title: customer-service business book|building a company culture around delivering happiness
text:
Building a company culture around delivering happiness does not start with scripts, slogans, or a wall covered in motivational posters. It starts with a decision: the people who work for you are not tools for producing transactions. They are the authors of your customer experience. If they feel trusted, respected, and supported, they will naturally create moments that customers remember. If they feel controlled, rushed, or unimportant, no clever policy manual will hide it.

You build this culture by making happiness a daily operating principle, not an annual theme. Every leader says customers matter, but your schedule, budget, and decisions reveal what actually matters. Do you spend time listening to frontline employees? Do you protect them from unrealistic productivity pressure? Do you celebrate employees who solve a problem creatively, even if the interaction took longer than average? Those choices teach the organization what you value.

Happiness in business is not about forcing cheerfulness. People can see through fake smiles, and customers can hear scripted enthusiasm. Real happiness comes from respect, progress, autonomy, and meaning. Your team wants to do good work. They want to know why the work matters. They want to be trusted to use judgment. Your job is to remove barriers, give them clear values, and then step back enough for them to act like human beings.

Begin by defining the kind of experience you want customers to feel. Not just fast service or accurate orders, although those matter. Do you want them to feel understood? Relieved? cared for? confident? Choose the feeling, then connect it to everyday decisions. A refund policy becomes easier when the goal is trust. A difficult conversation becomes kinder when the goal is respect. A complicated problem becomes worth solving when the goal is relief rather than merely closing a ticket.

But you cannot ask employees to deliver emotions they never experience. This is why culture begins inside the company. If leaders treat employees as disposable, employees will treat customers as interruptions. If leaders listen generously, admit mistakes, and invest in growth, employees are more likely to do the same. Culture is transferred through behavior. Your team watches what you do under pressure, especially during delays, complaints, and busy seasons.

Hire for character and curiosity, not just experience. Skills can be taught; warmth, humility, and good judgment are harder to train. During interviews, ask candidates how they have handled mistakes, awkward moments, and people with different communication styles. Look for people who take responsibility without becoming defensive and who naturally consider another person’s perspective. A team composed of caring people will outperform a team trained only in techniques.

Once hired, give employees context, not just commands. Tell them how their role affects customers, colleagues, and the larger mission. When people understand the purpose behind a rule, they make better decisions when the rule does not fit perfectly. Give them examples of excellent judgment, not just examples of forbidden behavior. If every training story is about punishment, employees will avoid risk. If stories celebrate learning and recovery, employees will take ownership.

Measurement also shapes culture. Track efficiency, but never at the expense of humanity. If average handle time is the main metric, calls will feel rushed. If surveys alone define success, employees may chase scores instead of solving root causes. Use metrics as signals, not gods. Measure repeat business, complaints resolved on first contact, internal health, customer effort, and stories of meaningful recovery. Numbers help you see patterns, but stories reveal the soul of the experience.

When mistakes happen, recover with grace. Customers do not expect perfection, but they remember how a company behaves after failing. Apologize clearly, fix what went wrong, and learn from the incident. Internally, conduct blameless reviews whenever possible. People who fear punishment hide problems. People who trust leadership expose problems early and help improve the system.

Finally, make gratitude ordinary. Thank employees for specific actions. Recognize patience, honesty, teamwork, and initiative. Tell customer stories in company meetings. When someone goes out of their way to help, let that become part of your shared history. Over time, these stories become the unwritten rules that guide behavior.

Delivering happiness is not softness. It is a disciplined way of running a business. It requires clarity, trust, accountability, and courage. But when your culture treats people as whole human beings, service stops feeling like a department and becomes the identity of the company.

title: habit-building book|starting with habits so small you can't fail
text:
Let me cut straight to the part no habit guru will tell you on their perfectly curated Instagram reel: three years ago, my “life-changing morning routine” lasted 47 hours.
I’d bought the fancy matcha, downloaded the 5 a.m. alarm tone that sounded like a monk humming over a rainforest, laid out my Lululemons, and even printed a habit tracker dotted with gold star stickers. By day three I hit snooze seven times, spilled the matcha all over my laptop, and ate three cold pop-tarts standing over the sink while scrolling TikTok at 7:45 a.m. I felt like such a failure I didn’t try to build a single new habit for six months.
Here’s the scam those gurus don’t sell you: big, flashy habit overhauls are built for people who already have their lives 80% together. For the rest of us—who forget to take our vitamins three days running, who still have a laundry pile that’s been evolving into its own ecosystem since last month—starting big is just setting yourself up to quit before you even hit the fun part.
I stumbled on the “can’t fail” habit method completely by accident, when I was so burnt out I could barely remember to brush my teeth some nights. I decided instead of vowing to “work out five days a week” or “read a book a week,” I would only commit to habits so tiny they were physically impossible to mess up.
No, I’m not exaggerating. My first workout habit was putting on my workout shoes. That’s it. I didn’t have to do a single squat, didn’t have to walk around the block, didn’t even have to stand up for more than two seconds. I just had to slip those sneakers on first thing when I got home from work. Then I could take them right off and binge Succession for four hours if I wanted.
You know what happened? Some days I did take them off immediately. Most days, though? Once they were on, I figured I might as well walk to the mailbox. Then walk around the block. Then maybe do two whole minutes of bodyweight squats before I face-planted on the couch. Within three months, I was going to three 30-minute yoga classes a week, without once having to “motivate” myself through a two-hour guilt trip about how I was lazy if I didn’t hit the gym.
The magic isn’t in the tiny action itself. It’s in the win you get every single time you show up, even for 10 seconds. Your brain stops seeing habits as a punishment you have to grind through, and starts seeing them as something easy, something you don’t have to be scared of messing up.
If you’re ready to stop the cycle of 3-day habit streaks followed by 3 weeks of guilt, start here:
1. Shrink your target habit until it sounds ridiculous. If you want to build a reading habit, commit to reading one single sentence a day. One. If you want to floss, commit to flossing one tooth. If you want to drink more water, commit to taking one sip. If you ever think “that’s too small,” make it smaller. There is no prize for starting bigger, only a prize for starting.
2. Anchor it to something you already do without thinking. I didn’t tell myself I’d “put my workout shoes on sometime every day.” I told myself I’d put them on the second I kicked my work shoes off after walking in the front door. You already do a hundred automatic things a day—make coffee, brush your teeth, open Instagram when you sit on the couch. Hook your new tiny habit to the end of one of those, and you won’t even have to remember to do it.
3. Celebrate the dumbest win, immediately. The second I got those sneakers on, I did a tiny little fist pump and thought “nailed it.” The second I flossed that one tooth, I grinned at myself in the mirror. Your brain is a dumb little golden retriever—it will do anything for a tiny, immediate reward. You don’t have to buy yourself a new purse for showing up; a silly little mental high five works just fine.
(Word count: 628)

title: personal finance book for young adults|automating your savings so you never have to think about it
text:
I’ll never forget the summer I tried to save money by “being more careful.” I was 22, living in an apartment where the kitchen window faced a brick wall, earning what felt like a decent salary until rent, groceries, gas, and late-night tacos did their thing. At the start of every month, I promised myself I’d save $300. At the end of every month, I checked my account and discovered, once again, that my money had developed legs, walked into a bar, ordered appetizers, and brought friends.

That’s when I learned the most boring, powerful, almost magical lesson in personal finance: willpower is garbage when it’s competing with convenience. The best way to save is to make saving automatic, invisible, and slightly annoying to undo.

Let me show you what changed.

I opened a separate savings account at a different bank—not the one linked to my debit card, not the one with the app I checked when I was bored, and definitely not the account that made transferring money back to checking take two taps. Then I set up an automatic transfer for $150 every payday. The money moved the same morning my paycheck landed. I didn’t see it. I didn’t approve it each time. I didn’t get a chance to negotiate with myself like, “Well, this weekend might be special.”

At first, nothing dramatic happened. I still bought coffee. I still went out. I may have eaten gas station nachos on two regrettable occasions. But after a few months, I looked at the savings account and saw $900 sitting there like a responsible little lawn gnome. I had not budgeted harder. I had not tracked every penny. I had simply moved the money before my brain could form an opinion.

That is the entire trick.

Automation works because it removes you from the decision. If saving is manual, you must choose it every week, every paycheck, every tempting sale. You are essentially running an emotional cage match between Future You, who wants security, and Present You, who wants the thing with the limited-time discount. Present You usually wins because Present You has enthusiasm, snacks, and a credit card.

So let’s make Future You win by default.

Start by choosing a percentage, not a dramatic round number that makes you feel heroic for one day. Five percent is enough to begin. If you earn $2,400 after taxes each month, five percent is $120, or $60 per twice-monthly paycheck. That’s one less random online order, not a life of poverty. As your income rises, increase it by one percent every six months. You can even set a calendar reminder for the day after your birthday. Nothing says personal growth like quietly raising your transfer rate while you eat leftover cake.

Next, split your accounts like a smart person hiding money from their own impulses. Keep checking for bills and daily spending. Have one savings account for emergencies, ideally at a separate bank. Have another account for specific goals: travel, a car, a security deposit, a laptop that doesn’t sound like a tiny jet engine. Name the accounts if your bank allows it. “Do Not Touch Unless Apartment Burns Down” is much harder to ignore than “Savings Account 0847.”

Then automate in the right order. Retirement first, especially if your job offers a match. If your employer matches contributions up to three percent of your salary, contribute at least three percent. Saying no to that match is like refusing free groceries because you enjoy struggling. After that, automate emergency savings, then debt payments above the minimums, then goals like travel or investing in a taxable brokerage account.

Here’s the part nobody tells you: you will feel slightly broke for about six weeks. That’s normal. Your checking balance will look smaller, and you’ll adjust your spending without needing a chart. You are not poorer. You are just no longer borrowing secretly from your future self.

Automation doesn’t make you rich by Friday. It makes you consistent for years. And consistency, when it happens quietly and automatically, is what turns ordinary paychecks into down payments, safety nets, and freedom.

Stop treating saving like a daily decision. Design your accounts so the decision is already made. Pay yourself first, move the money instantly, and then go live your life. The best financial system isn’t the one you constantly think about. It’s the one that works while you’re busy doing other things.

title: startup memoir|the early days of a search-engine company and its odd culture
text:
Excerpt from *Dogfood and Duct Tape: The Year We Built a Search Engine Out of Spite*
The office smelled like burnt microwave popcorn and regret the week we hit 12 million queries a day. That number sounds big now, back then it meant our server rack in the colo closet was overheating so bad the plastic label on Rack 3 melted, and our part-time sysadmin Javi was sleeping on a bean bag under his desk because his apartment had bed bugs and he couldn’t afford both a heat treatment and the replacement RAM we needed to stop returning cat litter results for people searching “local cancer treatment.”
We didn’t have an HR person. We didn’t have a health plan. We had a rule: if you brought a snack to share, you had to leave it on the rickety folding table by the door, and you weren’t allowed to yell if someone ate the last of it even if it was your mom’s homemade tamales. I broke that rule once, screamed at our intern Zara for eating the last pork tamale my abuela shipped from San Antonio, then apologized by giving her 0.02% equity that’s now worth enough to buy a small house in Oakland. She still texts me every Christmas to remind me I’m an asshole.
Our “culture deck” was a single Google Doc last edited in 2001 that said three things: 1) Dogfood every build, even if it crashes your laptop mid-porn, 2) No meetings before 1pm because half the team was up till 5am coding, 3) If you pitch a “synergy” with a pet supply brand you have to wear the dog cone we kept by the whiteboard for the rest of the day. The cone got used three times the month we turned down Yahoo’s first acquisition offer. Our head of sales, a guy named Rick who wore the same faded Pearl Jam hoodie every day for six months, put it on after he suggested we run banner ads for payday lenders, then left it on for three hours because he said it “cut down on screen glare.”
We didn’t track hours. We tracked how many times you fixed a bug that made the search bar turn neon pink when someone typed “boobs.” That was 17 times in March 2002. I fixed three of them. The worst one was the bug that auto-corrected “Hilary Clinton” to “Hillary Duff” for 48 hours before anyone noticed. We got 1,200 angry emails. We also got 400 fan emails from teens asking how to get the Duff filter as a browser extension. We didn’t respond to either. We were too busy arguing in the kitchen about whether our ranking algorithm was biased against vegan baking blogs. It was. Our lead engineer was a guy named Moe who hated vegan food with a passion usually reserved for people who kick dogs, and he’d tweaked the backlinks weight so any blog that mentioned “aquafaba” got pushed to page 7. We didn’t make him fix it for three weeks because he brought in homemade baklava every Friday, and none of us wanted to piss off the baklava guy.
The night we hit 15 million queries, the whole colo went down at 2:17am. Javi was passed out on the bean bag, so I drove over in my 1998 Civic with a broken heater, hauled three cases of Mountain Dew up three flights of stairs because the elevator was out, and sat on the concrete floor rewiring ethernet cables while Moe ranted about how Google’s PageRank was “for chumps who can’t code a better crawler.” A rat ran across my foot halfway through. I didn’t even flinch. I was too busy staring at the server monitor, watching the query ticker climb, thinking if this thing doesn’t die in the next six months I might be able to afford to fix my car heater.
Some VC guy came by the office that week, wore a tailored suit that cost more than our entire monthly server budget, and told us we “lacked professional cultural cohesion.” He offered us $2 million in seed money if we fired half the team, moved to a “real office” in SOMA with glass walls, and hired a “chief culture officer” who’d previously worked at Gap. We told him to get fucked. Zara put the dog cone on his head before he left. He didn’t think it was funny. We did.
(Word count: 598)

title: happiness and meditation guide|a ten-minute daily breathing practice for beginners
text:
Chapter 3: The 10-Minute Breath That Stuck (Even When My Life Felt Unstuck)
Three winters ago, I sat on the floor of my tiny Brooklyn apartment at 6:47 a.m., surrounded by half-packed moving boxes, a half-empty cold brew, and a to-do list so long it curled off the edge of my counter. I’d just quit a stable marketing job to write this guide, my subletter was arriving in 12 days, and I’d spent the previous night spiraling so hard about “ruining my life” that I’d woken up with a jaw ache so bad I could barely sip water. I’d read every meditation book on my shelf, tried every 30-minute “enlightenment in a week” challenge, and quit all of them by day three. That morning, I set one dumb, tiny rule: I would sit for 10 minutes, and I didn’t have to “empty my mind.” I only had to notice when I was thinking about moving boxes, and go back to breathing.
That 10 minutes didn’t fix my moving stress. It didn’t magically make my book deal appear, or unclench my jaw overnight. But when I opened my eyes, I realized I’d spent 10 whole minutes not catastrophizing. For 600 seconds, the boxes didn’t feel like a verdict on my bad choices. They just felt like cardboard. That’s the magic of this beginner practice: it doesn’t erase hard days. It gives you a small, steady anchor to hold onto when everything feels wobbly.
You don’t need a meditation cushion, a silent room, or any experience to do this. All you need is a timer (your phone works, just turn on do not disturb) and a place you can sit upright for 10 minutes—your couch, a desk chair, even the closed bathroom door if you live with noisy roommates or kids. Sit with your feet flat on the floor, hands resting gently on your thighs, and your spine straight but not stiff; you don’t need to sit cross-legged unless that feels good. Set your timer for 10 minutes, and close your eyes if that’s comfortable, or soften your gaze to a spot on the floor a few feet in front of you if closing your eyes makes you anxious.
Start by taking three slow, intentional breaths: inhale through your nose for four counts, feel your belly expand like a balloon, then exhale through pursed lips for six counts, like you’re blowing out a candle very slowly. After those three breaths, let your breath return to its natural rhythm—you don’t have to force deep breaths for the whole practice. Pick one spot to anchor your attention: the tingle of air moving in and out of your nostrils, the rise and fall of your chest under your shirt, or the soft push of your belly against your hands on every inhale.
Here’s the part no fancy app tells you: your mind will wander. A lot. You’ll think about the email you forgot to send, the laundry in the dryer, the awkward thing you said at a party three years ago. That is not failure. That is the whole point of the practice. Every single time you notice you’ve gotten pulled into a thought, that’s a tiny win: you’ve just woken up out of autopilot. Gently, without judging yourself or calling yourself “bad at meditation,” label the thought quietly in your head—“planning,” “worrying,” “replaying”—and guide your attention right back to the feeling of your breath. You might do this 80 times in 10 minutes. That doesn’t mean you’re doing it wrong. That means you’re practicing.
I did this exact practice every morning while I packed those boxes, and I still do it most days now, even when life feels calm. Some days my mind is so busy I spend almost the whole 10 minutes herding my attention back to my breath. Those aren’t “bad” meditation days. Those are the days that build the muscle: the muscle that lets you pause before you snap at your partner when you’re stressed, that lets you notice when you’re spiraling about the future before you lose an hour of sleep, that lets you feel small moments of happiness—a warm mug, sunlight through the window—without rushing past them to the next thing.
You don’t have to be good at this. You just have to show up for 10 minutes, one breath at a time.
(Word count: 698)

title: personal memoir with life lessons|a year of travel after a painful divorce
text:
I stood in the rain outside my old Portland bungalow at 6 a.m. on January 3, holding a garbage bag full of my ex’s leftover hoodies and a one-way ticket to Lisbon, and realized I couldn’t remember the last time I’d booked a trip that didn’t involve coordinating his work conference schedule or picking a rental with a garage for his stupid vintage motorcycle. The divorce papers had been signed 12 days prior. My best friend Lila had texted me the night before: “If you stay in that house another month you’re going to start talking to the sourdough starter like it’s your kid. Go.”
I thought travel would fix me, obviously. I thought I’d eat a pastel de nata, stare at a sunset, and magically stop reflexively reaching for a second wine glass at dinner. Spoiler: I cried through my first three pastel de natas. I got lost in the Alfama district at 2 a.m. wearing flip flops, tripped over a stray cat, and ended up sharing a bottle of vinho verde with a 72-year-old retired sardine fisherman who told me his wife of 48 years had left him for a competitive ballroom dancer when he was 50. “You think the hole in your chest is a permanent installation,” he said, passing me a salted sardine straight from a tin, “but it’s just a window. Stop trying to board it up.”
I spent the next 11 months bouncing: a month in a creaky Greek island cottage where the shower sprayed directly onto the toilet, two months teaching English to tiny, chaotic kids in northern Thailand, three weeks road-tripping around Iceland in a van that smelled like rotten skyr and regret, a long, lazy stretch in Mexico City where I ate so many al pastor tacos I genuinely thought I might give myself permanent heartburn. I made every dumb rookie travel mistake you can imagine, and a few extremely specific dumb divorce travel mistakes, too. Along the way I picked up three rules I still tape to my fridge now that I’m back home, no sourdough starter in sight.
1. Stop packing the person you used to be. I brought my ex’s favorite hiking boots on the first three legs of the trip, even though they gave me blisters, even though I hate hiking. I kept them “just in case” — just in case he showed up? Just in case I suddenly decided I was the kind of person who wakes up at 5 a.m. to summit a mountain for fun? I finally left them on a park bench in Chiang Mai, and a woman wearing a Muay Thai hoodie grabbed them before I’d even walked 10 feet. She waved, slipped them on, and took off running. It felt like a sign. You don’t have to carry the habits, the preferences, the oversized boots that don’t fit just because you once loved the person they belonged to.
2. The best meals are never the ones you plan. I booked a $180 tasting menu in Barcelona that I’d seen 17 influencers rave about, and it was fine — lots of foams, lots of tiny portions, lots of people taking photos of olive oil like it was a newborn. The best meal I had all year was a random plate of mango sticky rice I bought from a street cart outside a 7-Eleven in Bangkok at 1 a.m., after I’d missed the last train back to my Airbnb, sitting on a curb next to a group of college students who taught me how to do terrible TikTok dances while we ate. When you’re re-learning how to be alone, you don’t have to curate every second of joy to be Instagram-perfect. The messy, unplanned bits stick to your ribs longer.
3. It’s okay to leave before the party ends. I spent three weeks in a tiny surf town in Portugal, and I almost stayed. I made friends, I found a little apartment with a balcony, I was even getting sort of okay at standing up on a surfboard without face-planting. But one morning I woke up and realized I wasn’t staying because I loved the town — I was staying because I was scared to go home, scared to face the quiet of a house that was only mine, scared to prove I could build a life that didn’t feel like a rebound. So I booked a ticket home, and I cried on the flight, and it was the right call. Running away works great until you realize you’re the one carrying all your baggage with you, no matter how pretty the beach is.
I still have the crumpled napkin the sardine fisherman wrote his phone number on, tucked in the back of my passport. I texted him a photo of my first backyard garden last month — tomatoes, basil, no sourdough starter, no vintage motorcycle taking up half the garage. He wrote back: “Told you the window has a nice view.”
(Word count: 608)

title: Christian purpose-driven living book|serving others as the path to a meaningful life
text:
The other morning I spilled coffee all over my sermon notes, stepped on a kid’s Lego in bare feet, and walked into church only to find Mabel—a silver-haired woman who brings lemon bars to every potluck—crying by the donut table. Her ride to physical therapy had bailed, and she couldn’t bend her knees well enough to drive. Let’s be honest: my first thought wasn’t “What a divine appointment.” It was “I already have forty-seven things on my list today.” But I drove her anyway, and sitting in that PT parking lot for an hour, listening to her tell stories about her late husband’s terrible bowling scores, something shifted in me. That hour didn’t check a box on my agenda. It gave my day meaning I never could have scheduled.

If you’ve ever wondered why your life feels smaller than the one you imagined, I want to suggest something radical: you weren’t put on this earth just to build a comfortable life for yourself. You were created to serve. Ephesians 2:10 says we are God’s handiwork, created in Christ Jesus to do good works, which God prepared in advance for us to do. Notice it doesn’t say “good works you have to scramble to invent.” God has already lined them up. The question is whether we’ll slow down enough to notice them.

Here’s what I’ve learned after two decades of pastoring, parenting, and stepping on countless Legos: significance never shows up in the spotlight moments we chase. It hides in the mundane acts of serving nobody applauds. Let me give you some pictures. It’s your coworker who’s drowning after a new baby, and you leave a meal on their porch without posting about it. It’s the teenager in your small group who texts at 11 p.m., and you actually answer instead of waiting for morning. It’s forgiving the person who hurt you, not because they deserve it, but because Christ forgave you first. It’s volunteering in the church nursery when you’d rather sit in the service, or shoveling your elderly neighbor’s sidewalk, or listening—really listening—to the relative everyone else ignores at Thanksgiving.

A few years back I met a guy named David in our congregation who ran a successful landscaping business. He was miserable. Bigger trucks, bigger contracts, bigger emptiness. I challenged him to use his crew one Saturday a quarter to serve single moms and elderly homeowners for free. He resisted at first—said he couldn’t afford it. But he tried it. The first day, an eighty-two-year-old woman named Ruth came outside crying because nobody had tended her garden since her husband died. David told me later, “I’ve made a lot of money in this business, but I’ve never felt like I mattered the way I did in that moment.” Within a year, half his clients started asking how they could help. Serving didn’t shrink his business. It expanded his soul.

Want to know the secret nobody tells you? Serving isn’t something God needs from you. He’s God. He doesn’t need your casseroles or your skillset. Serving is something God wants for you. It’s the pathway he designed to make you like Jesus, to yank your eyes off yourself, and to plug you into a story way bigger than your own resume. Jesus himself said he didn’t come to be served, but to serve—and then he knelt down with a towel and washed his friends’ dirty, dusty feet. If the King of Kings did that, what makes us think we’re too busy or too important to do the same?

Start small this week. Don’t sign up for ten things and burn out by February. Pick one person. One act. One inconvenient, interrupting, grace-filled moment where you put someone else ahead of yourself. Make the call. Write the note. Forgive the debt. Bake the cookies and skip the social media post.

A purpose-driven life isn’t built on what you accumulate. It’s built on what you give away. And here’s the beautiful paradox Jesus keeps teaching me: when you spend your life serving others, you don’t lose yourself. You finally find the self God created you to be. Mabel still reminds me of that parking-lot day every time she hands me a lemon bar. I’m the one who drove her, but honestly? She’s the one who gave me the gift. That’s how grace works—and it’s the most meaningful way to live I’ve ever found.

title: negotiation book|finding out what the other side really wants
text:
Let’s cut the crap first. Half the “active listening” hacks you read in negotiation books are garbage. I once sat through a $4.2M commercial real estate deal in 2019 where a guy on the other side of the table spent 45 minutes nodding, paraphrasing, leaning in like he was about to ask me to prom, and he still walked away convinced I cared most about a 3% break on closing costs.
I didn’t give a shit about closing costs.
What I actually cared about? The 12 covered parking spots in the building’s garage, because my construction crew’s trucks kept getting ticketed $185 a pop on the street outside our current shop, and we’d racked up $11,000 in fines in six months. That’s $22k a year, easy, plus the time my foreman spent fighting tickets instead of running jobs. Those spots were worth more to me than a $75k price chop on the building. And he never asked. He was too busy performing “good listening” to notice I kept glancing at the garage entrance through the conference room window, kept making offhand jokes about “street cleaning being a racket,” kept asking about tenant access hours long after we’d moved on from that line item.
People don’t lead with what they actually want. Ever. If they tell you their top priority straight out the gate? It’s either a misdirect, or they’re so new to negotiating they haven’t learned to hide their cards yet. Most of the time, the thing they care most about is the thing they’re embarrassed to admit matters. It’s too small, too personal, too unprofessional to put on the official offer sheet.
I had a client a few years back negotiating a job offer with a SaaS startup. The hiring manager kept haggling over base salary, kept pushing back on extra PTO, kept acting like a $5k bump was going to break the whole company’s budget. My client was ready to walk, until I told him to stop talking comp for 10 minutes and ask about the team’s remote policy. Turns out? The hiring manager’s kid had severe autism, went to a special needs school 45 minutes from the office, and he needed to be able to drop him off every morning without getting written up for being 20 minutes late. The company had a strict “in office 9am sharp” rule for leadership, and he didn’t want to tell a candidate he couldn’t enforce a policy he was breaking himself. We traded a “flexible arrival window for all senior staff” clause written into the offer for a $7k lower base than my client initially wanted. Both sides left thinking they stole the deal.
You don’t find this stuff by running through a checklist of questions. You find it by shutting up for five minutes after they finish talking about the “official” terms. You find it by noticing what they circle back to when they think they’re making small talk. Last quarter I watched a supplier rep spend 20 minutes complaining about his kid’s travel soccer league travel costs right before he tried to jack up our material prices by 8%. We didn’t argue about the per-unit cost. We offered to comp his team’s hotel rooms for the three regional tournaments they had coming up that summer—cost us $1,200 total—and he locked in our rate for two years, no increase.
Stop looking for the big, obvious leverage. The real want is almost never the number written at the top of the offer. It’s the throwaway line, the offhand complaint, the thing they mention when they think the negotiation is paused. I once had a landlord hold out on a lease renewal for three weeks over a $150/month rent hike, turns out he just wanted permission to put his vintage 1972 Camaro in the unused back corner of the warehouse we were renting. We said yes, he cut the rent by $200 a month. He didn’t want to admit a stupid car mattered more than the rent number. None of us do.
Don’t wait for them to state it plainly. They won’t.

title: self-improvement book|dealing with procrastination and perfectionism
text:
Chapter 3: The Unfinished Manuscript That Taught Me "Good Enough" Moves Mountains
The cursor blinked at me like a judgmental eye. It was 2:17 a.m. on a Tuesday in 2019, and I’d spent three hours rewriting the first paragraph of the self-help zine I’d promised myself I’d launch by spring. First, the opening line felt too casual. Then too clinical. Then I decided the entire 500-word draft I’d written the week before was garbage—who was I to give anyone advice about showing up when I couldn’t even finish a 12-page pamphlet? I closed the laptop, poured a third glass of wine, and told myself I’d try again when I “had a clearer vision.” That “clearer vision” didn’t show up for 18 months.

I’ve told that story before, and people always assume the problem was laziness. It wasn’t. It was perfectionism wearing procrastination’s hoodie, hiding out in my brain so I’d never have to face the risk of making something mediocre. I thought waiting for the “perfect” first paragraph made me rigorous. It actually made me stagnant. The zine wasn’t just a zine, either: it was proof I could follow through on a promise to myself, and every time I hit delete instead of publish, I chipped away at my own self-trust.

The turning point didn’t come from a fancy productivity hack. It came from my friend Lila, a ceramicist who dragged me to her studio one rainy Saturday after I’d complained about my “writer’s block.” She set a lump of clay in front of me and said, “Make a mug. It has to be ugly. No exceptions.” I protested. I wanted to make a nice mug, one that didn’t wobble, one with an even handle. “That’s the rule,” she said. “If it comes out perfect, you have to smash it and start over.” My first mug tilted so far to the left it couldn’t hold liquid. The handle was lopsided, I carved a lopsided star into the side, and when it came out of the kiln, the glaze ran in streaks down the bottom. I still keep it on my desk. It leaks a little if you fill it too high, and it’s the best thing I made that entire year.

That day I learned perfectionism isn’t about high standards—it’s about fear disguised as standards. Procrastination is the coping mechanism we use to avoid ever having to test the false story we tell ourselves: *if I don’t finish, no one can call my work bad, and I get to keep believing I could be brilliant if I really tried*. The problem is that story costs you everything you actually could make, share, and become.

Over the years, I’ve landed on three small, actionable practices that pulled me out of that 18-month slump, and they work far better than any “hustle harder” mantra I ever tried:
First, run the “worst first draft” experiment. Pick the task you’ve been avoiding for weeks—the work presentation, the apartment cleanup, the text you need to send to a friend you’ve fought with. Give yourself 20 minutes to do the absolute sloppiest, most unpolished version possible. Typos allowed. Half-baked ideas allowed. Crooked wall art allowed. Perfectionism can’t survive when you intentionally give it nothing to fix right away. I wrote the entire first issue of that zine in three of those 20-minute sessions, typos and messy half-ideas included. It wasn’t brilliant. It was done, and people actually wrote back to say it helped them.
Second, define “good enough” before you start. Perfectionism moves the goalposts forever if you don’t pin them down. If you’re drafting an email, decide ahead of time: “This needs to state the request and the deadline, and I’m sending it after one read-through.” If you’re applying for a job, decide: “I’ll update my resume with these three projects, edit it twice, and submit no later than 6 p.m. Friday.” You don’t have to lower your standards—you just have to stop letting them expand endlessly the closer you get to finishing.
Third, schedule a “ship it” deadline that’s separate from your “tweak it” deadline. I now give myself two dates for every project: one day I stop making big changes, and two days later, I send it out into the world no matter what. The gap lets my perfectionist brain feel like it got a little extra time to fidget, but it removes the option to delay forever over tiny, meaningless adjustments.

That lopsided mug on my desk still reminds me: finished things get to hold coffee. Perfect things that never leave your head don’t get to hold anything at all. You don’t have to be great to start. You just have to start to get good. (Word count: 698)

title: leadership memoir by a former CEO|the hiring mistake that nearly sank the company
text:
You don’t forget the day you look at a quarterly report and realize the hire you fought so hard to make, the one you told your board was going to catapult the company to the next level, has burned through 40% of your operating cash in nine months with nothing to show for it. I was 12 years into running the supply chain software startup I’d built out of my garage, 18 months away from what we all thought was a surefire IPO, when I made that call.
We were stretched thin, our engineering team burning out building custom features for enterprise clients, and everyone on the leadership team kept saying we needed a seasoned president to scale operations, someone who’d taken a SaaS company public before. That’s how we found Eli. He had the perfect resume: 10 years at Oracle, a successful IPO exit at his last startup, wore the right tailored blazers to interviews, said all the right buzzwords about operational rigor and scalable growth. I ignored the quiet red flags because I wanted the easy win so bad. When our head of people pulled me aside after his final interview and said three of his former direct reports had mentioned he sidelined anyone who disagreed with him, I waved it off as “strong leadership for a high-growth phase.” When our CFO noted his compensation ask was 30% above our band, with a guaranteed bonus tied to no concrete metrics, I pushed the board to approve it, telling them you pay a premium for A players.
For the first three months, he felt like a miracle. He walked in with 90-day plans, restructured teams without endless debate, presented sleek slide decks to investors that had them asking if we could move the IPO timeline up. What I didn’t see, because I was so busy flying around to investor meetings and letting him “own operations,” was that he’d gutted the core customer success team to fund a flashy new AI product line no one had asked for. He’d fired two of our longest-tenured engineering leads when they pushed back that the new product would take resources away from the core platform our largest clients relied on, replacing them with his former colleagues who had no experience with our legacy code base. By the time our biggest retail client called to say they were pulling their $12 million annual contract because three straight product updates had broken their inventory tracking, the damage was already done.
I spent the next six months working 18-hour days, sitting in on support calls, apologizing to clients, rehiring the people we’d pushed out, and scraping together a bridge funding round that diluted every early employee’s stock by 22% to keep the lights on. We scrapped the IPO for three years. What haunts me most isn’t the money we lost or the delayed timeline; it’s the way I hid behind the myth of the “rockstar hire” because I was tired. I thought bringing in a big name would let me hand off the hard, messy work of listening to my team, of weighing tradeoffs, of showing up for the parts of the job that don’t make for good press hits. I stopped asking the quiet, critical questions because someone confident told me he had all the answers.
If you’re sitting across from a candidate who feels too good to be true, who checks every box on your job description but makes the people who built your company with you lean back in their chairs when he speaks, pause. You don’t hire a resume. You hire the person who shows up when the slide decks are put away, who listens more than he talks, who doesn’t treat the people who built the place before he arrived as obstacles to clear out. I learned that the hard way, and it nearly cost every single one of us everything we’d built.

title: personal finance book|why you should stop feeling guilty about lattes and focus on big wins
text:
Let me tell you about my friend Maya, who spent three years torturing herself over a four-dollar oat milk latte.

Every morning she’d walk into that café, and every morning she’d walk out feeling like she’d just betrayed her future self. She read the blogs, same as you probably have. The Latte Factor. The compound interest calculators showing that five dollars a day becomes a million dollars over forty years. She downloaded the budgeting app that judged her in cold, sans-serif type. She even bought a cheap espresso machine, which she used for eleven days before it became a very expensive dust collector on her counter.

And you know what happened during those three years? Maya stayed at a job that underpaid her by eighteen thousand dollars a year because she was afraid to negotiate. She kept twelve thousand dollars sitting in a checking account earning zero point zero one percent interest because investing felt “scary and complicated.” She renewed her lease twice without comparing prices, costing herself roughly two hundred and fifty dollars a month. And she beat herself up daily over coffee.

Do the math on the latte. Four dollars times twenty workdays a month. That’s eight hundred dollars a year. Serious money? Sure. Life-changing? Not even close.

Now do the math on the stuff she ignored. Eighteen thousand in unclaimed salary, compounded annually at seven percent over a decade, is well over two hundred thousand dollars. The idle cash, moved into a low-cost index fund even three years earlier, could have earned thousands. The rent overpayment alone ran her three thousand dollars a year, every single year, without a single blog post shaming her for it.

Here’s the dirty secret of personal finance nobody wants to tell you: scrimping on small pleasures is easy advice to sell because it feels productive. Tracking every coffee gives you a little dopamine hit of discipline. It makes virtue visible. But it mostly distracts you from the five or six decisions that actually determine whether you build wealth.

I call these the Big Wins, and there are really only five of them.

First, your earning power. Negotiating your salary, switching jobs at the right moment, learning a skill that doubles your market value — these move the needle in ways no coupon ever will. Maya finally asked for a raise after practicing the conversation with a friend, and she got twelve thousand dollars in a fifteen-minute meeting. Fifteen minutes. She could have skipped three thousand lattes and still not matched those fifteen minutes.

Second, your housing costs. The rule I like is simple: keep rent or mortgage payments under thirty percent of your take-home pay. One honest downsizing or roommate decision can free up hundreds of dollars every month, automatically, forever.

Third, your debts. A credit card at twenty-two percent interest isn’t a nuisance; it’s a financial emergency. Paying that off is the exact equivalent of finding a guaranteed twenty-two percent investment, which does not exist anywhere else in the known universe.

Fourth, your investments. You don’t need to be a genius. You need to automate a contribution to a low-cost index fund, increase it every time you get a raise, and leave it alone. That’s it. That’s the whole game.

Fifth, your major purchases. Cars, vacations, weddings, kitchens. These are the moments people quietly wreck their finances, usually while still feeling proud of skipping avocado toast.

Now please hear what I’m not saying. I’m not saying the latte is free, or that budgets don’t matter, or that small daily habits have no power. They do. But guilt is a terrible financial strategy, and deprivation without purpose almost always collapses in a spectacular late-night Amazon binge.

The question isn’t whether the latte is “worth it.” The question is whether the latte is making your life better enough to deserve your attention, because your attention is finite. If that warm cup in your hands at seven forty-five in the morning is one of the small joys that make your life feel livable, then enjoy it without apology. Buy it slowly. Savor it. Then redirect the guilt-energy toward one conversation, one transfer, one decision that could change your net worth by thousands.

Maya still gets the latte. She also has a raise, a brokerage account, and a cheaper apartment with a balcony. Last month she told me the coffee tastes better now.

That’s not magic. That’s just what happens when you stop negotiating against your happiness and start negotiating for your future.

title: personal finance book for young adults|automating your savings so you never have to think about it
text:
Let’s cut the crap first. You’re not going to “remember” to save money. I don’t care how many TikTok finance bros you watch while eating cold pizza at 1 a.m., how many fancy budget spreadsheets you built that one bored Sunday, how many times you’ve told yourself “next paycheck I’ll be responsible.” You won’t. I didn’t. None of my friends did. The 22-year-old version of me once blew $317 on a limited-edition Studio Ghibli skateboard I rode twice, then stared at my $12.47 checking account balance three days before rent was due and cried into a gas station burrito. Willpower is a scam invented by people who sell $40 productivity planners. If your savings relies on you making a good choice every single payday? You’re gonna lose.

The fix is so boring it feels like it can’t possibly work: automate every single dollar of your savings before you ever see it hit your checking account. No exceptions. No “I’ll move what’s left at the end of the month.” There will never be anything left. I promise you.

Let’s talk specific numbers, not that vague “pay yourself first” garbage your uncle rants about at Thanksgiving. If you’re making $42k a year right out of college, your take-home in a mid-cost state like Ohio or North Carolina is roughly $2,650 a month after taxes, health insurance, and your 401(k) contribution (and yes, if your job matches 401(k) contributions, you’re contributing at least enough to get the full match first—free money isn’t optional, don’t be an idiot). On payday, before you pay a single bill, before you scroll Amazon, before you send your friend $25 for that concert ticket you agreed to three weeks ago, 10% of that take-home goes straight to a high-yield savings account that is not linked to your main checking. That’s $265 a month. If your bank lets you split direct deposits? Do that. If not, set up an auto-transfer for 9 a.m. the day your paycheck hits. Not 9 p.m. Not the next day. 9 a.m., before your brain even boots up enough to check your balance.

Wait, hold on—10%? I know what you’re thinking. “I can’t afford to lose $265 a month, I’m already scraping by.” Bullshit. I want you to pull up your last three months of bank statements right now. Add up all the random shit you bought that you don’t remember: the $18 matcha lattes on mornings you were running late, the $3.99 TikTok shop impulse buys of silicone kitchen gadgets you never used, the $12 Uber rides you took because you didn’t want to wait 10 minutes for the bus, the two extra streaming services you signed up for to watch one show then forgot to cancel. I guarantee you it’s more than $265. When I did this at 23, I found I’d spent $412 in three months on vintage band tees from Depop. I still only wear three of them.

Here’s the trick no one tells you: you adjust. If that money never shows up in your spending account, you don’t miss it. You don’t have to white-knuckle your way through every weekend saying no to tacos. You’ll naturally skip the random third bar trip, you’ll make coffee at home one extra day a week, you won’t even notice the gap. I had a client a few years back who swore she couldn’t save more than $50 a month. We set up a $300 auto-transfer to her HYSA on payday, told her not to check the balance for six months. She texted me seven months later panicking because she thought she’d overdrafted, only to realize she had $1,872 sitting there, plus $42 in interest. She’d forgotten the transfer even existed.

Don’t overcomplicate the accounts, either. You don’t need a fancy robo-advisor for your emergency fund right now. You don’t need to split your savings into 12 different buckets for “new laptop” and “trip to Japan” and “future dog.” Just get a HYSA with no fees, no minimum balance, that takes two full business days to transfer money back to checking. That friction is on purpose. If you can move your savings to your spending account in 30 seconds, you will do it when you see a cute jacket go on sale, or when your friend begs you to split a weekend Airbnb. Two days? That’s enough time to remember you already have a perfectly good jacket, and that you can’t afford to blow your buffer on a trip that’ll leave you eating ramen for two weeks.

And for the love of god, don’t turn off the auto-transfer when you get a raise. When you get that 3% cost of living bump, or a $5k promotion, bump your auto-savings up by 50% of the raise first. If your take-home goes up $180 a month, add $90 to your savings transfer before you adjust anything else. You were living on the old amount just fine. You don’t suddenly need a $15 meal kit subscription and a premium gym membership you’ll use twice. I watched a coworker do this starting at 24: every raise, he upped his auto-transfer by half the new take-home, never touched the rest. By 30, he had $72k saved for a down payment, no side hustles, no inheriting money, just… not having to think about it. He still goes to every Bills game, still buys the good beer, still takes a week-long beach trip every year. He just never gave his dumb impulsive brain the chance to spend the money before it got stashed away.

Stop treating savings like a reward for being good with money. It’s not. It’s a bill you owe your future self, and you set it to auto-pay the same way you auto-pay your phone bill so you don’t get hit with a late fee. You don’t sit around every month debating if you feel like paying your electric bill, right? You don’t go “eh, I’ll pay what’s left after I go out this weekend.” Treat your savings the exact same way.

Last thing: if you mess up? If one month you have to pull $200 out because your car battery died and your tire popped on the same day (shoutout to 2022, when that happened to me on the way to a first date)? Don’t beat yourself up, don’t delete the auto-transfer, don’t decide the whole thing is broken and give up. Just let it keep running. Next month, the $265 will hit the account like it always does. You won’t even have to remember.

title: happiness and meditation guide|a ten-minute daily breathing practice for beginners
text:
Chapter 4: The 10-Minute Breath That Rewrote My Morning Routine
Three years ago, I woke up most days already behind. I’d slam my phone off the alarm, scroll 20 minutes of work emails before my feet hit the floor, and rush through burnt coffee while mentally drafting my to-do list. By 9 a.m., my shoulders were hunched up to my ears, and I’d snap at my cat for knocking over a pen—hardly the calm, joyful person I wanted to be. I thought meditation was for people who owned linen loungewear and could sit cross-legged for an hour without checking their watch. Then a rainy Tuesday, stuck waiting for a delayed bus with 10 minutes to kill and no cell service, I tried the simplest practice I’d ever read about: focused breathing. I didn’t feel enlightened. I did notice I didn’t mutter about the rain the whole ride, and that small shift stuck.

This 10-minute daily practice is built for total beginners—no special cushion, no quiet room required, no “clearing your mind” rule (that’s a myth, anyway). You can do it sitting on the edge of your bed, on a bus seat, or even in your parked car before work. All you need is a timer and the willingness to show up exactly as you are.

Start by setting your phone timer for 10 minutes, and place it out of arm’s reach so you won’t tap it mid-practice. Sit in a chair with your feet flat on the floor, spine straight but not stiff—you don’t need to twist into a lotus pose. Rest your hands gently on your thighs, palms down if you want to feel grounded, palms up if you’re open to whatever comes up. You can close your eyes, or soften your gaze to a spot on the floor three feet in front of you; there’s no “right” way here.

For the first two minutes, simply notice your natural breath. Don’t change it, don’t force deep belly breaths—just observe. Feel the cool air brushing the inside of your nostrils as you inhale, the warm air as you exhale. Notice your chest rise, your ribs expand, maybe the soft lift of your shoulders. That bus ride, I realized I’d been holding half-breaths all morning: shallow, tight sips of air that matched my rushed mood. You might notice the same, or you might notice your mind immediately jumps to your grocery list, an argument you had last week, or a show you want to watch. That is not failure. That is exactly how the practice works.

For the next six minutes, use a soft counting anchor to steady your attention. Inhale slowly through your nose to a count of four, hold that breath gently for a count of two, then exhale through pursed lips for a count of six. The long exhale is the secret here: it activates your body’s rest-and-digest response, melting that low-grade tension you might not even know you’re carrying. When (not if) your mind wanders, don’t judge yourself. In my first week, I’d plan three paragraphs of a work email, rehash a bad first date from 2019, and wonder if I’d left the stove on, all in one 10-minute sitting. Each time you notice you’ve drifted, silently say “thinking” to yourself without frustration, and guide your attention back to the count. That little act of returning is the meditation, not staying focused the whole time.

Spend the final two minutes dropping the count entirely. Let your breath return to its natural rhythm, and take a moment to notice how your body feels. Maybe your shoulders are lower, your jaw is unclenched, or that knot in your stomach has softened a little. You don’t have to feel “blissful”—some days you’ll still feel jittery, some days you’ll be bored, and that’s okay. When the timer goes off, don’t jump up right away. Wiggle your fingers and toes, take one more deep breath, and slowly bring your attention back to the room.

I still practice this 10 minutes every morning, usually while my coffee brews. Some days my mind races the whole time; some days I feel so calm I barely notice the timer. What changed isn’t that I never feel stressed anymore. It’s that I no longer start my days swept away by the rush before I’ve even said hello to myself. That 10 minutes isn’t an escape from your life—it’s a small, steady anchor that lets you meet every part of it with a little more kindness. (Word count: 698)

title: leadership memoir by a former CEO|the hiring mistake that nearly sank the company
text:
You think you know when you’ve found the one. You’re three years into scaling the SaaS company you built out of your garage, sleep-deprived, spread thinner than cheap butter on toast, juggling investor check-ins, product bugs, and a customer support team that’s still using a shared Gmail inbox. You’re desperate for a seasoned COO, someone who’s been through a hypergrowth phase at a bigger name, who can take the operational mess off your plate so you can focus on the product vision that got you here. That’s when the resume lands: 12 years at a FAANG adjacent firm, led a 200-person team through a 4x revenue jump, talked a good game about “lean process” and “people-first culture” in the first interview, nailed every case study you threw at them, even made you laugh when they joked about how all startup CEOs are terrible at reading P&Ls until it’s too late. Your board loves them. Your lead investor pulls you aside after the final interview and says this hire will take you to IPO in three years, no question. You ignore the tiny, niggling voice in the back of your head that noticed they never asked a single question about your core customer base, never asked to talk to the frontline support reps who’d been with you since day one, never mentioned the specific pain points you’d ranted about in your first conversation. You write that off as jitters, as them being too senior to get bogged down in small stuff. You offer them the job, with a compensation package that’s 30% higher than you initially budgeted, because you’re convinced they’re worth every penny.

For the first three months, it feels like magic. They roll out structured meeting agendas, fix your messy sales commission structure, hire a handful of solid operations leads that take a load off your overstretched managers. You start taking weekends off for the first time in three years. You tell your spouse you finally didn’t make a mistake, that you can stop carrying the whole company on your back. Then the cracks start to show. First, you hear from a long-tenured customer success rep that the new COO shut down their weekly check-in with small business customers, calling it “a waste of senior leadership time” that should be delegated to entry-level staff. Then your head of product pulls you aside, white-knuckled, to say the COO unilaterally cut the budget for your core accessibility feature, the one you’d promised your disabled user base you’d ship that quarter, because it “didn’t move the needle on near-term ARR.” You brush those concerns off as growing pains, as the old guard resisting necessary change. You tell yourself every scaling company goes through this, that you can’t be the CEO who meddles in every operational decision.

The wake-up call hits six months in, when you get a frantic 2 a.m. call from your head of finance. The COO had quietly restructured the sales team’s quota structure to prioritize only the highest-value enterprise contracts, fired 40% of the small business sales team without running it by you or HR, and signed off on a $2.4 million software contract for an enterprise resource planning tool your team didn’t need, all to hit a short-term quarterly bonus target tied to ARR growth. Worse, when you dig into the numbers, you realize they’d been fudging customer churn reports for two months, hiding that 22% of your core small business customers— the people who’d signed up when you were still building the product out of your garage, who’d given you feedback that shaped every feature—had left in the last quarter, angry that support response times had tripled and the features they relied on were being deprioritized for enterprise add-ons they’d never use. Your runway, which you’d thought was 18 months, was down to seven. Your most loyal engineers were updating their LinkedIn profiles, fed up with being told to build features that didn’t align with the mission you’d all signed up for. One of your earliest customers, a small bookstore owner who’d been your first paid subscriber, sent you an email saying they felt like you’d abandoned the people who got you here, and it made you sick to your stomach.

You don’t sleep for 72 hours after that. You sit in your office, staring at the handwritten note that first customer sent you when you launched, taped to your monitor, and realize you made the mistake every founder is warned about: you hired the resume, not the person. You were so desperate for someone to take the weight off, so eager to look like a “real” company to your investors, that you didn’t vet for value alignment. You didn’t ask the hard questions about how they’d treated entry-level staff at their last job, what they considered a non-negotiable tradeoff for growth, how they defined success beyond spreadsheets and quarterly targets. You assumed a big name on a resume meant they cared about the same things you did, and that blindness almost cost you everything you built.

You fire the COO two days later, eat the cost of that useless software contract, and spend the next three months personally calling every churned customer to apologize. You roll back the commission structure, rehire the small business sales team, and move the accessibility feature back to the top of the product roadmap. It takes 18 months to get back to the churn rate you had before that hire, and you never take another full weekend off for two years, because you learn the hard way that leadership isn’t about handing off the hard parts to someone who looks good on paper. It’s about showing up, even when you’re tired, to make sure the people who trust you—your employees, your customers, the people who showed up before you had a fancy title or a board—never get sidelined for a quick win or a fancy resume. You’ll make a hundred more hiring mistakes after that, but you’ll never again ignore that quiet voice asking if the person across the table actually cares about the thing you built, not just the title and the paycheck that comes with it. That mistake cost you nearly $3 million, half your core customer trust, and a year of progress, but it taught you the lesson no business school ever could: the most dangerous hire you’ll ever make is the one you’re too relieved to find to vet properly.

title: Christian purpose-driven living book|serving others as the path to a meaningful life
text:
I used to think a meaningful life looked like a spotlight.

You know the version I mean: bigger platform, better book deal, perfect kitchen shelves, Bible journaling that looked like a craft store had a revival in my notebook. I wanted my life to feel important, and I wanted everyone within a 40-mile radius to notice.

Then God, in His great patience and slightly disruptive sense of humor, placed me next to Marlene.

Marlene was 82, used peppermints like currency, and had a habit of calling me “Karen” for two entire years despite my name being on a casserole dish I brought her. She needed help with groceries, her TV remote, and occasionally understanding why her phone was suddenly in French.

I would show up at her apartment with my little Christian service checklist, fully prepared to “be a blessing” and leave spiritually glowing in under 20 minutes.

Instead, Marlene wanted to talk.

About her husband. About her knees. About the neighbor who played music too loud. About whether the apostle Peter was dramatic or just “very passionate.” She made me instant coffee that tasted like warm cardboard and asked me questions I could not rush past.

Somewhere between the third grocery run and the 400th explanation of volume buttons, I realized something uncomfortable: I was not serving Marlene to love her. I was serving Marlene to feel meaningful.

And Jesus gently tapped me on the shoulder and said, “Let’s try this again.”

Purpose-driven living is often sold to us as a strategy. Discover your gifts. Clarify your calling. Build the plan. Maximize your impact. Those things are not wrong, but sometimes we turn following Jesus into a productivity system with better vocabulary.

But Jesus did not say, “Whoever finds the most efficient life mission will save it.”

He said, “If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me” (Matthew 16:24).

Then He did this wild thing throughout the Gospels: He kept defining greatness by service. “Whoever would be great among you must be your servant” (Matthew 20:26). Not whoever sounds most anointed on a podcast. Not whoever has the most impressive testimony. Whoever serves.

That changes everything.

Because service is not one category of the Christian life; it is the posture of the Christian life. It is love with its shoes on. It is faith carrying something heavy. It is the Holy Spirit working through our ordinary hands, our messy schedules, and our remarkably average cooking.

I learned more about purpose sitting in Marlene’s sticky kitchen than I did from every personality test I have ever taken. And I have taken them all. I was “winsome” in one, “a beaver” in another, and in one truly strange assessment, I came out as a pastoral spreadsheet.

Still, Marlene taught me that meaning is not usually found in a mountaintop moment. It is found in the repeated choice to love the person in front of me.

If you want to stop drifting into self-centered living, here are a few things that helped me.

1. Start with the person already assigned to your life.

You do not need a ministry empire. You might need a text message. A meal. A ride. A quiet visit. The person God has placed near you is not a distraction from your purpose; often, they are part of the answer to your prayer for purpose.

2. Serve without filming the testimony.

Some service should be invisible. Make the coffee. Clean the kitchen. forgive the rude comment. Do not announce your humility like a billboard. Matthew 6:3 says do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing, which is hard because my hands are both dramatic.

3. Pay attention to small needs.

Meaning rarely arrives wrapped in a dramatic assignment. It looks like helping a child with shoes, listening to a grieving friend, returning the cart, forgiving again, or sitting with someone whose life cannot be fixed in one conversation.

4. Let service expose your selfishness.

It will. Mine showed up impatient, proud, and checking the clock. Do not panic. Confess it. God is not surprised by your mixed motives. He sanctifies us as we obey, not after we become spiritually impressive enough to serve.

5. Remember whom you are really serving.

Colossians 3:23–24 says whatever you do, work heartily, “as for the Lord and not for men,” knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance. You are not serving ungrateful people for their approval. You are serving Christ, who sees every hidden act and never wastes one.

Marlene eventually learned my name. Sort of. She called me “Karen, but the good one.” I chose to receive it as an anointing.

The truth is, she served me more than I served her. She let me enter the slow, holy work of loving a real person instead of performing a polished purpose.

A meaningful life is not the life that gets noticed. It is the life poured out.

And when we pour ourselves out in Jesus’ name, we discover the strangest, most beautiful paradox of the kingdom: the life we lose for His sake is the life we finally find.

title: personal finance book|why you should stop feeling guilty about lattes and focus on big wins
text:
Excerpt from *Stop Pinching Pennies and Start Stacking Cash*
Let’s cut the crap right now. If you’ve spent the last three years lying awake at 2 a.m. replaying the $5.75 oat milk latte you bought on your way to work, beating yourself up for “throwing away” your shot at early retirement? I need you to take a deep breath, roll your eyes at the last finance bro who yelled at you about lattes, and listen up. That guilt is garbage. It’s designed to keep you small, to make you blame yourself for a system that’s rigged to make big wins feel out of reach while you nickel-and-dime yourself out of every tiny daily joy that makes 60-hour workweeks bearable.

Don’t get me wrong. I’m not saying you should blow every paycheck on artisanal coffee and matcha croissants. I am saying the math on the “latte factor” is straight-up bullshit, and the people peddling it know it. Let’s run the numbers, no fancy compound interest trickery designed to make a $5 purchase look like a million-dollar mistake. Let’s say you buy one latte every single workday—260 days a year, no skipping, no free office coffee swaps. At $6 a pop after tip? That’s $1,560 a year. Even if you invested every single one of those dollars at a 7% annual return, after 10 years you’d have… wait for it… $22,600. Nice! Don’t get me wrong, that’s a solid chunk of change. But it’s not early retirement money. It’s not a house down payment in 90% of American cities. It’s not going to make or break your financial future if you’re also blowing $400 a month on a car you don’t need, or paying 22% APR on a credit card you never bothered to do a balance transfer on, or leaving $12,000 a year on the table by not negotiating your starting salary.

Wait, let’s talk about that last one. I had a client a couple years back, Mia, 28, working in marketing in Chicago. She came to our first coaching session red-faced, carrying a crumpled spreadsheet tracking every coffee, every pack of gum, every $3 metro ride she’d taken for three months. She’d cut out lattes entirely, was bringing instant coffee to the office in a chipped mason jar, skipping happy hours with her team, and still couldn’t scrape together more than $300 a month in savings. She told me she felt like a failure, like she was “bad with money” because she couldn’t stick to the zero-based budget some TikTok guru sold her for $47.

We didn’t talk about coffee once in that first meeting. We talked about her job. She’d been at the company two years, hadn’t asked for a raise since she was hired, was making $78,000 a year. I made her do the research: people in her role with her experience at comparable firms were making $90k to $95k. She spent two weeks prepping her ask, walked into her boss’s office, walked out with a $14,000 raise and a 10% annual bonus structure. That’s $15,400 a year, before taxes. Let me repeat that: that’s TEN TIMES the annual cost of her daily latte habit. She started buying lattes again the next week, still puts 20% of that raise straight into her Roth IRA, and last year she put a down payment on a condo. She didn’t get there by skipping coffee. She got there by going for the big win.

Let’s talk about other big wins, because they’re everywhere, and we’re trained to ignore them because we’re too busy squinting at our bank apps for $4 charges to judge ourselves for. When’s the last time you shopped your car insurance? I did this last year, went from paying $187 a month to $112, same coverage, same car, same driving record. That’s $900 a year back in my pocket, no skipping lattes required. What about that subscription box you signed up for during the pandemic that you never open? The $130 a month gym membership you’ve used twice since January? The 401(k) match your job offers that you’re not contributing enough to get? I had a guy in my audience last year who realized he was leaving $4,500 a year on the table in unclaimed 401(k) match because he’d only set his contribution rate to 3% instead of the 6% required to get the full company match. That’s free money! He didn’t even know it was there, because he was too busy feeling guilty about the two beers he bought at the baseball game the weekend before.

Here’s the dirty secret the latte police don’t want you to know: shaming you for small purchases is easy. It’s content you can crank out in 10 minutes, no nuance required, that makes people feel guilty enough to click, to buy the $200 budget course, to sign up for the fancy app that tracks every penny you spend. Going for the big wins? That’s hard. It requires having an awkward conversation with your boss about pay. It requires spending two hours on a Saturday making phone calls to insurance companies instead of watching Netflix. It requires pulling your credit report, looking at the big scary number that is your student loan balance or your mortgage, and making a plan instead of distracting yourself by policing your own tiny, trivial purchases.

I’m not saying small expenses don’t add up. They do! But they add up to a fraction of what the big wins are worth. And if you cut out all the small things that make your life worth living? You’re going to burn out before you ever hit those big goals. I’ve seen it a hundred times: people go on extreme budget kicks, cut out every coffee, every takeout meal, every concert ticket, last three months, then blow $3,000 on a weekend bender in Vegas because they’re so deprived they can’t take it anymore. That’s way more expensive than a daily latte.

Last thing: I drink a latte every single morning. I get it from the same shop down the street from my house, the barista knows my order, I tip a dollar every time. That’s $7 a day, $1,820 a year. Do I lose sleep over it? Hell no. Because last year I refinanced my mortgage, knocked 1.25% off my interest rate, and saved $420 a month on my house payment. That’s $5,040 a year. That covers the lattes, my monthly book budget, the occasional fancy dinner with my partner, and still leaves me with an extra $2,000 a year to throw at my kid’s college fund. If I’d skipped the lattes but never bothered to refinance? I’d be out $5k a year, and I’d be miserable drinking bad office coffee every morning.

Stop feeling guilty for the small stuff. Stop letting people make you feel like your daily joy is the reason you’re not rich. The reason most people aren’t rich isn’t the lattes. It’s that they’re too busy counting pennies to reach for the dollars sitting right in front of them.

title: entrepreneurship book|launching a small business with almost no money
text:
Chapter 3: The $12 Flyer Strategy That Launched My First Business

When I lost my barista job in March 2020, I had $47 in my checking account, a beat-up laptop, and a landlord who’d already sent one polite-but-terrifying “rent concerns” email. I didn’t have savings for ads, a website, or even a formal business license right away. What I did have was a decade of helping my grandma fix wobbly chair legs, patch drywall, and assemble IKEA furniture for her neighbors in our small Ohio town. I called the idea “Neighborly Odd Jobs” — no fancy branding, no niche, just “I’ll fix the small stuff you don’t want to.”

My first mistake was waiting three days for “the perfect logo.” I sketched 20 versions in a notebook, compared free Canva templates until my eyes burned, and almost gave up entirely because none felt “professional enough.” Then my roommate Lila leaned over my shoulder, grabbed the notebook, and tore the logo pages out. “No one hires a handyman because of a logo,” she said. “They hire him because they know he’ll show up and not charge $150 to hang a curtain rod.” She was right. That day, I spent $12 on black-and-white flyer printing at the library — 50 copies, 24 cents each — and wrote my cell phone number in Sharpie at the bottom of every single one.

Here’s what I didn’t do: I didn’t buy tools. I already owned a basic hammer, screwdriver set, drill, and tape measure from my teen years helping Grandma. For jobs I didn’t have gear for, I told clients upfront, “I don’t own a ladder tall enough for your gutter — if you have one I can use, I’ll knock $10 off the hourly rate.” Every single person said yes. I didn’t build a website. I made a free Facebook page with one photo of me holding a hammer and a two-sentence bio: “Local, reliable odd jobs. No job too small. Free quotes.” I didn’t register an LLC until I’d made $1,200 in cash, enough to cover the $100 state filing fee without touching grocery money.

I spent three hours after printout taping flyers to community bulletin boards: the laundromat, two grocery stores, the senior center, the apartment complex lobby down the street, and the library itself. I didn’t tape them to mailboxes (that’s illegal in the U.S., by the way — a $200 fine I absolutely could not afford) or leave them on car windshields, where 90% get thrown away immediately. Instead, I targeted places where people who needed small home help actually spent time: the senior center’s book swap table, the laundromat’s folding counter, right next to the “for rent” ads at the grocery store.

My first call came 18 hours later. Mrs. Henderson, 78, needed three curtain rods hung and a loose bathroom towel bar resecured. She’d seen the flyer at the senior center. I quoted her $25 an hour, showed up 10 minutes early with my drill, and finished both jobs in 45 minutes. She paid me $20, insisted I keep the extra $5, and gave me a chocolate chip cookie. More importantly, she told three of her friends at bridge night that week. By the end of the first month, I had 11 clients, $780 in cash, and zero spent on advertising beyond that initial $12.

That experience taught me the core rule of no-money launches: *pre-solve trust before you spend a dollar on polish*. When you have no capital, your most valuable assets aren’t a fancy website or branded swag — they’re proximity to your community, transparency about what you can and can’t do, and willingness to start ridiculously small.

Three actionable takeaways from that $12 flyer run still work for every lean service business I’ve launched since:
1. Validate before you formalize: Don’t register an LLC, buy bulk inventory, or pay for software until you have three paying customers. If no one will pay you for the unpolished version, no one will pay you for the “professional” one either.
2. Use shared, free, or client-owned assets first: Borrow tools, use free social media pages, print low-cost flyers at public libraries, and trade skills for gear if you have to. I traded six hours of shelf hanging for a used 6-foot ladder two months in — no cash exchanged.
3. Target high-trust, low-competition micro-channels first: Skip expensive social media ads when you’re starting. Community boards, local Facebook groups, word-of-mouth referrals from your first three clients, and even handwritten notes to nearby neighbors cost almost nothing and convert far better for local service work.

I still have one of those original flyers tucked in the back of my desk drawer — lopsided clip art, misspelled “assembley” in the service list, Sharpie number bleeding through the paper.
