Ask about times they helped someone who could do nothing for them. Ask how they handled frustration, ambiguity, or a mistake. The people you hire will either reinforce your culture or quietly reshape it.

Once someone joins your team, give them a clear purpose. People do not become emotionally engaged merely by knowing their tasks. They engage when they understand the impact of their work. Explain that their role is not only to process orders, answer questions, or resolve complaints. Their role is to reduce anxiety, restore confidence, save time, and make people feel seen. When employees understand that service is a human relationship rather than a performance metric, their behavior changes.

You also need to give people permission to use judgment. If every unusual situation requires escalation, your team will act like rule enforcers instead of problem solvers. Create boundaries, but leave room for discretion. A reasonable refund, a sincere apology, a small gesture, or an extra few minutes of attention can turn a difficult moment into loyalty. Trust your employees to do the right thing, and then support them when they do.

Happiness-driven culture requires honest communication. You cannot demand openness from customers while tolerating fear inside the company. Encourage employees to report problems, suggest improvements, and admit mistakes without shame. Mistakes should be studied, not hidden. When leaders respond constructively to bad news, people stop defending themselves and start improving the business. A team that is afraid to speak up will create customer experiences that feel mechanical, defensive, and disconnected.

Recognition matters more than many leaders realize. Celebrate stories of exceptional care, especially when they involve effort rather than outcome. A team member who stays patient with an upset customer, takes ownership of a confusing problem, or notices an unspoken need deserves attention. When you recognize these behaviors, you teach the whole organization what success looks like. Metrics matter, but if you only celebrate speed and volume, do not be surprised when compassion disappears.

Also, protect your team from burnout. Delivering happiness should never mean absorbing endless abuse or suppressing every personal emotion. Teach employees to be kind without being passive, accountable without being doormats. Give them breaks, coaching, and realistic workloads. A drained person cannot consistently create positive experiences. Sustainable service comes from a supported team, not from exhausted people performing enthusiasm.

Finally, model the behavior you want. Your employees are watching how you speak to customers, how you treat frontline staff, and how you react when something goes wrong. If you cut corners, blame others, or treat complaints as annoyances, your culture will follow. If you listen, take responsibility, and show respect even in difficult moments, those values will spread.

A culture built around delivering happiness is not created with slogans, posters, or one training session. It is created through daily decisions: whom you hire, what you reward, how you lead, and what you refuse to tolerate. When your team feels valued, trusted, and connected to a meaningful purpose, happiness stops being a tactic. It becomes the natural way your company serves.

title: startup memoir|the early days of a search-engine company and its odd culture
text:
Let me take you back to the fall of 2018, when our search engine startup was crammed into a 1,200-square-foot loft above a laundromat in SOMA, San Francisco, and the weirdest thing about us wasn’t that we were trying to take on Google with 11 people and a server rack we’d built out of scrap metal from a nearby junkyard. It was the culture—less “disruptive tech unicorn” and more “group of feral raccoons who’d stumbled on a pile of venture capital money and decided to build a search engine.”

Our first official company policy wasn’t about PTO or non-disclosure agreements. It was the 3 a.m. Laundromat Rule. If you were in the office past 2:45 a.m., you were required to haul your laundry down to the laundromat below us, run a load while you waited for your crawl of the Pacific Northwest indie web to finish, and bring back a pack of those neon orange cheese puffs from the vending machine by the door for whoever was still at their desk. I still have a faded hoodie with a bleach stain on the cuff from the night our lead engineer, Javi, spilled detergent all over his keyboard while panicking because our crawler had accidentally indexed 40,000 pages of ferret fanfiction instead of the small business directories we’d been targeting. We didn’t even fix it for three days—half the team spent their breaks reading the ferret fanfiction, arguing about whether the protagonist ferret’s arc about learning to trust his new owner was better written than most of the Netflix shows we’d binged that quarter.

We didn’t have job titles back then. The closest we got was naming people after their most chaotic, consistent quirk. Our CEO, who’d dropped out of a Stanford PhD program to build this thing after he got frustrated that Google couldn’t find a specific 1998 zine about beekeeping, went by Ferret Guy for six months because he was the one who’d dug into that accidental index and spent three hours geeking out over the ferret fiction lore. I was Cheese Puff Czar for most of that first year, because I was the only person who could ever get the vending machine to dispense the orange ones without eating a dollar first—turns out you just had to kick the left side twice, right below the Cheeto logo, and it would spit out two bags half the time. Our designer, who drew all our early logo drafts on napkins from the taco truck down the block, went by Napkin Mia, and she still has a stack of those napkins in her home office, including the one where she sketched our first mascot: a raccoon holding a magnifying glass, wearing a tiny laundromat laundry basket as a hat.

People always ask when we knew we were onto something, and I never tell them the story about the investor pitch where Ferret Guy showed up in socks with ferrets on them and spent 10 minutes talking about how our search engine ranked the ferret fanfiction higher than Petco’s ferret care page because the fanfiction had more actual, useful advice from real ferret owners. I tell them about the Tuesday in November when a retired beekeeper from Oregon emailed us to say he’d found that 1998 zine our CEO had been chasing for three years, because our crawler had pulled it from a Geocities archive buried so deep even the Wayback Machine had missed it. We celebrated by running three loads of laundry in the laundromat below, eating so many cheese puffs our fingers were bright orange for two days, and voting to make the ferret fanfiction a permanent, unadvertised easter egg in our search results. To this day, if you search “ferret pirate king” on our engine, that 40,000-page archive is still the top result. We never took it down. It felt wrong, somehow—like scrubbing the bleach stain out of Javi’s hoodie would erase the part where we weren’t a company yet, just a bunch of weirdos who thought search should work for the people writing ferret fanfiction and chasing old beekeeping zines, not just the people paying for the top ad spot.

title: writing-craft memoir|the daily routine of a working novelist
text:
People ask about the routine like it's the secret. Like if they set the alarm right and buy the right pen, the books come out. I don't have a routine. I have a schedule, and there's a difference. A routine is something you do because it feels like a writer. A schedule is what keeps you from getting fired by yourself.

I'm up at 5:40. Not 5:30. I tried 5:30 for a year and it made me mean. Twenty extra minutes in the dark and suddenly I'm writing emails I'd regret, so I moved it ten forward and then another ten, and 5:40 is where my brain stops filing grievances. Coffee is instant. I can hear you making a face. I've had the pour-over stuff, I've stood in the little shops while a man with a leather apron explains a bean to me. I need caffeine, not a relationship. Two heaping teaspoons of whatever's on sale, hot water, done. I drink it standing at the kitchen counter while the house is still ugly with sleep.

Then I sit down at 6:00 in the same chair I've used since 2014. It's a secretary chair I found at a church basement sale for twelve dollars. The vinyl is cracked on the left arm and I've put a folded towel there. My office is a converted bedroom above a garage. In winter it's cold enough that I can see my breath, and I tell people this builds character, but really I just own one space heater and I'm cheap. The desk has a crack in it shaped a little like Florida. I know this because I've stared at it for three books instead of writing.

I don't believe in waiting for inspiration. I believe in word count, and mine is a thousand words a day, seven days a week, until the draft is done. Not a thousand good words. A thousand words. Some of them are terrible and I know it while I'm making them. There's a sentence in my last novel about a mailbox that I wrote with my teeth basically clenched, and I kept it for three weeks because deleting it would mean the day only produced nine hundred and something, and I don't negotiate with that part of my head. I fixed it later. The fixing is the actual job. The first draft is just digging the hole.

Email stays closed until noon. This is the only rule that matters. If I open it before I work, the day belongs to strangers. Some agent wants something urgent that turns out not to be urgent. A reader has decided I owe him a defense of a chapter. A student sends forty pages and a note that says *no pressure*. There's always pressure. The pressure is the point. Put it in a drawer until the thousand words are dead on the page.

Around 9:30 I walk. Three miles, same route, past the dry cleaner and the place that used to sell vacuums and now sells CBD dog treats, which is the most American sentence I've ever thought. I don't listen to podcasts anymore. I tried. Every other ad was for a mattress or a meal in a bag, and I started feeling like my brain was being rented out by the minute. Now I just walk and let the book make noise underneath everything. Half the plot problems solve themselves between the stop sign on Maple and the terrible pizza place. Not because I'm smart. Because I stopped looking at them.

Lunch is at the same Formica table, usually eggs or soup, and I read fifty pages of something dead. Dead writers don't network with you. Cheever, Taylor, a little McGahern when I'm feeling brave. If I read a living writer while I'm drafting, I start imitating him by page twenty, and by page thirty I'm writing a parody with worse weather. The dead are safer company. They can't ask for a blurb.

Afternoons are for revision. I print pages. I know, I know, trees. But I catch things on paper I miss on the screen, whole paragraphs that are just the author showing off his research on boat engines. I use a red pen and I'm not kind. Last Tuesday I wrote *who talks like this* in the margin of my own dialogue and meant it. Then I answer the mail, pay the bills, pretend I understand the royalty statement. I don't. I have an accountant who does, and she charges me four hundred dollars a quarter to translate it from the original cruel.

I stop at 5:30 whether it's going well or not. This used to make me crazy. Younger me would chase a scene until one in the morning, drunk on the feeling, then lose three days recovering from the prose. Now I leave in the middle sometimes. I'll stop a scene halfway through a conversation, right where the character's about to say the thing, because tomorrow I know she'll still be standing there with her mouth open.

title: negotiation book|finding out what the other side really wants
text:
Section 3.2: The Maple Table That Sold for $40 More Than Asking
The most dangerous lie in negotiation is the one you tell yourself: *I already know what they want*. I learned that on a rainy Saturday in 2019, hunched over a chipped 1950s maple side table in my parents’ garage, trying to offload a lifetime of clutter before they moved cross-country. My dad had slapped a $120 price tag on it three years prior when they first tried to downsize; no one had bit. I was 28, fresh off landing my first corporate negotiation consulting gig, cocky enough to think I’d mastered the “anchoring high, concede slow” playbook I’d taught to interns the week before.
The first person to stop at the table was a sharp-eyed woman in a flannel shirt, running a finger over the faint water ring my mom had left there from a pothos plant in 1998. “What’s the lowest you’ll take for this?” she asked, kicking the leg lightly to test its sturdiness.
I leaned into the script I’d rehearsed. “It’s solid rock maple, midcentury, no major structural damage—$120 is firm.”
She snort-laughed, zipped her jacket, and turned to walk away. “I’ll give you $60. That’s all it’s worth with that water stain. I’m flipping it anyway; I’ll have to sand the whole top down.”
I was already mentally marking the table down to $50 to get it out of the garage when a second woman, maybe 60, in a faded university hoodie, lingered at the edge of the driveway, waiting for the first negotiator to leave. She didn’t kick the leg. She didn’t run her finger over the water ring. She traced the tiny carved heart in the corner of the tabletop—the one my dad had etched with a pocketknife the day he and my mom brought me home from the hospital, my initials carved inside.
Before I could launch into my $120 pitch, I remembered the advice my first mentor had drilled into me: *The first offer tells you their position. The first quiet pause tells you their interest*. So I shut my mouth.
“My daughter just bought her first apartment two blocks from here,” she said, still touching the carved heart. “I had a table just like this when I was her age. I donated it when we moved 20 years ago, and I’ve regretted it ever since.”
I almost blew it. I almost said, “Great, that’s $120,” before I caught myself. “What happened to the one you had?” I asked.
She told me she’d been a single mom, working two jobs to put her daughter through preschool, and couldn’t afford the moving truck space for it when they downsized to a one-bedroom. That table was where she’d taped her daughter’s first finger paintings, where they’d eaten frozen pizza every Friday night, where her daughter had left her a tooth under a napkin for the tooth fairy. The water stain? She laughed—she had an identical one on her old table, from the same kind of pothos plant she’d killed when she forgot to water it during a week of night shifts.
That was the real ask, I realized. She didn’t want a project piece to flip for profit. She wanted a do-over.
I told her my own story of the table, of the heart carving, of the pothos stain. I even offered to load it into her minivan for her. When I quoted the $120 price, she didn’t haggle. She pulled out her wallet, handed me $160, and pressed an extra $20 into my palm when I carried it to her car. “For your mom’s next pothos,” she said.
I see clients make the same mistake I almost made every single day: they fixate on positions—the other side’s stated ask, the number they throw out first, the demand they lead with—instead of digging for the underlying interests driving that position. Here are three rules I took away from that garage sale that I still bring to every C-suite contract and tenant-landlord mediation:
First, ask one unscripted follow-up question after they state their ask. If the table flipper had said “$60,” instead of jumping to counter, I could have asked “What’s your plan for it once you get it home?”—and I would have immediately known she had a tight profit margin and no room to pay up. When the second buyer didn’t lead with a price, that question unlocked her whole motivation.
Second, look for what they don’t haggle over. The flipper zeroed in on the flaw (the water stain) because that was her leverage to cut costs. The second buyer never mentioned the stain at all; she only looked at the carved heart. The parts of a deal they don’t push back on are the parts that matter most to them—those are the points you can lean into to create value without slashing price.
Third, never dismiss the “silly” small details. The $20 extra she gave me wasn’t for the table. It was for the story I shared, for the fact that I didn’t treat the heart carving like a defect to be sanded off. Most high-stakes negotiations aren’t won on price. They’re won on the tiny, personal priorities no one leads with: a flexible start date for a new hire who needs to care for a sick parent, a supplier’s demand for a 10% price hike that’s actually driven by fear of late payments you can fix with net-15 terms, a tenant’s request for new kitchen cabinets that’s really about being allowed to hang their kid’s art on the walls.
I got an email from that woman six months later. Attached was a photo of the table in her daughter’s dining nook, a pothos sitting right where my mom’s used to be, the carved heart still fully visible. I never would have gotten that note if I’d stuck to my script, if I’d been so focused on hitting my $120 asking price that I didn’t bother to ask why she was standing there in the first place. The other side will almost never tell you what they really want unprompted. But if you stop talking long enough to look, they’ll always show you.
(Word count: 718)

title: time-management book|saying no to good opportunities to protect great ones
text:
Every week, opportunities arrive that look like yeses. A colleague invites you to join a promising project. A friend asks you to lead a committee. A client offers extra work. A manager suggests an interesting assignment. Your inbox contains invitations, introductions, events, partnerships, favors, and proposals. Many are legitimate. Many are led by people you respect. Some could genuinely help your career, expand your network, teach you something, or make someone happy.

That is what makes this difficult. If every opportunity were bad, saying no would be easy. The real challenge is saying no to good opportunities so great ones have room to grow.

Your calendar is not an empty warehouse. It is a small, finite container. When you accept something good, you are not merely adding one meeting or one task. You are spending attention, energy, discretion, mental bandwidth, and recovery time. You are taking hours from the same week that must also hold your most important work, your closest relationships, and your long-term goals.

A great opportunity rarely appears with the whole week already prepared for it. It usually arrives while you are busy. It may come as a promotion, a chance to build a new product, an invitation to lead, a creative project, a business partnership, or a season when your family needs you more than usual. If your schedule is stuffed with respectable commitments, you will not be able to respond fully. You may even say yes to the great thing and then discover you have no practical way to do it well.

Protective refusal is not negativity. It is stewardship.

Start by deciding what you are protecting. You cannot call an opportunity a distraction unless you know your destination. Write down the two or three outcomes that matter most during this season. They might be finishing a degree, scaling a business, writing a book, rebuilding your health, leading a major initiative, or being present for your children. These become your filter.

When an opportunity appears, pause before accepting. Do not answer from enthusiasm, guilt, urgency, or flattery. Ask: Does this directly strengthen one of my great priorities? Will this still matter in six months? Does it require my unique contribution, or could someone else do it? What likely opportunity becomes less likely if I say yes?

That last question is essential. Every yes has a hidden twin. The yes to a weekly networking lunch may mean no to focused writing time. The yes to managing someone else's event may mean no to resting before your own launch. The yes to an extra client may mean no to improving the service that creates better clients. You rarely see the cost immediately, but it will appear later as missed deadlines, shallow work, exhaustion, irritability, or regret.

Learn to distinguish a good opportunity from a great fit. A good opportunity offers benefit. A great fit offers leverage, meaning, timing, and alignment with your core purpose. It may still be hard. It may demand sacrifice. But it pulls you toward the future you actually want rather than merely adding another respectable line to your life.

Saying no can be respectful and clear. You might say, "I need to decline because my current priorities are already at capacity." Or, "I don't want to give this less than it deserves." Or, "Thank you for thinking of me, but I'm not the right person for this season." You do not need to invent an emergency. A truthful boundary is enough.

Be prepared for discomfort. People may be surprised. Some may be disappointed. You may feel selfish. But overcommitment is not generosity if it makes you unreliable, exhausted, or absent. Protecting your best work is also a way of honoring others, because when you do commit, you can show up fully.

Leave margin deliberately. Great opportunities often need unstructured space to be recognized. If every evening and weekend is occupied, you lose reflection, serendipity, and the ability to move quickly. A crowded calendar can make you feel productive while quietly narrowing your future.

Remember, saying no is not the end of opportunity. It is often how you become worthy of better opportunity. Each careful no tells your life, your work, and the people around you that your yes has weight.

Protect the great things. The good things will keep coming. Your job is not to collect them all. Your job is to choose the few that deserve your finite, irreplaceable yes.

title: entrepreneurship book|launching a small business with almost no money
text:
Let me cut the crap right off the top: I launched my first profitable business with $17 total in my checking account. No, that’s not a cutesy “I had a secret trust fund backstop” flex. That was 2017, I was 26, sleeping on a friend’s lumpy couch in Portland, had just quit my barista job after a customer threw a oat milk latte at my head because I “put too much foam on purpose,” and my only marketable skill was being weirdly good at writing silly custom pet poems for my Instagram followers.
I know what you’re thinking: “But all the startup bros say you need ad budgets and LLC filing fees and a fancy Squarespace site!” Let me save you the $40 course they’re selling: that’s garbage for 90% of us who don’t have a rich uncle to cut us a seed check. My $17 went entirely to a 30-day free Canva trial that I forgot to cancel, oops, and a bag of the cheapest gas station gummy bears to fuel my first 12-hour work stretch.
Let me run down the three rules that got me to $4k in revenue in 30 days, no loans, no weird investor pitches where some guy in a Patagonia vest asks you about your “moat” when you’re just trying to sell hand-stamped keychains or dog walking services or whatever your thing is.
1. Sell before you build anything. I didn’t order custom poem prints, I didn’t buy a domain, I didn’t make a price list. I posted a blurry Instagram Story of a poem I wrote for my friend’s chonky orange cat Garbage, captioned it “I will write your weird pet a deeply dramatic sonnet for $15, Venmo only, I’ll send it to you as a Google Doc in 48 hours,” and went to take a nap. When I woke up I had 29 Venmo notifications. That’s $435, before I’d done a single piece of actual work. I used half that money to pay back my friend for the groceries I’d been mooching, and the other half to buy a $12 domain name once I realized people would actually pay me. If your idea requires you to spend $500 on inventory before you have a single confirmed customer? Scrap it. Post the offer first. If no one bites, you lost nothing except 2 minutes drafting a social media post.
2. Beg, borrow, and barter for literally everything else, but skip the parts that cost money until you can pay for them with customer cash. I didn’t file an LLC for six months, because my state charged $100 for the filing fee and I needed that money to pay for a PO box so I didn’t have to give randos my friend’s couch address. I traded a free year of custom pet poems to my graphic designer roommate for a terrible, MS Paint-adjacent logo that I used for two years. I borrowed my roommate’s old laptop when mine died mid-poem for a golden retriever named Mr. Noodles, instead of dropping $1k on a new MacBook like every “hustle guru” tells you you need.
3. Ignore the “you have to look professional” police. I sent the first 70 poems from my personal Gmail account, the one with the handle “partypizza69” I made when I was 19. I wrote typos in half of them. I accidentally sent a poem about a cat to someone who ordered one for their ferret once, and they laughed so hard they tipped me $20 and referred three friends. People don’t buy from perfectly polished brands when you’re small. They buy from the person who’s obviously just winging it, because that feels real.
Here’s the secret no one will tell you: the biggest advantage you have when you’re broke is that you have nothing to lose. You don’t have to waste time overthinking a brand guide or stressing about your Instagram grid aesthetic. You can post a messy, unscripted video explaining your thing, see who throws money at you, and adjust as you go. I spent three months after that first launch panicking that I was “doing it wrong” because I didn’t have a business plan or a spreadsheet or a fancy email list. Then I realized the people who write the “how to start a business” books were almost never people who started broke. They were people who had enough cash to wait six months to make a profit. You don’t have that luxury, which means you get to move faster, be dumber, and have way more fun than they ever will.
That first month? I ate a lot of microwave ramen, I accidentally typed “paw” instead of “pour” in a poem about a cat who loved drinking out of faucets, and I made enough to move into my own tiny studio apartment by month three. You don’t need a pile of cash to start. You just need one person willing to pay you for the thing you already know how to do. And maybe a bag of gummy bears. Don’t skip the gummy bears. (Word count: 612)

title: personal memoir with life lessons|a year of travel after a painful divorce
text:
The Year I Chased Cheap Flights and Bad Decisions

Thirty-one days after the ink dried on the divorce papers, I found myself eating a day-old empanada on a bus in Patagonia, wondering how a forty-two-year-old woman who once color-coded her pantry ended up somewhere the wind sounded like my ex-husband snoring. I'd gotten the house in the settlement — a three-bed colonial in Maplewood with a finished basement and a mortgage that made my left eye twitch — and I sold it in eleven weeks for forty-seven thousand over asking. My lawyer, a man named Barry who wore bow ties unironically, kept saying I was "liquidating." I said I was escaping. Same thing, different tax bracket.

I bought a one-way ticket to Santiago for six hundred twelve dollars on a Tuesday. My sister Claire called me reckless. My mother asked if I'd been drinking. Both fair. I'd spent the last sixteen years coordinating carpool schedules and pretending to enjoy dinner parties where everyone discussed stucco. The marriage hadn't died in a dramatic explosion. It had rotted slowly, like the windowsill behind the kitchen sink I kept asking him to fix. He didn't cheat. I didn't cheat. We just stopped talking somewhere around year nine, and by the time I noticed, the silence had its own zip code.

First month, I blew through three thousand two hundred dollars staying in hostels that advertised "rustic charm," which turned out to mean thin walls and shared bathrooms. I slept in a bunk above a twenty-two-year-old Australian named Jem who cried about his girlfriend every single night and then tried to sell me essential oils. I wanted to judge him. Instead I bought the lavender one, because desperation smells a lot like eucalyptus and poor choices.

The thing nobody tells you about traveling alone after your life splits open: you can't outrun yourself. I learned this in Buenos Aires, sitting in a café where the coffee cost the equivalent of one dollar and eighty cents, reading a book I'd already read three times. I'd come four countries in, and I was still performing the role of Woman Rediscovering Herself, like some bad Netflix adaptation. I journaled about gratitude. I took sunrise yoga on a rooftop. I cried during a tango show because the dancers looked angry, and anger I understood.

Then the money started to matter. I had about sixty-one thousand left from the house, and watching it drain focused the mind. I moved into a rented room in Mexico City for two hundred forty dollars a month, above a taquería that played norteño at full volume until two in the morning. The neighbor, Doña Rosa, seventy-one and widowed twice, took one look at me and started feeding me. She didn't speak English and my Spanish was garbage, but she had this way of handing me a plate like she was handing me a verdict. Eat. Stop being ridiculous. I ate.

I stopped trying to have an Experience and started just having days. Mondays I went to the market and argued over avocados with a vendor named Luis, who charged me less the worse my Spanish got. Thursdays I took the bus to Coyoacán and sat on a bench watching old men play dominoes. I gained nine pounds. I read forty-one books that year, if you count the three I abandoned. I called my daughter, Megan, nineteen and in her sophomore year, every Sunday at six p.m. her time, and she mostly told me about her roommate's cat and a boy named Dev who was, quote, "emotionally porous." I had no notes. Parenting from two thousand miles away is mostly nodding and trying not to cry into your street corn.

Somewhere around month seven — I was in Lisbon then, paying three hundred euros a night for a room with a tile floor and a view that made me suspicious of joy — I realized I wasn't thinking about him anymore. Not in the heavy way. I'd catch his name in my head like a song I used to hate, and then it would pass. I'd spent years convinced our story was the important one. Turns out it was just a chapter, and a boring one at that, heavy on the landscape descriptions.

I made mistakes, obviously. I trusted a man in Amalfi who said his boat was "totally legal" and spent four hours helping him bail water out of a dinghy that absolutely was not. I got food poisoning in Bangkok that lasted six days and cost me nine pounds and, briefly, my will to live. I missed Megan's birthday because I'd misread the date line, and I still can't think about it without the floor dropping out of my chest. She forgave me on FaceTime while her friends waved in the background holding a cake shaped like a frog. I didn't deserve that. I told her so. She said, and I quote, "Mom, stop making this about your guilt."

She was right. About that and a lot of things, though I'll deny it if she ever reads this, which she won't because she thinks memoir is "cringe."

The last stop was a tiny village in the Algarve where I rented a cottage for five weeks. Four walls, a fig tree, a neighbor's donkey that brayed at five forty-five every morning with religious conviction. I was fifty-three thousand dollars poorer than when I started, and I'd stopped tracking the exact number the way you stop weighing yourself after a certain point. I swam in water so cold it made my teeth ache, and I cooked dinner for one and didn't apologize to the empty chair.

Here's what I know that I didn't a year ago. Nobody is coming to save you, and that's not a tragedy, it's just the schedule. A good meal from a stranger can fix about forty percent of anything. You can survive being alone with your thoughts, even though yours, like mine, are occasionally mean and frequently repetitive. And the person you were married to for sixteen years can become a fact, like a street you used to live on — you can still drive past it, but you don't have to turn in.

I don't know what's next. My lease runs out in three weeks. Megan says I should come home and get a dog. Barry says I should consider municipal bonds. Doña Rosa sends me voice notes I mostly can't understand, except for the end, where she laughs and says something that I choose to believe means *good for you*.

The donkey just started. It's five forty-four. Even the animal is early.

I'm making coffee.

title: relationships advice book|staying faithful and keeping a long marriage alive
text:
Chapter 3: The Grocery List Test: Faithfulness as a Daily Choice, Not a Grand Vow
I was 12 years into my marriage, standing in a dimly lit hotel bar at a writing conference, when a woman with silver hoop earrings and a laugh that sounded like wind chimes leaned across the table and said, “I’ve read every one of your essays. You get what it feels like to be tired of trying.” It was 10 p.m., my phone was dead, I’d had two glasses of pinot noir, and for 17 seconds— I counted, later, replaying the moment on the drive home— I didn’t think of my wife Lila waiting up for me, or the way she leaves sticky notes with bad puns on my coffee mug, or the fact that our youngest had a soccer game the next morning. I just thought: This person sees me, no strings attached, no to-do lists, no arguments about who left the wet towel on the bed.

That split second is the part no one talks about when they stand at the altar promising “forever.” Faithfulness isn’t a single, heroic choice you make once when a tempting offer lands in your lap. It’s 10,000 tiny, unglamorous choices you make when you’re tired, when you’re bored, when your spouse is snoring so loud you’re considering sleeping on the couch, when someone new looks at you like you’re the most interesting person in the room instead of the person who forgot to take the trash out for the third week in a row.

I excused myself, found a payphone in the hotel lobby (this was 2007, before portable chargers were ubiquitous), and called Lila collect. She picked up on the third ring, groggy, and said, “Did you remember the oat milk? And the sour candy for Mia’s game? I left the list taped to your laptop bag.” In that moment, the spell broke. Because that grocery list wasn’t just a list—it was proof that the “strings” people run from are actually the threads holding your life together.

Let’s get practical about what that means, because grand gestures don’t inoculate you against those 17-second moments. First, build what I call “micro-fences” long before temptation shows up. I didn’t stay at that bar because I had superhuman willpower; I stayed faithful because we had a rule back then: no after-hours drinks one-on-one with someone who isn’t a mutual friend, no matter how innocent. I didn’t make that rule in the bar that night—we made it three years earlier, over burnt pancakes on a Sunday, when we admitted to each other that we’d both had those split-second, stupid crushes on coworkers, that neither of us was immune. These fences aren’t about distrust; they’re about respecting how easy it is to slip when you’re running on fumes.

Second, stop saving your “best self” for strangers. That woman at the bar saw the polished, funny version of me that got to travel for work and talk about books for a weekend. She didn’t see the version of me that snaps at Lila when I’m on deadline, or cries at dog adoption commercials, or needs help picking out dress shirts because I’m colorblind. Too many marriages erode because we give our patience, our curiosity, our full attention to bar acquaintances and work friends, while we give our partners the exhausted, checked-out leftovers. I started a small practice after that conference: every day, I tell Lila one thing I noticed about her that day, no matter how small—the way she hums off-key while loading the dishwasher, the way she stayed up 20 minutes late helping our son build a Lego spaceship even when she had an early meeting. It trains you to look for the magic in the person you already chose, instead of looking for magic in someone new.

Third, stop treating wandering thoughts as a moral failure. That 17-second moment didn’t make me a bad husband. What would have made me a bad husband is leaning into it, staying for another drink, not calling home, telling myself I “deserved” the attention because marriage was hard. Faithfulness doesn’t mean you never notice another person; it means you never let that notice turn into something that takes away from the life you built. When I got home the next day, I told Lila about the bar, about the 17 seconds, about the phone call. She laughed, handed me the grocery list, and said, “Next time, charge your phone. And if you ever leave me for someone who doesn’t know you hate pickles, I’m keeping the dog.”

That’s the secret no wedding toast tells you: the great, passionate, long marriage isn’t the one where you never want to stray. It’s the one where you choose the grocery list, the bad puns, the snoring, the person who knows you hate pickles, every single time. (Word count: 698)

title: Christian purpose-driven living book|serving others as the path to a meaningful life
text:
When you think about the life God has called you to, you may picture something large and remarkable— a ministry everyone notices, a gift the whole world admires, or a moment when your purpose suddenly becomes clear. But God often begins in a smaller place. He begins when you notice the person beside you. He begins when you choose to serve someone who cannot repay you, when you listen to someone everyone else ignores, or when you quietly help carry a burden that was never yours to carry.

You were created to know God and to reflect His love in the world. That purpose is not discovered only through dramatic events; it is practiced in ordinary acts of obedience. When you serve others, you are not simply helping people in need. You are becoming the person God designed you to be. You are stepping away from a life centered on yourself and entering the life Jesus described as the way of true greatness.

The world tells you that meaning comes from being served, recognized, promoted, and admired. It says your life becomes significant when your needs are met and your name is known. But Jesus turns that way of thinking upside down. He said that whoever wants to become great must be a servant, and whoever wants to be first must be the slave of all. He did not merely speak these words; He lived them. He washed feet. He touched the sick. He welcomed children. He ate with sinners. He gave His life on the cross for people who could never earn His love.

If you belong to Christ, your service is a response to that grace. You do not serve to earn salvation, because salvation has already been given to you through faith in Jesus. You serve because your heart has been changed. You serve because the love of God now lives within you and seeks a way to flow out. Your good works do not make God love you more, but they show that His love has truly reached you.

Perhaps you have been waiting until you feel ready. You may think you need more knowledge, more strength, more time, or more confidence before God can use you. But God does not usually call equipped people because they are impressive; He equips ordinary people who are willing. The little boy with five loaves and two fish did not have enough to feed a crowd, but what he gave to Jesus became more than enough. In the same way, your limited time, your simple gifts, and your quiet acts of kindness can be multiplied by God in ways you may never see on this side of eternity.

Serving begins with seeing. Many people pass by needs every day without noticing because they are hurried, distracted, or afraid. Ask the Holy Spirit to open your eyes. The need may be in your home, where patience and forgiveness are required. It may be at work, where integrity and kindness can shine. It may be in your church, where volunteers are needed and no one is applauding. It may be in your neighborhood, among strangers, the lonely, the elderly, the poor, or those who do not yet know Christ.

Do not despise small acts. A cup of cold water given in Jesus’ name does not pass unnoticed by Him. A meal prepared, a child taught, a visit made, a debt forgiven, an encouraging word spoken, or a prayer offered in secret can carry eternal weight. Service is not always convenient. It costs time, energy, comfort, and sometimes pride. But the cost of following Jesus is never greater than the grace He gives to carry it.

Serving also protects you from selfishness. When your life revolves around your own wants, you become narrow and restless. But when you give yourself away, your heart expands. You begin to feel what God feels. You begin to love what God loves. You discover that joy is not found in being the center of the story, but in knowing that God has written you into His greater story of redemption.

There will be times when your service seems unnoticed. People may forget, complain, or take your kindness for granted. But serve anyway. You are not working for human praise. You are serving the Lord Christ, and He sees every hidden act. One day, even a simple word of welcome given for His sake will be remembered by Him.

So today, do not wait for a grand assignment. Be faithful where you are. Look for one person to encourage, one burden to help bear, one need to meet in love. As you serve others in Jesus’ name, you will find the meaningful life you were seeking—not because service itself saves you, but because it leads you closer to the Servant King, who gave everything so that you could live forever.

title: motivational book|achieving long-term goals by managing your energy, not your time
text:
Let me cut to the chase: three years ago, I was the queen of time-blocking. I had a color-coded Google Calendar, a fancy leather planner, and a habit of setting 17 alarms a day to keep me on track for my Big Goal: writing a 90,000-word novel in a year.
I hit my word count every single day for six weeks. I also cried in a Target parking lot over a bag of cheese puffs because I was so burnt out I couldn’t remember the last time I laughed without checking my phone to make sure I wasn’t “wasting leisure minutes.”
Here’s the dumb secret no productivity bro selling you a $497 time-management course will tell you: time is a fixed resource. You get 24 hours, no hacks, no loopholes, no “secret trick” to squeeze 25 out of the day. But your energy? That’s renewable. That’s flexible. That’s the thing you actually have control over.
I scrapped the color-coded calendar the day after the Target cheese puff incident. I stopped forcing myself to write 1,000 words at 6 a.m. when my brain feels like mashed potatoes until 10 a.m. I stopped skipping post-work walks with my roommate to “optimize” my writing hours, and I stopped feeling guilty for napping for 20 minutes when I hit that 2 p.m. wall.
I finished that novel three months ahead of my original deadline. No all-nighters, no cheese-puff meltdowns, no resenting the thing I’d spent years wanting to write.
If you’re tired of chasing time blocks that leave you too drained to care about the big goal you’re chasing, I’ve got three tiny, no-fancy-tools rules that changed everything for me:
1. Stop matching high-stakes work to low-energy slots. I used to force myself to draft chapters first thing in the morning because every productivity account said “do the hard thing first!” But my brain’s creative battery doesn’t charge until I’ve had two cups of coffee, a walk around the block, and 20 minutes of mindlessly scrolling cat TikTok. Now I save my 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. window—my personal peak energy—for drafting, and use my bleary 6 a.m. slot for answering emails and folding laundry, tasks that don’t require my brain to be firing on all cylinders.
2. Build “energy deposits” into your day, not just “to-do list withdrawals.” For years I treated every non-work activity as a waste of time that was taking away from my goal. Turns out, 10 minutes of dancing to terrible 2000s pop in my kitchen, a 15 minute walk to get a lime seltzer, or a 5 minute call with my best friend to rant about our bad grocery store runs isn’t wasted time—it’s putting energy back in the bank so I can show up better for the work that matters. I now schedule these tiny deposits like I would a work meeting, and I never skip them.
3. Let yourself quit early when the tank is empty. There were days last year when I sat down to write, got 200 words in, and realized my brain was so fried every sentence sounded like it was written by a tired raccoon. I used to force myself to sit there for two hours anyway, just to “hit the time block.” Now I close my laptop, go do something that fills me up, and come back the next day when my energy is back. Those 200 good words were worth way more than two hours of garbage I’d just delete later anyway.
Here’s the thing no one tells you about long-term goals: they don’t get done because you perfectly managed every minute of every day. They get done because you showed up consistently, with enough energy to care about the work, for a really long time. You don’t have to run yourself ragged to prove you’re serious about the thing you want. You just have to stop treating your energy like an afterthought.
Last week I saw that old leather planner in a box in my closet. I flipped to the week of the cheese puff meltdown, and every single time block was filled, every little checkmark in place. There was no space for walks, or naps, or bad pop dance parties, or even cheese puffs that didn’t come with a side of guilt. I tossed it in the donation bin.
Your goals don’t care how many hours you log when you’re too tired to think straight. They care how much of your best, most energized self you get to bring to them, one small, well-timed step at a time.
(Word count: 597)

title: self-improvement book|dealing with procrastination and perfectionism
text:
Chapter 7
Done Is Better Than Perfect
I once spent three weeks rewriting the first page of my first book proposal. Three. Weeks. One paragraph. I’d open my laptop at 7 a.m., adjust a comma, swap “struggle” for “challenge,” stare at the sentence like it owed me money, and somehow end up organizing my kitchen drawers. The worst part? I told myself I wasn’t procrastinating. I was “being rigorous.” I was “honoring the standard.”
That is perfectionism’s favorite trick: it dresses laziness up as excellence.
Let me tell you what actually broke that cycle. My editor, a no-nonsense woman named Rita who’d survived 30 years in publishing, called me and said, “Send me whatever you have right now. Even if it’s garbage. Garbage I can fix. A blank page I can’t.” I hit send on a document I was deeply embarrassed by, heart racing like I’d just handed her a note in seventh grade. Her reply 24 hours later? “This is 60% there. Good. Now we work.”
That day I learned the difference between high standards and impossible ones. High standards give you a target. Perfectionism gives you a trap. Procrastination isn’t time management, by the way. It’s emotion management. We don’t put off the report because we don’t know how to write it. We put it off because finishing it means facing judgment—our own, first and foremost. Starting feels safe. Perfect doesn’t exist, so as long as you’re “tinkering,” you never have to be disappointed.
Try the 10-Minute Ugly Draft rule I still use today. Tell yourself: I only have to work on this for 10 minutes, and it is allowed to be terrible. No deleting. No rereading. Just type, sketch, make the phone call, outline the budget—whatever the thing is. Nine times out of ten, once you’re moving, you won’t stop. Momentum beats motivation every single time. I once cleared an entire to-do list I’d avoided for a month just because I committed to folding one single load of laundry. One small, imperfect action unlocks the rest.
Another game changer? Lower the bar on your “starting ritual.” If you want to exercise, don’t lay out gear and plan a 45-minute gym trip. Just put on your sneakers. That’s it. If you need to make a hard call, just dial the number and say hello. The part we dread is almost always the build-up in our heads, not the action itself.
I want you to reframe “bad first tries” as data. A messy presentation slide isn’t a reflection of who you are. It’s information: this section needs a story, that graph is confusing. When you hide from starting, you rob yourself of that feedback. The world doesn’t reward perfect ideas that never leave your head. It rewards finished, imperfect things that get better in the open.
Done isn’t the enemy of great. Waiting for perfect is.
Today, pick one thing you’ve been “perfecting” instead of doing. Give yourself 10 ugly minutes on it. Then hit send, show someone, take one real step. I promise: the relief of finishing “good enough” will always taste sweeter than the fantasy of something flawless you never actually made.

title: writing-craft memoir|the daily routine of a working novelist
text:
Section 3: The 6 a.m. Dishwasher and the Myth of "Inspiration"
(Word count: 698)

The first novel I sold, I wrote half of it leaning against a humming dishwasher at 6 a.m., because that was the only 75 minutes of the day no one in my rented Portland group house needed the kitchen. At the time, I was waiting tables 32 hours a week, editing a friend’s poetry zine for free, and had a recurring panic that I was wasting the last of my mid-20s not being a “real writer”—the kind who had a sunlit garret, a grant, and the luxury of waiting for inspiration to strike before they typed a sentence.

That winter, I’d spent three months stuck on the same 17-page chapter about a lighthouse keeper who couldn’t stop leaving jars of pickles on her dead sister’s porch. I kept waiting for the muse: I went for long rainy walks, reread all my favorite Virginia Woolf passages, even bought an expensive beeswax candle I couldn’t afford to light while I “contemplated tone.” I wrote 114 usable words in those three months. Then, in late January, my roommate Lila—who worked night shifts at a psychiatric ER—started leaving her unwashed ceramic coffee mug in the sink every morning at 5:45, right before she collapsed into bed. I’d stumbled down for a glass of water one Tuesday, tripped over her work boots, found myself staring at the dishwasher, and thought: I might as well load it. If I’m going to stand here waiting for the kettle to boil, I might as well open my laptop.

That’s the lie no one tells you when you’re starting out: inspiration doesn’t show up for people who are waiting for it. It shows up for people who are already doing the boring, unglamorous work of showing up, even when the space is imperfect, even when you haven’t had coffee, even when the story feels like a pile of wet cardboard you’re trying to sculpt into a house. That first morning by the dishwasher, I wrote 427 words. Most of them were bad. The pickles were still bad. But the lighthouse keeper paused while setting a jar down, and noticed a snail crawling up the porch rail, and I realized she wasn’t leaving pickles out of grief—she was leaving them because she was scared her sister would forget the sound of her laughing, the way they’d stolen pickles from their grandma’s pantry as kids. I wouldn’t have found that if I’d been sitting in a garret waiting for it to tap me on the shoulder.

Here’s the practical part, the stuff I still follow 12 years later, even with a home office and a book deal that doesn’t require me to write next to kitchen appliances: stop curating the perfect writing conditions. My routine has no “writerly” rituals: no special pen, no mandatory playlist, no meditation cushion. I write for 75 minutes first thing, before I check email, before I scroll social media, before I remember all the emails I have to answer for my kid’s elementary school PTA. I set a cheap kitchen timer, and I don’t get up until it dings, even if all I’m writing is a list of complaints about how the story isn’t working.

The second rule: the bad words are non-negotiable. Those 400 bad words I wrote that first morning by the dishwasher? They were the scaffolding. I can’t get to the line that makes me cry, that makes me lean back in my chair and think oh, that’s why I’m doing this, unless I wade through 300 lines of garbage first. Inspiration is the reward for writing when you don’t feel like it, not the prerequisite.

I kept that dishwasher routine for 18 months, until I could afford a studio apartment with a desk that didn’t wobble when the heat turned on. Last year, I got a letter from a reader who said the pickle jar scene made her call her own sister, who she hadn’t spoken to in three years. She asked if I’d written it in a burst of divine inspiration. I thought about writing back to tell her about Lila’s coffee mug, about the way the dishwasher would rattle so hard I had to hold my laptop with one hand, about the 114 words I’d labored over for three months before I stopped waiting for the muse to show up. I didn’t, though. I just wrote back and told her that the best scenes never come when you’re waiting for them. They come when you’re already loading the dishwasher, already writing, already there.

title: career advice book|quitting a stable job to do work you care about
text:
You have probably sat at your desk on a Tuesday afternoon, doing work you could do in your sleep, and felt a quiet question rise up: Is this all? The job is stable. The pay is predictable. Your boss likes you, or at least tolerates you. Your benefits are decent, your commute is manageable, and nobody in your family understands why you would ever want to leave. And yet some kind of work keeps calling to you—a cause, a craft, a business, or simply a version of your life that feels more honest than the one you are living now.

Let us start with what this chapter is not. It is not a speech telling you to hand in your resignation tomorrow, cash out your savings, and trust the universe to provide. That is not courage; that is recklessness wearing courage’s clothes. Quitting a stable job to do work you care about is one of the most meaningful decisions you can make, but meaningful does not have to mean impulsive. The goal is not escape. The goal is direction.

First, understand the difference between dissatisfaction and calling. Sometimes the pain is not the work itself but a bad manager, a toxic team, exhaustion, or a season of life that has become too heavy. Before you leave an entire field, ask whether you are running from something specific or toward something real. If you cannot describe the work you want in concrete terms—what you would do each day, who it serves, how it might pay, and why it matters to you—then you may be in love with the idea of freedom rather than prepared for its practice.

Do your imagining before you do your quitting. Start the project on nights and weekends. Take the course. Conduct the interviews. Build the portfolio. Volunteer in the area that interests you. Sell the first service, write the first chapters, make the first prototypes, or meet the first clients. The people who make successful transitions usually do not leap from certainty into blank space. They build a bridge while still standing on solid ground. They test whether the work they romanticize also survives contact with reality.

Get practical in a way that does not embarrass your future self. Know your numbers. How much do you need each month for rent, food, insurance, debt, and basic dignity? How long can you survive without a regular paycheck? A reasonable reserve is not weakness; it is the fuel that lets you make better choices. Desperation often pushes people back into the exact jobs they left. Savings give you patience, and patience is one of the most underrated advantages in meaningful work.

You should also think carefully about identity. A stable job can provide more than money. It gives you status, routine, colleagues, and a ready answer to the question, “What do you do?” When you leave, some of that disappears. You may feel exposed. Some people will not understand. Others will admire you but secretly wait for proof. Do not let either reaction become your compass. Your task is not to perform boldness. Your task is to create work that fits your values and can sustain your life.

When the time comes, leave well. Do not burn down the bridge simply because you are finally crossing a different one. Finish your responsibilities. Tell your employer with respect. Document what you can. Offer a proper transition. The professional world is smaller than it feels, and the people you leave today may become clients, references, partners, or friends tomorrow. Quitting does not require anger; in fact, the cleanest exits are often made by people who have already stopped blaming their old job for their future.

Once you leave, expect a strange mixture of fear and aliveness. Meaningful work is not automatically easy work. It may involve rejection, slow income, confusion, and days when the old stable life looks extremely attractive. That is normal. A calling is not a permanent mood; it is a commitment you return to when the excitement fades.

You do not need certainty to begin. You need evidence, savings, humility, and a plan you can adjust. Stability is a gift, but it can become a cage when it asks you to spend your one life pretending not to want something more. If the work matters enough to prepare for, it may matter enough to pursue. Prepare seriously, move thoughtfully, and when the bridge can hold your weight, walk.

title: leadership memoir by a former CEO|the hiring mistake that nearly sank the company
text:
Let me set the scene: 2017, our little project management startup was flying. We’d just closed a $12M Series A, had 40,000 paying users, and our office had that sparkly “we might actually make it” energy. You know the vibe—cold brew on tap, a rescue dog named Muffin who napped in conference rooms, engineers high-fiving when they fixed a bug at 2 a.m.

I was stretched thinner than a cheap yoga mat. I was doing sales calls, investor updates, approving snack orders, even mediating a fight about whether our weekly lunch should be tacos or sushi (tacos won, obviously). Our head of people pulled me aside one Tuesday and said, “You need a COO. Badly.”

She was right. I’m the idea guy—the guy who rants about bad software in coffee shops and turns those rants into products. I’m not the guy who builds org charts or remembers to file quarterly taxes. So we started the search.

Thirty-seven interviews later, we found him. Let’s call him Chad (because of course his name was Chad). He’d been at a big enterprise software company, wore tailored suits even on casual Fridays, used words like “synergize” and “leverage” without irony. He walked into his final interview and presented a 50-slide deck on “scaling frameworks.” I was dazzled.

I hired him on the spot.

Here’s where I messed up. I was so desperate for someone to take the “boring CEO stuff” off my plate that I didn’t listen to the people who actually knew our company. Our head of engineering, a quiet guy named Raj who’d been with me since we were working out of my garage, pulled me aside after Chad’s team interview. “He kept asking about our ‘exit strategy’,” Raj said. “He didn’t ask a single question about our users.”

I laughed it off. “That’s because he’s a big-picture guy,” I said. “We need that.”

Our customer support lead, Mia, who answered every support ticket personally in the early days, said, “He made fun of our ‘no corporate jargon’ Slack channel. Said it was ‘unprofessional’.”

I waved that away too. “He’ll get used to our weird little culture,” I said.

Spoiler: He did not get used to our weird little culture.

First, he banned Muffin from the office. Said “pets create liability issues.” Then he canceled Taco Tuesday because “it’s a waste of resources that could be allocated to sales outreach.” Then he rolled out a 90-page employee handbook that had rules about “appropriate desk decor” (no funko pops, apparently) and required manager approval for any Slack message sent to more than 10 people.

Worse? He started pushing us to pivot. “Small business users don’t scale,” he’d say in every leadership meeting. “We need to chase enterprise clients. Six-figure contracts. That’s where the real money is.”

I let him. Because I was tired, and he sounded so confident, and I thought that’s what “grown-up CEOs” did—they hired people who knew more than them and got out of the way.

Three months later, our user churn jumped from 3% to 18%. Half our customer support team quit. Raj gave his notice, saying, “This isn’t the company I joined.” Muffin started moping by the front door of my house like she knew something was wrong.

The breaking point came when I got an email from a user named Sarah who’d been with us since we were in beta. She ran a small bookstore in Portland. “I don’t recognize your product anymore,” she wrote. “You used to care about people like me. Now it feels like you’re building software for people who wear suits to work.”

I sat at my desk and cried. Not pretty, snotty crying, the kind where you have to blow your nose on a paper towel because you can’t find a tissue. Then I called an emergency board meeting and fired Chad that afternoon.

It took us 18 months to recover. We brought back Taco Tuesday. We let Muffin come back (and gave her a custom “Chief Morale Officer” bandana). We killed the enterprise pivot and doubled down on small business users. We even added a “jargon jar” where people had to put a dollar every time they said “synergize.” We used the money to buy Muffin fancy dog treats.

Now when I talk to founders about hiring, I tell them three things:

1. If a candidate doesn’t ask about your users in the interview, run. Don’t walk. Run. Anyone who cares more about exit strategies than the people actually using your product will kill what makes your company special.
2. Listen to the quiet people. The ones who don’t give flashy presentations or use big words, the ones who’ve been there since the garage days. They see things you don’t, especially when you’re tired and desperate for help.
3. Culture isn’t about ping pong tables or free snacks. It’s about Muffin the dog and Taco Tuesday and the Slack channel where people make fun of corporate jargon. If someone calls that “unprofessional,” they don’t get to work there.

I still have Sarah’s email printed out and taped to my desk. It’s a reminder that the best hire you’ll ever make isn’t the one with the fanciest resume or the shiniest deck. It’s the person who gets why you started this whole crazy thing in the first place.

(And for the record? Muffin is now retired, but her puppy, Bagel, is our current Chief Morale Officer. She’s even better at her job than Chad was at his.)

title: time-management book|saying no to good opportunities to protect great ones
text:
Chapter 8: Say No to the Good So You Can Say Yes to the Great

Here’s something nobody tells you about success: the closer you get to it, the more dangerous your inbox becomes.

Early in my career, I said yes to everything. I was flattered. Somebody wanted me on a podcast? Yes. Somebody wanted a one-hour “pick your brain” coffee? Yes. A startup wanted me to advise them, a conference wanted a keynote, a nonprofit wanted a board member, a friend wanted feedback on a business plan—yes, yes, yes, yes.

I thought I was being generous. I thought I was building relationships. I thought every open door was an opportunity I was supposed to walk through.

Then one Tuesday, I sat in my kitchen with a calendar that looked like a game of Tetzus played by a toddler. I had seventeen calls that week, three trips, two speeches, and zero uninterrupted time for the book I claimed mattered most. My “great opportunity” was getting the leftover minutes while every “good opportunity” got my best energy.

That’s when the principle clicked: you protect the great by saying no to the good.

Let me tell you about the lunch that changed my mind. A mentor I admired invited me to dinner, and I arrived proud of my busy schedule. I listed projects, partnerships, podcasts, and panels. I expected applause. Instead, she looked at me over her soup and said, “You’re not impressed. You’re scattered.”

Ouch.

Then she asked a question I now ask myself weekly: “Which of these would you invent a reason to do if it weren’t already on your calendar?”

I scanned the list. Most of it was good. Genuinely good. That was the painful part. Bad opportunities are easy to reject. Good opportunities are dangerous because they dress themselves in momentum, politeness, and fear of missing out.

I went home and did something uncomfortable. For the next ninety days, I protected my number one priority: finishing the proposal for a book that could reach people I’d never meet. Every request had to pass one question: *Does this make the great thing more likely, or less?*

Two weeks later, I was invited to speak at a well-known industry summit. Great exposure. Nice people. Nice hotel. Nice badge with my name on it. But preparation would take three full days, plus travel. When I checked my calendar, those three days were the exact block I needed to finish two chapters.

I said no.

The organizer sounded surprised. “Are you sure? This is a really good opportunity.”

“I know,” I said. “That’s why it’s hard.”

That sentence became my shield. Not every no means the request is bad. Some nos mean the request is good—but not priority.

Here’s a practical script you can borrow. When someone invites you to something worthwhile, say: *“Thank you. That sounds meaningful, but I’m protecting a major commitment right now, so I can’t give this the attention it deserves.”* Notice what that does. It honors the opportunity, honors the person, and honors your priority without pretending you have unlimited capacity.

Another example: A former colleague asked me to join an advisory call every month. The company was interesting, the team was talented, and the equity sounded exciting. But when I imagined twelve monthly calls, follow-up emails, and emergency strategy sessions, I realized I’d be renting out my future in small pieces. I declined, but offered one specific introduction instead. It took ten minutes and helped them without chaining me to a calendar I didn’t want.

Saying no is not a lifestyle of refusal. It’s an act of loyalty to what you said yes to already.

Your calendar is a budget, and attention is the currency. Every “maybe” costs something. Every half-yes steals focus. Every polite yes given in weakness becomes a resentful obligation paid in weeks.

So identify your “great.” Name it plainly. Is it launching the business? Finishing the degree? Rebuilding your health? Being present for your family? Writing the album? Growing into the role you’ve been given?

Once you know what it is, opportunities become easier to judge—not by how attractive they are, but by what they protect.

The goal isn’t to do fewer things because ambition is bad. The goal is to do fewer competing things so the right thing has room to become exceptional.

You don’t need more discipline tomorrow morning. You need one honest no today.

Because great opportunities rarely shout. They usually stand quietly behind a closed door you were brave enough to protect.

title: leadership book for new managers|giving honest feedback without crushing morale
text:
Let’s cut the crap first. If you’re here because you think “honest feedback” means sandwiching a gripe between two fake compliments about someone’s Slack emoji game, you’ve already lost half your team before you open your mouth. I once watched a new sales manager at a SaaS startup I consulted for pull a rep aside after a quarter where she missed her quota by 22% and lead with, “I love how you always bring extra coffee to team standups! But… your close rate is garbage. Also, that hoodie you wore to the client call last week? Great color!” That rep quit 10 days later. Took three job offers with her, all from our competitors. The coffee compliment? She told HR later it made her feel like he thought she was a kindergarten kid who needed a sticker before getting a time-out.

Here’s the rule nobody prints in the corporate HR playbooks: people don’t quit over hard feedback. They quit over hard feedback that makes them feel like you don’t see them as a full person, that you’re just waiting to pounce on their mistakes to justify a performance plan. I’ve run numbers on 1,200 manager-direct report pairs across 17 companies over the last eight years. Teams where managers gave unvarnished, specific feedback without the fluffy filler had 32% lower voluntary turnover, and 47% higher self-reported engagement scores, than teams where managers hid criticism behind niceties. Wait, hold on—don’t take that as permission to storm over to someone’s desk and yell that their Q3 report was dogshit. That’s not honesty. That’s being an asshole, and there’s a line thinner than the cheap office printer paper between the two.

Let me tell you what works, because I’ve messed this up enough times to know. Back when I was 26, running my first content team, I had a writer named Javi who kept turning in blog posts that read like he’d pulled them straight from a 2017 Wikipedia dump. I pulled him into a conference room, closed the door, and said, flat out, “These last three posts are unreadable. If you turn in another one like this, we’re going to have to talk about whether this role is a fit.” He sat there, face red, didn’t say a word for 45 seconds, then nodded and walked out. I thought I nailed it! No fluff, straight to the point, clear expectations. Turns out? His mom had been in the ICU for two weeks, he was driving 45 minutes each way to the hospital every night after work, and he’d been pulling all-nighters just to hit his deadlines, too proud to ask for an extension. I didn’t ask. I just dumped my frustration on him, because I was so focused on being “honest” I forgot to be human.

We fixed it, eventually. But that misstep cost us six weeks of his best work, and almost cost us a really talented employee. Here’s the tweak I started using after that, no fancy framework, no acronyms: lead with the specific, verifiable fact first, no judgment, no lead-up. Wait 10 seconds. Let them respond before you say another word. When Javi and I reset, I didn’t lead with a compliment about his great meme game in the team channel. I said, “I noticed the last three posts you turned in had 12+ factual errors each, and the draft for the client case study didn’t include any quotes from the customer success team we talked about last week. That’s not the bar we set for this role. What’s going on?” That’s it. No “but,” no fake praise, no jumping straight to consequences.

You’d be shocked how many people will tell you exactly what’s getting in the way if you don’t immediately put them on defense. Last year I worked with an engineering manager who had a senior dev missing 60% of his sprint commitments for two months. He was this close to putting him on a PIP, until he sat down, skipped the “you’re such a rockstar” opener, laid out the exact ticket numbers that had slipped, and waited. Turns out the dev had been reassigned to help put out three different production fires every week that no one was tracking, because the other two devs on his team were out on parental leave, and he didn’t want to seem like he couldn’t handle it. They adjusted his sprint load, he hit 100% of his commitments the next quarter, and led the team that shipped the feature that drove 18% of the company’s new annual recurring revenue that year.

Don’t get me wrong—sometimes the answer isn’t a caregiving crisis or unassigned work. Sometimes someone is checked out, or cutting corners, or just not a fit for the role. You still don’t need the sandwich. You don’t need to soften the blow so much they walk out of the room not realizing they’re three weeks away from losing their job. I once had a customer support rep who was averaging 4.1/5 on CSAT when the team average was 4.8, and who had 11 instances of closing tickets without resolving the customer’s issue in one month. I sat down, laid out the ticket numbers, the CSAT scores, the exact feedback customers had left, and said, “This isn’t meeting the standard we need for this role. I want to help you get there, but if we don’t see these numbers move up to the team average in 30 days, we’re going to have to part ways.” No fluff, no compliment about how nice he was to the office dog. He didn’t quit. He asked for a shadow schedule with the top rep on the team, put in the work, and 18 months later he’s running the entire support department.

The thing no one tells you about being a new manager is that your team doesn’t need you to be their friend. They don’t need you to be the “nice” boss who never says a hard thing. They need you to be predictable. They need to know that when you pull them aside for feedback, you’re not going to lie to them to spare their feelings, and you’re not going to take a bad day out on them. Stop treating honest feedback like it’s a bomb you have to wrap in cotton balls to keep from blowing up morale. Morale doesn’t die when people know exactly where they stand. Morale dies when people waste six months guessing why you’re mad at them, when they think their hard work is going unnoticed because the only time you talk to them is when something goes wrong, when they find out you’ve been complaining about their work to other people behind their back instead of saying it to their face.

Last stat, then I’ll get off my soapbox: 92% of employees in that same 1,200 person dataset said they’d take corrective feedback over vague praise any day, as long as it was specific, and delivered without personal judgment. So skip the sandwich. Skip the fake small talk about their weekend before you drop the hammer. Just show up, tell the truth, and stay long enough to listen when they talk back.

title: productivity book|single-tasking in a world built for distraction
text:
You sit down to write. Three tabs open, phone face up, a notification glowing like a small emergency. You tell yourself this is how work happens now - responsive, connected, always available. But twenty minutes later you cannot name one thing you have made. You have read six headlines, answered a message that could have waited until Thursday, ordered laundry detergent, and learned how a former classmate felt about the weather. The document remains a blinking accusation.

The world was not arranged by accident. Every application on your screen was designed by very smart people to capture a slice of your finite attention, and those slices are sold, measured, and optimized. Your focus is not drifting because you lack discipline. It is drifting because drifting is the intended outcome of the system. The first relief of single-tasking is the relief of blame: you are not weak. You are outnumbered.

But you are not powerless. Single-tasking is not a retreat from modern life. It is the deliberate practice of placing one thing at the center of your mind and refusing to let the rest of the world climb onto the table. It sounds almost too simple, because simplicity is precisely what makes it difficult. You have grown accustomed to the comforting friction of multiple demands. Busyness has become a costume you wear to prove your importance.

Begin by choosing one task. Not a category, not a role, not an intention large enough to hide inside. One task. Draft the introduction. Review the contract. Cook dinner without a lecture in your headphones. Listen to your friend without planning your reply. If the task would look ridiculous written on a sign above your head, it is still too vague. Make it small enough that your mind can close around it.

Then set a boundary that exists in the physical world. Close the door. Put the phone in another room, not face down on the desk, because face down still belongs to you and you still belong to it. Set a timer for twenty-five minutes if timers help, but do not worship the number. The purpose is not to achieve an impressive duration. The purpose is to create a protected interval during which the task is allowed to be enough.

Your mind will rebel. It will offer urgent questions. What did that email say? What is that noise? Is that symptom serious? Should you book the flight now before prices rise? These are not genuine emergencies. They are withdrawal sensations dressed as responsibility. Write each interruption on a piece of paper beside you and return. The paper performs a quiet miracle: it proves the thought can wait without disappearing. Most of what felt essential at minute three will seem trivial at minute twenty-three.

Do not confuse single-tasking with slowness, though slowness may arrive as one of its rewards. It is often the fastest way to work because error decreases, rework shrinks, and the costly ramp-up between tasks disappears. Every switch demands a tax. You may not see the tax when you glance at a message for nine seconds, but you pay it during the minutes afterward as your brain searches for the road back to the thought it was carrying. Returning is work. Protecting yourself from unnecessary return is strategy.

Single-tasking also changes what you notice. When you walk without a podcast, the walk begins to speak. When you eat without a screen, taste returns. When you speak to someone without divided attention, they can feel the difference immediately, and so can you. Attention is not merely a tool for production. It is the substance of how you spend a life. An hour fully given to one thing is larger than an hour shattered across ten.

You will fail often. The habit is not a destination but a daily re-entry. Notice the scatter without drama, gently collect yourself, and begin again. That recovery is the practice. Every time you return, you strengthen the muscle that says no to the noise and yes to the matter at hand.

Tonight, choose one thing. Let everything else wait its turn. The world will continue without your supervision. Your work will not.

title: writing-craft memoir|the daily routine of a working novelist
text:
I used to think novelists spent their days draped across velvet chaises, sipping single-malt scotch and waiting for the muse to tap them on the shoulder with a perfectly turned metaphor. That was before I sold my first book, back when my biggest professional deadline was getting a TikTok about bad book boyfriends up before 7pm so it would hit the algorithm sweet spot. Now I’m three years and two novels in, and my “muse” is a 12-pound tabby named Mochi who chews through my laptop charger if I don’t give her a treat at 9:15am sharp.
I wake up at 7, no alarms, because Mochi has decided that’s the exact minute my bladder is a perfectly acceptable trampoline. I don’t check my phone first. Wait, no—let me be honest. I check my phone first, but only for 10 minutes, strictly to scroll cat rescue accounts and delete the 47 PR emails asking me to promote weight loss gummies to my bookish audience. If I open Twitter before I’ve had two sips of coffee, I will see a take so bad (“all third person POV is elitist”) that I’ll waste three hours drafting a subtweet instead of hitting my word count. I learned that the hard way.
