I do my writing in 45-minute sprint blocks, no exceptions, because my attention span was permanently deep-fried by six years of making 15-second social media content. I used to brag I could knock out 2,000 words in a single sitting if I was “in the zone,” until I realized those “zone” sessions were 70% me scrolling Zillow for fictional character apartments and 30% writing sentences that sounded good in the moment but made me cringe so hard the next day I’d delete the whole chapter.
I have three non-negotiable rules for these sprints, the kind I used to mock when fancy MFA authors posted them on Substack:
1. No internet on my writing laptop. I installed a blocker that locks me out of every site except my Google Doc, and I gave the password to my best friend who lives three time zones away. The last time I begged her for it mid-sprint because I “needed to fact-check what kind of snack a 1998 skateboarder would eat,” she made me Venmo her $20 before she sent it, then texted me a meme of a raccoon in a trash can that said “u are not researching u are procrastinating.” She was right. The snack was Cheetos. I already knew that.
2. I don’t save the “good lines” for later. I used to hoard pretty turns of phrase in a notes app, convinced I needed to save them for a “better scene,” until I had 400 disconnected lines and zero finished chapters. Now if a line pops into my head about the way my protagonist’s mom burns toast every Sunday, I write it right into the scene I’m working on, even if that scene is a high-stakes car chase. Turns out the toast detail makes the car chase hit harder, because you remember the guy driving has a mom who burns toast. Who knew?
3. I stop when the timer goes off, even if I’m mid-sentence. I used to write until I ran out of steam, which meant I’d end days stuck on a dead end, staring at a half-written paragraph with no clue how to move forward. Stopping mid-sentence means when I sit down the next day, I don’t have to ramp up from zero—I just finish the thought, and I’m already rolling. It’s the same trick I used to use for blog posts, back when I’d leave a half-written joke at the end of a draft so I had a reason to come back and finish it the next morning.
People always ask if I miss blogging, if the rigid routine of novel-writing kills the fun of making things up. It doesn’t. The fun isn’t in the chaise or the scotch or the viral take. It’s in the boring, repeated bits: the 9:15 cat treat, the $20 Venmo fines, the half-written sentences waiting for me when I sit down, the way a throwaway line about burnt toast can make a whole scene feel real. Yesterday I wrote a scene where my protagonist cries over a broken coffee maker, and it was better than any viral tweet I ever posted, because I didn’t write it for likes. I wrote it because my own coffee maker broke last week, and I cried over it too.

title: motivational book|achieving long-term goals by managing your energy, not your time
text:
Chapter 7: Your Calendar Is Lying to You — Energy Is the Real Currency
I used to wear my 5 a.m. wake-up like a badge of honor. Back when I was building my first side business while working a full-time sales job, I mapped every 15 minutes of my day like a drill sergeant. 6:00 to 7:30 a.m.: draft client proposals. 12:00 to 12:45 p.m.: film social media content. 8:00 to 10:00 p.m.: answer emails and tweak my website. I’d stare at my color-coded planner on Sunday nights, convinced I’d cracked the code to quitting my job within a year.
Three months in, I was burnt to a crisp. I’d sit at my kitchen table at 5:15 a.m., coffee gone cold, staring at a blank proposal draft for 40 minutes before typing three garbage sentences. I’d film “motivational” reels on my lunch break while slouching against a office bathroom stall, my eyes glazed over, and re-record the same line 17 times because my brain felt like it was stuffed with cotton. Worst of all, I started resenting the business I’d once daydreamed about. My calendar said I had 20 hours a week to pour into my goal. My body and brain were showing up with about two good hours, max.
That’s when my mentor Rita, a 72-year-old former marathon runner who built three successful businesses after raising four kids, laughed at my crammed planner over lunch. “Honey,” she said, pushing my notebook away, “you don’t manage your way to a big goal by counting minutes. You manage your energy. Time ticks the same for everyone. Your energy? That’s the stuff you actually get to spend.”
Most of us treat our energy like it’s a flat, constant battery, right? We assume every hour holds the same value. But I tested Rita’s advice for two weeks, and it flipped everything upside down.
First, I stopped forcing deep work at 5 a.m. I’d spent years telling myself I was a “morning person,” but the truth was, I rolled out of bed groggy, skipped breakfast, and dragged myself through the first two hours of my day. Instead, I used those slow first 30 minutes to walk around my neighborhood, eat a protein-heavy breakfast, and listen to dumb comedy podcasts. I saved my proposal writing for 9:30 to 11:00 a.m. at work — the window where I’d historically crushed sales calls, when my focus was sharpest. I got more high-quality work done in those 90 minutes than I’d squeezed out of three whole early mornings.
Then I stopped treating my lunch break like a content marathon. I split it: 20 minutes to film two short reels, back when I felt chatty and energized after talking to teammates, and the other 25 minutes I sat outside and ate without scrolling. Before, I’d trudge back to my desk feeling more drained than before I took a break. After? I’d knock out my afternoon admin work twice as fast, freeing up mental space I didn’t know I had.
I also built in tiny, deliberate energy refills instead of waiting until I crashed. I used to power through 90-minute stretches answering emails at night, slouched on my couch, until I’d pass out mid-sentence. Now I set a 25-minute timer, and after every work block, I do one thing that actually recharges me: play fetch with my terrier Muffin for five minutes, do three silly dance moves to my favorite 2000s pop song, or even just stand on my balcony and breathe fresh air. Those little stops don’t “waste time.” They keep my battery from hitting zero.
Within six months, I hit my revenue goal to quit my job three weeks early. I didn’t add a single extra hour to my weekly schedule. I just stopped spending my best energy on meaningless busywork, and stopped forcing my worst energy to do hard things.
Long-term goals aren’t won by who has the most hours in a day. They’re won by showing up with your best energy, one well-matched task at a time. Stop worshipping your to-do list. Start checking in with your battery.

title: leadership memoir by a former CEO|the hiring mistake that nearly sank the company
text:
Excerpt from *Scrappy: How We Built, Nearly Broke, and Salvaged PipeWrench* (2024)
Let’s cut the crap: I hired Jake because he made me feel like less of a rube.
It was 2019. We’d just hit $42 million in ARR selling industrial pipe sensors to oil and gas outfits out of a cinder-block office in Tulsa, 127 employees, no HR department to speak of, just a part-time bookkeeper who brought pecan fudge to all-hands and yelled at anyone who printed more than two pages a day. Our lead engineer, Ray—guy who’d built the first prototype in his garage over three cases of Coors Light—was burning out. We’d already blown two VC offers because the partners kept side-eyeing my worn work boots like I didn’t know a P&L from a PVC joint. I was tired of being the scrappy guy. I wanted to look like a real CEO.
Jake blew into the interview in a tailored Tom Ford blazer, Harvard MBA, 11 years at GE Digital, talked a mile a minute about “scalable org design” and “churn reduction flywheels” and “enterprise value unlock.” He didn’t even flinch when Ray showed up late in a grease-stained Carhartt, muttering about a fried sensor out in the Permian. Afterward, our head of sales, Marisol, pulled me aside and said, “That guy’s never held a wrench in his life. He’ll eat us alive.” I laughed it off. Told her we needed to grow up.
I paid him $325k base, 1.2% equity, a $50k signing bonus, gave him the COO title, told him to fix the operational mess I didn’t have the patience for.
First 90 days, it felt like magic. He rolled out OKRs. Got us a real enterprise Slack plan instead of the free tier we’d been freeloading on for three years. Hired three recruiters, talked the board into greenlighting a 40-person headcount expansion across sales and account management. The VCs stopped giving me the side-eye. I started getting invited to speak at SaaS conferences. Bought a stupid custom suit. Felt like I’d finally made it.
Then the cracks showed.
Jake fired Ray three days before Christmas. Said he was a “cultural misfit” who resisted process. I found out when Ray texted me a photo of the cardboard box he was carrying out to his truck, snow sticking to his flannel. I was in Aspen, at a CEO retreat, halfway through a overpriced cabernet, and I just… didn’t call him back. Told myself Jake knew what he was doing. That we couldn’t let one guy hold the whole company back.
Six weeks later, our biggest client—Chevron, 21% of our annual revenue, the contract that had kept us afloat when we were three months from missing payroll in 2017—sent a termination notice. Their custom sensor fleet had been glitching for three weeks, all the new support reps Jake had hired were reading off scripts no one had vetted, and there wasn’t a single engineer left who knew how the legacy code worked. Ray had written 70% of that code. The new engineering lead Jake hired had spent his last job building yoga class booking apps.
The numbers got ugly fast. Churn spiked to 18% a month. We burned through $1.9 million in cash in Q1 2020, right as COVID hit and every oil and gas client froze their budgets. We had 21 days of operating cash left when I finally pulled the plug on Jake’s whole little empire. I walked into his corner office—he’d demanded we build it for him when he started, took out a wall to put in a floor-to-ceiling whiteboard he never used—and told him he was out. He had the nerve to ask for a 12-month severance. I told him he’d be lucky if I didn’t sue him for negligence.
I drove out to Ray’s house that night. He was on his porch, grilling brats, drinking a Coors Light, same as always. He didn’t even say I told you so. Just handed me a beer, said he’d come back if we fired every last one of Jake’s leadership hires, nixed the OKRs, and let him run engineering his way. I didn’t argue.
I sat on that porch for two hours, watching smoke curl off the grill, thinking about how I’d almost thrown away six years of 18-hour days, of sleeping on the office couch during launch weeks, of pecan fudge from the bookkeeper, all because I’d wanted some guy in a fancy suit to make me feel like I belonged in the big leagues. The wind was coming off the Arkansas River, cold enough to make my ears burn, and I couldn’t even look Ray in the eye when he said he’d draw up a plan to fix the Chevron sensors by the end of the week.
We didn’t make payroll that month. I took out a second mortgage on my house, sold the stupid custom suit, dumped the enterprise Slack plan. Marisol drove out to Chevron’s Midland office with a cooler of Oklahoma craft beer and a handwritten apology, sat in their lobby for seven hours until the operations VP would see her.
(Word count: 598)

title: self-improvement book|dealing with procrastination and perfectionism
text:
Chapter 3: The Unfinished Manuscript – When “Perfect” Becomes the Enemy of “Done”
Three years ago, I sat at my kitchen table with a half-written book proposal, a blank document labeled “FINAL DRAFT (NO MORE EDITS),” and a growing pit in my stomach. I’d spent six months polishing the first 10 pages: tweaking sentences until they sang, rearranging paragraphs at 2 a.m., even reworking the opening line 47 times (I counted). The rest of the proposal? Ninety pages of scattered notes, half-baked arguments, and voice memos I’d never transcribed. I told myself I was “striving for excellence.” What I was actually doing was hiding.
I’d landed a book deal two years prior on the strength of a messy, passionate 20-page sample—one I’d banged out in three weeks between client sessions, no second-guessing. But when the time came to deliver the full proposal, perfectionism wrapped its familiar hand around my throat. What if the rest wasn’t as good as the opening? What if publishers laughed at my unpolished ideas? What if I turned in something “good enough” and it proved I was a fraud? So I procrastinated: I deep-cleaned the fridge, reorganized my bookshelf by color, took on three extra clients, and told anyone who asked that I was “taking my time to get it right.”
The wake-up call came when my agent emailed, gentle but firm: “The editors love your voice. They don’t need perfect. They need the rest of the story.” I realized then that my “pursuit of perfection” wasn’t about quality—it was about fear. Procrastination was my safety blanket: if I never turned in imperfect work, no one could reject it. Perfectionism gave me a socially acceptable excuse to avoid vulnerability.
If you’ve ever stalled on a work project because you didn’t know where to start, rewritten a text three times before sending it, or put off a hobby because you “weren’t good at it yet,” you know this cycle. The good news? You don’t have to choose between “perfect” and “slacking.” You just have to learn to ship the messy version. Here’s what pulled me out of my spiral—and what I still use today.
 The 20-Minute “Garbage First” Draft
Perfectionism demands that your first attempt be your best. Reverse the rule: give yourself 20 minutes to write, draft, or build the worst possible version of the task you’re avoiding. When I restarted my proposal, I set a timer and typed, “This part is about how procrastination isn’t laziness—it’s fear. I don’t know how to prove it yet, but I have a client story about a teacher who graded papers late.” It was clunky, full of gaps, and objectively bad. But it was something. Perfectionism can’t argue with a task you’ve already labeled garbage—and once you have raw material, editing feels far less scary than creating from nothing.
 Lower the “Success Bar” for the First Step
We procrastinate when our brain sees a task as too big, too vague, or too high-stakes. My mistake was framing my daily goal as “write a perfect book chapter.” Instead, I started setting absurdly small, non-negotiable goals: open the document and type one sentence. Pull one client quote from my notes. Write three bullet points for the conclusion. On my hardest days, I only did that one tiny step. But 80% of the time, once I’d crossed that ultra-low bar, I kept going. Perfectionism hates small, unimpressive wins—but those wins stack into finished work.
 Schedule a “Hard Stop” for Polishing
For tasks where quality matters, set a strict time limit for edits before you even start. For my proposal, I gave myself two hours total to revise each section: one hour for structural tweaks, 30 minutes for line edits, 30 minutes to fact-check. When the timer went off, I hit save and walked away. I also adopted a “two sets of eyes” rule: I only asked one trusted peer to review a draft, not three (a trap I’d fallen into before, chasing endless feedback to avoid finalizing). The goal isn’t to make work flawless—it’s to make it good enough to share, then improve it later if you need to.
I turned in that proposal three weeks later. It had awkward sentences, underdeveloped sections, and a conclusion I still wanted to rework. But the editors offered me the contract. One told me, “The messy parts felt human. The polished opening felt like you were trying too hard.”
Perfectionism promises you safety: if you never release imperfect work, you’ll never fail, never be judged, never feel like you’re not enough. But it also robs you of the chance to be seen, to grow, and to finish the things that matter. Done isn’t the opposite of excellent. It’s the only way excellence ever gets the chance to exist.
(Word count: 698)

title: personal finance book|negotiating a raise and why most people never ask
text:
Let me cut to the chase: I left $14,200 on the table at my first corporate job because I was scared to ask for a raise.
I know the exact number because I found the pay band spreadsheet in a shared drive three months after I quit, right after I’d cried in my Honda Civic for 20 minutes because I couldn’t afford to fix the AC that blew only hot air in 90-degree Atlanta summers. For two years, I’d stayed late every Thursday to fix my boss’s botched client reports, trained three new hires who got hired at $5k more than me, and brought in two small accounts that added $70k in annual revenue. And I never said a word.
Why? Because I’d bought the lie we all get fed: if I just worked hard enough, someone would notice. Someone would tap me on the shoulder, slide a better offer across the desk, and reward my grind without me having to make a fuss.
Spoiler: No one is keeping track of your grind like you are.
A 2023 Glassdoor survey found 60% of workers never negotiate a raise, ever. I get it. I’ve been the person practicing the ask in the shower for three weeks, then bailing the second my boss asked “how’s it going?” by rambling about the office coffee being weird that week. We’re scared we’ll sound greedy. We’re scared they’ll say no. We’re scared we’ll get fired for even asking (pro tip: you won’t. If they fire you for asking to be paid fairly, that job was a ticking time bomb anyway).
I finally worked up the nerve to ask at my next job, after a friend who worked in HR told me the company budgeted 3-5% annual raises for people who didn’t ask, and 10-15% for people who came with receipts. I spent three nights putting together a one-page doc: the social media campaigns I’d run that grew engagement 40%, the client who specifically asked to work with me, the process I built that cut our weekly meeting time in half. I didn’t lead with “I need more money because my rent went up.” I led with “Here’s the extra value I’ve delivered that’s above the job description I was hired for, and here’s the number that matches that value.”
I got a 12% raise, plus a $1k one-time bonus. I cried in my car again, but this time it was because I could finally afford to replace the broken passenger side window that had been held together with duct tape for six months.
If you’re sitting there sweating just thinking about having that conversation, let me give you the three no-BS rules I’ve used every time since, that have helped me and hundreds of my blog readers lock in raises without awkwardness:
1. Never ask out of the blue. Time the convo for right after a win: when you just closed that big client, when that project you led launched to great feedback, when your boss just sang your praises in a team meeting. Don’t wait for annual review season, when budgets are already locked in.
2. Come with receipts, not feelings. Your rent going up, your student loans being due, your cat needing expensive vet bills? Those are your problems, not your employer’s. The only thing that matters is the extra value you deliver that they aren’t paying you for yet. Keep a running folder of wins, kudos from clients or coworkers, and metrics that move the needle, so you don’t have to scramble to remember them when it’s time to talk.
3. Ask for a specific number, not “more money.” Studies show people who ask for a precise, targeted number (say, $82,500 instead of $80k) get higher offers, because it signals you’ve done your research and know your worth. Look up pay bands for your role on Glassdoor, Levels.fyi, or even by asking a few trusted coworkers what they make (yes, it’s legal to talk about pay in the US, and no, it’s not rude).
Here’s the thing no one tells you: the worst that happens is they say no. And if they say no? You just got free intel that it’s time to start looking for a job that will pay you what you’re worth, instead of wasting another year grinding for a company that sees you as a line item instead of the person keeping the lights on.
I still get a little nervous before I have these conversations, by the way. Last year I practiced my ask while walking my dog around the block so many times he started giving me judgmental side-eye when I rambled about campaign ROI. But the 10 minutes of awkwardness is worth thousands of dollars a year, every year, that compounds into down payments, vacations, and not having to choose between fixing your car AC and buying groceries. Stop waiting for someone to notice your work. They’re busy noticing their own work. It’s your job to advocate for the person who shows up for you every day: you.
(Word count: 598)

title: startup memoir|the early days of a search-engine company and its odd culture
text:
The first rule of SearchNook, the search-engine startup I joined above a laundromat in Palo Alto, was simple: never trust a desk that faced the wall.

I learned this on a Tuesday in April 2007, when I showed up wearing a button-down shirt and carrying a leather notebook. The office had no receptionist, no logo, and, as far as I could tell, no adults. A man in socks was kneeling beside a server rack, feeding a goldfish. Nearby, three engineers argued over whether the perfect search result should feel like a librarian, a blackjack dealer, or a dog carrying a slipper.

“You’re the marketing guy?” the sock man asked.

I said I was.

“Great. Marketing is now your problem. Also, the fridge is sacred. Don’t move Maya’s chia drink.”

That was Dane, the founder. He had dropped out of two PhD programs and spoke about web crawlers the way other people spoke about childhood summers. His theory was that search was not really technology. It was psychology, religion, and customer service, with occasional math.

The company culture made no sense, which is probably why it worked for a while.

We had stand-up meetings at 11:11 every morning, because Dane believed arbitrary timekeeping “kept people alert.” Anyone late had to bring breakfast for the team. The breakfast could not be boring. Plain bagels were considered an insult. One engineer, Paulo, arrived eleven minutes late after an all-night crawl failure and brought seven flavors of pudding. Dane called it “a masterpiece of accountability.”

The office itself looked like a garage sale held inside a spaceship. Whiteboards covered every wall, covered in diagrams, index-size formulas, and hostile notes to future ourselves: “Latency is a mood,” “Stop ranking spam,” “Why is a candle site winning?” Desks moved constantly. If your code caused an outage, your chair got relocated closer to the dryer vents downstairs. It was childish, inconvenient, weirdly effective.

My first project was writing a company slogan. I proposed “Find Everything Faster.”

Dane looked physically pained.

“That sounds like a truck with a website,” he said.

So I sat among the engineers and watched users try our prototype. A retired nurse searched for her cat’s symptoms and got medical journals, a pet forum, and an ad for industrial refrigerators. A high-school kid typed “why do hands look weird” and found a philosophy paper, a guitar lesson, and a Reddit argument about mittens. The web was already infinite. The hard part was not finding pages. It was understanding the trembling human behind the query.

That became our odd obsession. Every Friday, the entire company answered support tickets. Dane insisted. Even our infrastructure lead, a quiet woman named Priya who could debug load balancers without opening her eyes, had to answer emails from confused users. One man wrote from Winnipeg to say our search engine had helped him locate a replacement part for a 1994 rice cooker. He included a photograph. We printed it and taped it beside a server. For months, that rice cooker was the closest thing we had to a mission statement.

Not everything was charming. Money ran low in autumn. The fancy coffee vanished first, then the snacks, then the pretense that payroll was guaranteed. Dane stopped shaving. Paulo began writing code by candlelight during a planned power saving period, not because it was romantic, but because he refused to go home. Priya calculated runway on a napkin and said, “We have until Thanksgiving, or possibly the afterlife.”

Yet there was a strange innocence to those months. We believed every query deserved dignity. We believed speed was kindness. We also believed, with remarkable confidence, that office decisions could be settled by rock-paper-scissors, provided the loser updated the documentation nobody read.

By winter, our little search engine had grown faster and stranger. Queries began returning answers that felt almost intuitive. The team celebrated with cold pizza and a ceremonial ranking of pizza-related websites. A local pizzeria came in first, which Dane called proof of intelligence. A national chain threatened to sue, which he called proof of impact.

Looking back, the laundromat years were less a business plan than a collective fever dream. But somewhere between the sacred chia drink, the pudding fines, and the rice cooker photograph, we stumbled onto something true: building search was never about mastering machines. It was about understanding people in their most impatient, unpolished, searching moments.

And if that required socks, servers, and an unhealthy amount of dried fish food, so be it.

title: personal finance book|negotiating a raise and why most people never ask
text:
Let’s cut the crap. 70% of people who ask for a raise get one. That’s not a stat from some bro finance TikTok bro—that’s from Glassdoor’s 2024 employee survey, pulled from 160,000 real worker responses across every industry from warehouse ops to SaaS sales. You know how many people actually ask? 35%.
Do the math. That means almost two out of three of you are leaving free, earned money on the table because your throat goes tight when you walk past your manager’s office.
Don’t give me that “the economy is bad” line. I asked for a 12% raise in 2009, when our company was laying off 10% of the department every quarter. I walked in with a one-page list: 18% of the quarter’s new client upsells came from accounts I’d fixed after the last account rep bailed, I’d trained the two new hires who were already outperforming their 90-day targets by 30%, I’d stayed late 19 nights in three months to fix the broken client report template no one else would touch, and that mess had been costing the team 5 collective hours a week. I didn’t say “I think I deserve more money.” I said “Here’s exactly how much value I’ve delivered above my job description in the last six months, here’s market rate for someone doing this work in this city, which is 15% higher than my current pay, and I’d like to lock in a 12% raise effective next pay period, plus a $1,500 bonus for wrapping up that template project early.”
I got the 12%. I got the bonus. My manager later told me half the team was complaining about being underpaid over Slack, but no one else had brought a single concrete number to a conversation that year.
Most of you won’t ask because you’re scared of awkwardness. Not scared of being fired—wait, let’s kill that boogeyman right now: less than 2% of people who ask for a reasonable, evidence-backed raise face any negative repercussions at work. No demotions, no cold shoulders, no being first on the layoff list. That’s not my opinion, that’s data from Wharton’s 2023 workplace dynamics study. You’re not scared of consequence. You’re scared of 10 minutes of slightly weird energy with the person who signs your timesheet. You’ll spend three hours scrolling Zillow and seething that you can’t afford the apartment with the in-unit laundry, but you won’t spend 45 minutes prepping a one-page document of your wins because that would mean having to say the words “I’d like to discuss my compensation” out loud in a closed room.
I had a friend, a graphic designer making $72k a year at a DTC sock brand, who spent two years venting to me over happy hour beers that she was underpaid. She redesigned their entire packaging line, which drove a 22% lift in Amazon sales in six months. She trained the intern who ended up running their whole TikTok account. When I told her to ask for $85k, she froze. Said “What if they think I’m greedy? What if they say no and then treat me differently?” She waited six more months, got a 3% “cost of living” raise that didn’t even cover the year’s rent hike, and left for a $92k job at a competing brand three months later. Her manager told her during the exit interview, “We would have matched that if you’d asked. We didn’t know you were unhappy.”
Don’t do that performative “well if they valued me they’d just pay me” garbage. Your boss is not your mom. They are not sitting around noticing all the little extra things you do, keeping a running tally of your wins so they can cut you a bigger check out of the goodness of their heart. Their job is to keep labor costs as low as possible to hit their own quarterly bonus, same as your job is to pay as little as possible for a gallon of milk or oil change without getting ripped off. They’re not evil. They’re just busy. They’re managing 12 people, putting out three fires a day, forgetting half the stuff their own boss asks them to do by lunch. They will never, in a million years, care as much about your bank account as you do.
Wait, let’s get specific about the other dumb reason people don’t ask: they wait for the “right time.” There is no right time. You don’t have to wait for performance review week. You don’t have to wait until you have 100 wins lined up. You don’t have to wait until you’re so burnt out you’re secretly scrolling LinkedIn on company time during team meetings. The right time is when you can point to three specific, measurable things you’ve done that made or saved the company more money than the raise you’re asking for.
I know a guy in commercial construction who thought he had to wait until he’d been at the company five years to ask for more pay. He’d been there 18 months when he noticed the crew was wasting $800 a week on misordered lumber because no one was cross-checking the delivery manifests against the project blueprints. He fixed the process in two weeks, saved the company $41,000 in a single quarter, walked in and asked for a $5 an hour raise (that works out to $10,400 a year, for the math averse). He got it on the spot. His foreman told him, “I didn’t even realize that waste was that bad until you brought it up.”
Stop treating your pay like some kind of reward for being a polite, uncomplaining worker bee. It’s a number, negotiated between two people who both want the best deal for themselves. The worst thing that happens is they say no. If they say no, you get to ask exactly what you need to do to get that raise in three months, get that list in writing, and then either do it and get the money, or take that exact same one-page win sheet to the next company that will pay you what you’re worth.
I’ve had people tell me “But I’m bad at negotiating!” Cool. So was I the first time. My voice cracked when I said the number. I was so nervous I forgot to mention one of my biggest wins, the client I’d saved from churning right before renewal. I still got the raise. No one cares if you’re smooth. They care if you’re right.
You know who never gets a raise without asking? People who wait for someone to notice how hard they work. People who think bringing donuts to the team meeting once a month is a substitute for hard numbers that prove you’re worth more. People who’d rather leave $10k, $15k, $20k on the table every single year than deal with 10 minutes of awkward conversation.

title: personal finance book|negotiating a raise and why most people never ask
text:
Chapter 7: The Question That Stays Stuck in Your Throat

Let me take you back to a fluorescent-lit conference room in Chicago, 2014. I had spent nine months rebuilding a broken client onboarding process, training two new hires who were originally assigned to a different manager, and quietly covering half my boss’s work while she cared for a sick parent. Our team had beaten every quarterly target by wide margins. My performance review opened with the words “exceed expectations,” and my raise: 3%. A cost-of-living bump, dressed up as a reward.

I nodded politely, said thank you, and walked back to my desk with a strange burning sensation behind my eyes. For two weeks I rehearsed a negotiation conversation in the shower, on the train, even while microwaving lunch. I never had it. I told myself stories: *The budget is fixed. My boss will think I’m greedy. Maybe I’m just lucky to have a job.* Then a colleague in a similar role left for a competitor making 22% more. That was the day I understood: the company was never going to voluntarily pay me what I was worth just because I deserved it. I had to make the ask.

Most people never negotiate their salary, and the reasons are rarely about logic. Surveys of working professionals consistently find that only about 30–40% of employees ever negotiate a starting offer or a raise, even though a large majority of employers expect some back-and-forth and leave room in their initial number. Women and people of color negotiate at even lower rates, partly because of very real social penalties—assertiveness is often judged differently depending on who displays it. But underneath the demographics sits a universal tangle of fears: fear of conflict, fear of seeming ungrateful, fear that asking will somehow put the job itself at risk.

Here is the reframe that changed everything for me: a salary negotiation is not a confrontation. It is a business conversation about the value you already deliver. Companies do not pay people based on effort, seniority, or how many years they have been loyal. They pay to retain someone whose departure would create measurable pain. Your job is to document that pain in calm, specific language before you ever walk into the room.

Start with a brag file, not a list of grievances. Keep a running document of outcomes you can quantify: revenue added, costs cut, hours saved, clients retained, projects delivered ahead of schedule, problems solved before they reached your manager. When I finally negotiated my next role, I walked in with a one-page summary: rebuilt onboarding had cut client churn by an estimated 18%, I was managing three accounts worth $2.4 million, and I had trained four people. None of these were feelings. They were evidence.

Next, anchor to a market number, not a percentage increase over your current pay. Use Levels.fyi, Glassdoor, industry salary surveys, and—most powerfully—casual conversations with peers and recruiters. When a recruiter told me my skill set commanded $95,000 while I was earning $72,000, the ask stopped feeling arrogant and started feeling factual. Aim for the top of the realistic range; the person who names a specific, well-researched number first usually pulls the final outcome toward it.

Timing matters more than most people realize. Ask after a visible win, not during a bad week. Schedule a dedicated conversation; never spring a raise discussion on your manager in a hallway. Frame it around the future, not the past: “Here’s what I’ve delivered, here’s what I’m ready to take on, and I’d like to align my compensation with that scope.”

If the answer is no, make it a beginning, not a dead end. Ask what specific milestones would justify the number you want, and when the company can revisit it. Get it in writing. If six months pass, you hit every target, and nothing changes, the conversation has quietly become about your exit plan—which is itself leverage, but only if you are genuinely prepared to walk.

That 3% raise I never challenged cost me far more than the few thousand dollars that year. Because raises compound, and future offers often anchor to prior pay, one unmade ask can echo through a decade of earnings. The person across the table negotiates budgets every day. They are not nervous. Give yourself the same permission.

title: personal memoir with life lessons|a year of travel after a painful divorce
text:
You don’t pack for a year of travel the way you pack for a vacation, not when the divorce papers are still warm in your kitchen drawer and the ring indent on your left finger hasn’t quite faded. You throw in the frayed hiking boots you bought on a whim three years earlier, the ones your ex said were “too rugged for date nights,” the tattered copy of Mary Oliver poems you hid on the top shelf of your closet because he teased you for reading “sad tree poetry,” and a stack of postcards you have no intention of mailing. You leave the good china, the framed wedding photos, the couch you picked out together for the new renters who don’t know the way he used to leave half-drunk coffee mugs on the armrest until the wood stained. You lock the door behind you and don’t look back, not because you’re strong, but because if you stay, you’ll dissolve into the carpet that still holds the echo of the fight that ended it all.

The first month, you sleep on a friend’s couch in Lisbon, and you cry so hard into a plate of pasteis de nata that the old lady at the next table slides you an extra espresso and pats your hand without saying a word. You think you’ll never stop feeling that sharp, hollow ache under your ribs, the one that makes you flinch when a couple holds hands on the tram, that makes you reach for your phone to text him a photo of the sunset before you remember you blocked his number. You walk until your feet blister, because if you keep moving, you can’t sit still long enough to unpack the anger and the grief and the quiet, shameful relief that you don’t say out loud to anyone.

You learn the first lesson outside a tiny village in the Scottish Highlands, when the rain comes out of nowhere and soaks you to the bone halfway up a hill, and you huddle under a pine tree next to a shepherd who offers you a sip of whiskey from a dented flask. He doesn’t ask why you’re traveling alone, doesn’t say you’ll “find yourself” like all the cheesy Instagram captions promise. He just says the rain never lasts forever, even when it feels like the sky’s forgotten how to stop. You sit there for 40 minutes, cold and shivering, and when the sun breaks through, it paints the heather purple so bright it hurts your eyes, and you realize you haven’t thought about the divorce for a full hour.

The second lesson hits you in a market in Oaxaca, when you fumble through terrible high school Spanish to ask for tamales, and the vendor laughs and pulls you behind her stall to show you how to fold the corn husks right, her granddaughter braiding daisies into your hair while you work. You’d spent 12 years in that marriage shaping yourself to fit what he said you should be: quieter, neater, less likely to get flour on your shirt when you cook, less eager to talk to strangers. For the first time, you don’t feel like you have to shrink to take up less space. You eat three tamales standing up, grease on your chin, and you don’t apologize for it.

There are hard nights, of course. The night you get food poisoning in a hostel in Hanoi and throw up for six hours straight, no one there to hold your hair back. The night in New Zealand when you camp under the stars and suddenly feel so lonely you can’t breathe, because for a second you wish someone was there to see the Milky Way with you, and then you realize you don’t need that someone to be him. You hike a volcano at dawn, you learn to surf badly and wipe out a hundred times, you dance to bad reggaeton in a beach bar in Costa Rica with a group of backpackers you’ll never see again, and slowly, the indent on your finger fades.

When you get home 12 months later, you don’t move back into that old house. You rent a tiny apartment with a fire escape where you can grow tomatoes, you hang the Mary Oliver poems above the stove, you buy a set of chipped mugs from a thrift store that don’t match, because you don’t care about matching anymore. You learn that travel doesn’t fix you. It doesn’t erase the hurt, or the years you spent loving someone who didn’t love all of you. What it does is show you how much of you was still there, under the version of yourself you built to be someone’s wife. It shows you that you can ask for directions when you’re lost, that you can fix a flat tire on a rental bike in the rain, that you can laugh so hard you snort in a room full of strangers and not feel embarrassed. It shows you that home isn’t a person, or a couch, or a house with a white picket fence. It’s the part of you that sat under that pine tree in the rain, that learned to fold tamales, that got back up every time you fell off that surfboard. You still have the postcards you never mailed. You don’t need to send them. You already got the message.

title: happiness and meditation guide|a ten-minute daily breathing practice for beginners
text:
Let me tell you about the morning I almost lost my mind in a grocery store parking lot. I was thirty-three, newly self-employed, and so wired from stress that I sat in my car for twelve minutes just gripping the steering wheel, unable to remember why I'd driven there. That night, a friend — the calm kind who always has tea brewing — said four words that changed everything: "Just breathe, you idiot." She was smiling, so I forgave her, and she taught me the ten-minute practice I still do today. It wasn't magic, but it was close enough.

Here's the practice, the whole thing, in plain language. Set a timer for ten minutes, because clock-watching defeats the purpose. Sit somewhere you won't be interrupted — a chair, a couch, even the floor propped against a wall. I used to sit on a folded blanket in the narrow corner of my apartment kitchen, because it was the only spot my then-cat hadn't claimed. Upright but relaxed is the goal, not some pretzel pose. Shoulders soft, hands resting however they like, eyes gently closed or softly focused at the floor in front of you.

Now bring your attention to the breath. Don't change it yet. Simply notice it — the cool air touching the rim of your nostrils, the rise of your chest, the way your belly moves. This is the part people skip, and it matters more than anything. For the first week or two, you'll spend most of the ten minutes remembering that you're supposed to be breathing, because your mind will bolt like an untrained puppy. Mine used to compose emails, rehearse arguments, and suddenly remember the dentist appointment I'd forgotten. That's not failure. That's the whole exercise.

When you notice you've wandered — and you will, dozens of times — gently congratulate yourself for noticing, and return to the breath. No drama, no scolding. Think of it as lifting a feather back onto a table. Each return is one repetition, one small strengthening of the muscle of attention. Over time, you might begin counting breaths: one on the inhale, two on the exhale, up to ten, then starting again. If you lose count, simply begin at one. A meditation teacher I adore calls this "giving your mind a bone" — enough of a job that it stops rummaging through the garbage.

Here's what surprised me. Around week three, I noticed the practice leaking into the rest of my day. Someone cut me off on the highway, and I caught myself taking one conscious breath before reacting. My sister said something snippy at dinner, and I paused instead of snapping back. The ten minutes on the cushion were teaching my nervous system a new habit — that I could feel pressure without becoming pressure.

A few practical notes. You will feel restless, bored, even emotional sometimes. Boredom, I've learned, is just excitement wearing a dull coat; sit through it anyway. If you're congested or anxious, exhale slightly longer than you inhale — a four-count in, six-count out calms the body like nothing else. And please, skip the guilt when you miss days. I've gone weeks without practice and simply come back, the way you'd return to a friendship after a busy season. Beginners often think meditation is about emptying the mind. It isn't. It's about befriending what's already there, one breath at a time.

Ten minutes. A timer. A quiet corner. That's all you need to begin.

title: personal finance book for young adults|automating your savings so you never have to think about it
text:
From *I Got Paid, Now Why Am I Broke?* (2024)
Let me tell you about the dumbest mistake I made at 22, fresh out of college with my first real $42k a year office job: I waited until the end of the month to save. I’d pay rent, blow $80 on Taco Bell and post-concert Uber rides, drop $120 on fast fashion I’d wear twice, then look at my bank account on the 30th and go “oh, guess I can’t put anything into savings this month. Next month for sure.” Next month never came. I did that for 18 whole months. Saved $147 total. Not a typo. I could’ve cried when I ran the numbers later.
Here’s the thing no boomer finance bro will tell you straight: willpower is a scam. You don’t have it. I don’t have it. The guy who writes those FIRE blogs with the spreadsheet tabs for every grocery purchase? He doesn’t have it either—he just automated his shit so he doesn’t have to fight the urge to blow his emergency fund on a limited-edition sneaker drop. You don’t have to “be good with money” to save. You just have to be good at setting it and forgetting it, like that weird crockpot chili you forgot about in the fridge for three days (wait, no, throw that out. But the savings part works).
Let’s get specific, no vague “pay yourself first” garbage. The day your paycheck hits—*not* three days later, not after you’ve paid your Spotify bill—your bank should be moving money out of your checking before you even see the balance. How much? Let’s skip the 10% lie for anyone making under $60k a year. If you’re pulling in $38k after taxes working front desk at a chiropractor’s office? 5% is fine. That’s $28 a week if you get paid biweekly. $28. That’s two overpriced matcha lattes. You won’t miss it. If you make $65k? Knock it up to 8%. Wait, don’t roll your eyes. I didn’t say you have to stick it in a stupid high-yield savings account earning 0.01% at the bank your mom set up for you when you were 12. Open an HYSA right now—Ally, Marcus, whatever, they’re all mostly the same—earning 4.5% right now? Let that money sit there and make free money while you scroll TikTok.
Wait, pro tip that changed my life: set the auto-transfer for 2 a.m. the day after payday. I know, 2 a.m.? Why? Because if you set it for 9 a.m., you might wake up, see that $1,200 hit, Venmo your roommate $200 for concert tickets before the transfer goes through, overdraft, and pay $35 in fees because you’re an impulsive dumbass (guilty. Did that three times in 2019). 2 a.m.? The transfer clears while you’re passed out after happy hour. You wake up, your checking says $1,144 instead of $1,200, and you adjust your budget for the two weeks accordingly. No drama. No internal fight about whether you “deserve” that new video game instead of saving. The money’s already gone.
And don’t stop at the emergency fund, for Christ’s sake. If your job offers a 401(k) match? Auto-enroll right now to contribute enough to get the full match. That’s free money. I don’t care if you think your 22-year-old self doesn’t need to think about being 67. If your job matches 50% of your contributions up to 6% of your salary, that’s a 50% instant return. You would not leave a $50 bill lying on the sidewalk, don’t leave that on the table. Set the contribution to come out pre-tax, so you don’t even see it on your pay stub. When I finally did that at 24, I thought I got a raise for three months until I realized I just wasn’t noticing the 6% coming out before my check hit.
Wait, what about fun? Oh, right, the “but I want to enjoy my 20s” crowd that comments on every one of my Reels like I’m telling them to live on ramen for 10 years. Auto-transfer for fun, too! I have a separate savings bucket labeled “dumb bullshit” that gets $30 a week auto-dropped into it. Last month I used it for that terrible pop-punk festival where I waited in line for an hour for a $17 lemonade. No guilt! The money was already there, earmarked for garbage. I didn’t have to choose between that and my car repair fund, because the car repair fund was getting its own $25 a week auto-transfer right alongside it.
Don’t overcomplicate it. You don’t need 17 savings accounts with color-coded spreadsheets. You don’t need to check your balance every day. I spend approximately 47 seconds a month thinking about my savings now, compared to the three hours a week I spent at 22 panicking because I didn’t know how I’d afford a new tire when my old one went flat. Once I set those transfers up? I stopped having those 2 a.m. panic sweats where I’d log into my bank app and stare at the screen like it would magically grow more money. Last year, when my cat ate a hair tie and needed a $1,200 emergency vet visit? I didn’t have to put it on a credit card. I didn’t have to call my dad to borrow money. The cash was just there, sitting in the account I’d been auto-feeding $25 a week into for three years, earning $187 in interest while I wasn’t paying attention.
You know what the worst part was? When I finally checked how much I’d saved after that first year of automating? It was $2,142. That was more than 14 times what I’d saved in the year and a half I was trying to “be disciplined” about moving money manually. I’d spent all that time thinking I was bad with money, that I was the kind of person who would never be able to save, and all I’d needed to do was take 10 minutes out of my Sunday to set up a few recurring transfers and then stop thinking about it.
Oh, and one last thing: don’t turn the auto-transfer off when you get a raise. I know. When you get that $3 an hour bump, the first thing you want to do is upgrade your apartment, or get a new car, or start ordering the fancy cocktail every time you go out. Just bump the auto-savings up by 1% every time you get a raise. You won’t notice the difference in your checking, but five years from now? You’ll be sitting on a down payment for a condo, or a six-month emergency fund, or enough cash to quit the job you hate and take that road trip you’ve been daydreaming about since sophomore year, and you won’t even remember how it got there. I have a friend who did that starting at 23, auto-increasing her 401(k) by 1% every six months, and she’s on track to retire at 62 with $1.2 million, and she still goes to every Taylor Swift show, still buys overpriced coffee, still takes a beach vacation every year. She doesn’t budget for fun. She doesn’t track every penny. She just set the automation up and let it run.
Last week I got a DM from a kid who read my first TikTok about this, said he set up a $15 a week auto-transfer to a savings account six months ago, and when his laptop died last week he had $390 saved to buy a new one without putting it on a 22% APR credit card. Said he didn’t even realize the money was adding up. That’s the magic of it. You don’t have to be a finance guru. You don’t have to give up all the stuff that makes your 20s worth living. You just have to get out of your own way, set the transfers up before you have a chance to spend the money, and then go live your life. The money will take care of itself. Wait, no—don’t take that as an excuse to never check your accounts, obviously. Don’t be the person who has $10,000 sitting in savings and still pays overdraft fees because you forgot to make sure your rent cleared. But the day-to-day? The “am I saving enough this month” spiral? You can kiss that goodbye. I haven’t had that spiral in four years, and I’m still the same person who once spent $65 on a limited-edition Squishmallow without thinking twice. The difference is, that $65 came out of the dumb bullshit fund, not my rent money, not my savings. It was already allocated, automatically, before I even saw the Squishmallow on the shelf.

Not 9 a.m.—I learned the hard way that if you wait until 9, you’ll wake up, see that $1,200 hit, Venmo your roommate $200 for concert tickets before the transfer clears, and get smacked with a $35 fee for being an impulsive dumbass. 2 a.m.? The transfer goes through while you’re passed out after happy hour. You wake up, your checking says $1,144 instead of $1,200, and you adjust your two-week budget accordingly. No drama. No internal fight about whether you “deserve” that new video game instead of saving. The money’s already gone.
If your job offers a 401(k) match? Auto-enroll right now to contribute enough to get every cent of it. That’s free money. I don’t care if you think your 22-year-old self doesn’t need to stress about being 67. If they match 50% of your contributions up to 6% of your salary, that’s a 50% instant return. You wouldn’t leave a $50 bill lying on the sidewalk, don’t leave that on the table. Set contributions to come out pre-tax, so you don’t even see it on your pay stub. When I finally did that at 24, I thought I got a raise for three months until I realized I just wasn’t noticing the 6% coming out before my check hit.
And for the “but I want to enjoy my 20s” crowd flooding my comment section like I’m telling you to live on ramen for a decade: auto-transfer for fun, too! I have a separate savings bucket labeled “dumb bullshit” that gets $30 a week auto-dropped into it. Last month I used it for that terrible pop-punk festival where I waited an hour for a $17 lemonade. No guilt! The money was already there, earmarked for garbage, so I didn’t have to choose between that and my car repair fund, which got its own $25 a week auto-transfer right alongside it.
I spend approximately 47 seconds a month thinking about my savings now, compared to the three hours a week I spent at 22 panicking because I didn’t know how I’d afford a new tire when mine went flat. Last year, when my cat ate a hair tie and needed a $1,200 emergency vet visit? I didn’t put it on a credit card. I didn’t call my dad to borrow cash. The money was just there, sitting in the account I’d been auto-feeding $25 a week into for three years, earning $187 in interest while I wasn’t paying attention.
Wait—don’t turn the auto-transfer off when you get a raise. I know, when you get that $3 an hour bump, the first thing you want to do is upgrade your apartment or start ordering the fancy cocktail every time you go out. Just bump the auto-savings up by 1% every time you get a pay bump. You won’t notice the difference in your checking, but five years from now you’ll be sitting on a down payment, or a six-month emergency fund, or enough cash to quit the job you hate and take that cross-country road trip you’ve been daydreaming about since sophomore year.

title: leadership book for new managers|giving honest feedback without crushing morale
text:
Chapter 3: The Conversation That Felt Like a Failure—And What It Taught Me About Honest Feedback
Early in my first management role, I inherited Priya, a top-performing marketing specialist who’d been passed over for promotion twice. Her campaign analytics were flawless, but cross-functional partners quietly complained she dismissed input and rushed timelines without looping in the design team. I knew I had to say something, but I’d spent my first three months terrified of driving away my highest-output team member. So I did what many new managers do: I softened the blow until the message was unrecognizable.

Over coffee one Tuesday, I said, “Priya, your work is incredible. One tiny thing to maybe think about? Some folks might feel a little left out if you move too fast, but honestly, it’s just because you’re so much more efficient than everyone else.” I patted myself on the back for being “nice.” A month later, Priya missed out on the promotion a third time. She stormed into my office, eyes wet with frustration, and said, “You told me I was doing great. No one ever said this was holding me back. Why didn’t you just tell me the truth?”

That moment stung because I realized my “kindness” wasn’t kindness at all—it was cowardice. I’d protected my own discomfort instead of giving her the information she needed to grow. Honest feedback doesn’t have to crush morale, but vague, sugarcoated feedback almost always does. Over 15 years of leading teams, I’ve landed on four rules that turn hard conversations into trust-building moments.

First, separate the observation from the judgment. When I finally circled back to Priya to reset, I didn’t say, “You’re bad at collaboration.” I said, “In the last two product launch syncs, you shared final campaign copy three days before the design deadline, and the design lead noted they didn’t get a chance to weigh in on brand alignment. That led to 12 hours of last-minute rework and a one-day launch delay.” Stick to specific, time-bound, factual details anyone in the room would agree happened. Judgments (“you’re arrogant,” “you don’t care about the team”) trigger defensiveness; observations create shared ground.

Second, name the impact, not just the action. Most people don’t show up to work trying to let their teammates down. Priya had no idea her rush to hit targets was creating extra work for people she liked. When you tie behavior to tangible impact—for the team, for their own goals, for the business—you turn feedback from a criticism into a problem-solving conversation. For Priya, I added: “This is the exact skill the promotion panel is looking for: leading cross-functional work without creating bottlenecks. Fixing this isn’t just about making the design team happy; it’s about getting you the role you’ve worked for.”

Third, invite dialogue before you jump to solutions. New managers often treat feedback like a performance review monologue: talk at the person for 10 minutes, then send them on their way. But people receive feedback far better when they feel seen. After I laid out the facts and impact for Priya, I paused and said, “What’s your perspective on those launches?” She explained she was juggling three urgent executive requests and assumed the design team preferred getting final copy instead of half-baked drafts. That context changed everything: the problem wasn’t that she was dismissive, it was that she was overloaded and had no shared process for flagging tradeoffs. We landed on a solution together— a 15-minute early check-in with design for all future campaigns—instead of me handing down a rule she resented.

Finally, end with clear support and accountability, not a vague “keep it up.” I told Priya I’d block 10 minutes in our weekly 1:1 to debrief cross-functional check-ins, and that I’d connect her to a peer in the design org to build rapport. A month later, when she ran her first collaborative launch with zero rework, I called out that win publicly in our team all-hands. Feedback isn’t a one-time dump; it’s a cycle of honest input, support, and recognition of progress.

Priya got that promotion six months later. She still teases me about the coffee chat where I “said nothing and everything at once.” That line always reminds me: Your job as a manager isn’t to be liked in the moment of a hard conversation. It’s to be the person who respects your team enough to tell them the truth, and cares enough to help them act on it. (Word count: 698)

title: personal finance book|negotiating a raise and why most people never ask
text:
Let’s start with the statistic that made me write this chapter: 70 percent of people who ask for a raise get one, according to data from Payscale and Glassdoor, and yet 60 percent of working adults never ask at all. I’ve sat across the kitchen table from friends making $85,000 a year who will spend three hours clipping coupons to save $40 on a grocery run, but won’t set aside 30 minutes to prepare for a conversation that could net them a $10,000 to $15,000 annual raise, money that compounds for every year they stay in the role, funds retirement contributions, and raises the baseline for every future job offer they get. I’ve been that person too: early in my career, I waited 18 months for a “merit raise” that never came, convinced if I just worked hard enough, my boss would notice and reward me without me having to say a word. That mistake cost me roughly $22,000 in lost wages before I finally spoke up, money I could have used to pay off my student loans six months early.
Most people don’t ask not because they don’t deserve more, but because three quiet fears stop them before they even open their mouth. The first is the fear of looking greedy or ungrateful. You tell yourself your boss already pays you fairly, that bringing up money will make you seem like you don’t care about the team, that you’ll be labeled high-maintenance. Let’s be clear: your employer does not set your pay based on how grateful you are. They set it based on the market rate for your work, the value you deliver, and the least amount they can pay to keep you in the role without you leaving. Asking for fair compensation is not greedy—it’s the same calculation your company makes every single quarter when it sets prices, negotiates vendor contracts, and decides on annual budgets. The second fear is that you’ll be rejected, and that rejection will ruin your relationship with your manager. But the data tells the opposite story: managers expect these conversations. Most budget for raise requests every year, and they respect employees who can make a clear, evidence-based case for their value far more than employees who quietly stew about being underpaid for months before quitting without warning. The third fear is that you don’t have a “good enough” reason to ask. You don’t need to have a life crisis, a competing job offer, or a major promotion to ask for more. You just need to be able to point to concrete, specific value you’ve delivered that goes above the job description you were hired for: the process you streamlined that cut 10 hours a week of admin work for the team, the client you retained that was at risk of leaving, the new hire you trained who got up to speed two weeks faster than expected.
When you do have the conversation, skip the personal pleas. Don’t lead with your rising rent, your kid’s daycare costs, or the fact that your coworker makes more than you. Lead with your value. Come with three to five specific, quantifiable wins from the last six months, a realistic number tied to market rates for your role in your area (check Glassdoor, Payscale, and your local professional network to get that number, don’t guess), and frame it as a conversation about alignment, not a demand. Say something like, “I’ve really loved growing in this role over the last year, and I wanted to talk about adjusting my pay to match the work I’m doing now. Over the last six months, I led the X project that came in 15 percent under budget and drove 20 percent more sign-ups than we projected, and I’ve taken on managing our intern program which used to take five hours a week of your time. Based on the market rate for this level of work and the value I’m delivering, I’d like to talk about moving my salary to $X.” If they say no right now, don’t storm out. Ask what specific, measurable goals you need to hit to get to that pay level in the next six months, and get that timeline in writing.
The worst outcome is almost never that they say no. The worst outcome is that you stay silent, leave tens of thousands of dollars on the table over the course of your career, and wait for someone to notice your hard work when no one is paid to look out for your bottom line except you. That raise is not going to land in your lap because you deserve it. It’s going to land in your lap because you asked for it, clearly and confidently, with the evidence to back you up.

title: time-management book|saying no to good opportunities to protect great ones
text:
Here’s the thing nobody tells you about being ambitious: the danger isn’t only bad opportunities.

Bad opportunities are easy to reject. The scammy partnership. The “exposure” gig. The cousin who wants you to quit your job and sell luxury pickles.

No, the real trouble comes from good opportunities.

The interesting project. The fun podcast. The paid speech in a city you’ve never visited. The introduction to someone impressive. The favor for a friend that would only take “a quick weekend.”

Those are the ones that sneak into your calendar wearing respectable shoes.

Early in my blogging career, I said yes to almost everything. I was flattered. I was also convinced that every open door led to destiny, instead of sometimes leading to a conference room with bad coffee and a man named Todd who wanted to “pick my brain about synergies.”

One year, I agreed to speak at an event, write a short ebook, help launch a friend’s product, join a mastermind, and redesign my website—all during the same six weeks I was supposed to finish my actual book proposal.

Naturally, I did what any mature professional would do. I bought a new notebook, made a color-coded schedule, and pretended I had become a different human being through the power of gel pens.

Spoiler: I did not become a different human being. I became the same human being, but more irritable and behind on laundry.

Every opportunity was individually reasonable. Together, they were a conspiracy against the one thing that mattered most.

That’s the hidden math of time management. A yes isn’t only a yes to the thing in front of you. It’s a no to whatever your future self was planning to protect. Deep work. Rest. Family dinner. The creative project that scares you. The business bet with the huge upside. Sometimes even your ability to be pleasant at a grocery store.

Great opportunities rarely shout. They usually require patience, repetition, and blocks of uninterrupted attention. Good opportunities, meanwhile, are charming, urgent, and socially rewarding. They arrive with deadlines and compliments. They make you feel in demand.

But being in demand is not the same as being on purpose.

I eventually finished the proposal, by the way. It required canceling two things, delaying one, and admitting to my friend that I could not save her launch with the sheer power of my retweets. She survived. So did I. The world did not collapse, which was both reassuring and slightly offensive.

Since then, I’ve used a few goofy but useful filters before saying yes.

1. Ask, “Does this make my main thing easier or harder?”  
If the opportunity is exciting but pulls energy from the commitment I’ve already declared great, it’s probably a no, even when it’s good.

2. Use the “hell yes or future regret” test.  
If I’m not genuinely enthusiastic, I imagine looking back after six months. Will I be glad I did it, or just glad to have survived it?

3. Stop treating novelty as destiny.  
New things sparkle because they are new, not because they are important. Most shiny opportunities are just glitter with an invoice.

4. Buy time before answering.  
I rarely decide on the spot anymore. I say, “Let me check my calendar and get back to you.” This prevents my mouth from signing contracts my nervous system cannot cash.

5. Protect the great thing visibly.  
I schedule the work that matters before the fun stuff arrives. If my calendar already contains the book, the product, the family time, or the recovery period, a new request has to compete with something real instead of stealing from empty space.

Saying no to good opportunities feels awkward because people are used to ambitious people saying yes. But every meaningful achievement I’ve seen came from someone protecting a narrow, unsexy priority from a bunch of attractive distractions.

You don’t need more discipline as much as you need a clearer target.

When you know what great looks like for this season, protecting it gets easier. Not easy—you’ll still miss parties and disappoint people and occasionally wonder if Todd had the synergies of a lifetime—but easier.

A full calendar can look impressive from the outside. The best life rarely comes from filling every gap.

It comes from guarding the few yeses that count.

title: entrepreneurship book|launching a small business with almost no money
text:
Let’s cut the crap first. The “you need $50k to launch a business” grift is peddled by two groups: people who sell $497 “launch blueprints” and people who’ve never sold anything that didn’t come with a W-2 attached. I launched my first profitable business— a curbside junk removal service for suburban hoarders—for $187 total, back in 2017. No loan, no angel investor, no “side hustle savings fund” I’d spent three years hoarding. I had $212 in my checking account, a 2004 Honda Civic with a busted passenger window, and a rent payment due in 12 days.
Here’s the breakdown of that $187, because vague “spend less” advice is useless: $42 for 500 full-color flyers from the local print shop (the guy behind the counter gave me 100 extra because I told him I was broke and would bring him donuts if it worked— I did, two weeks later), $25 for a 30-day basic Craigslist posting in the “labor and hauling” section, $97 for a used hand truck off Facebook Marketplace (the seller threw in a pair of work gloves for free when I showed up 20 minutes early in the rain), and $23 for a pack of heavy-duty contractor bags and a roll of duct tape from the dollar store. That’s it. No website. No LLC. No branded t-shirts. No Canva logo that looks like every other cheap service business logo on Instagram.
Wait, hold on—people lose their minds when I say no LLC first. Let me be clear: if you’re making less than $10k gross in the first 90 days, spending $300 to register an LLC is a waste of money that could buy you gas, supplies, or a week’s worth of groceries so you don’t tap out before you get your first client. File a DBA for $25 if your state makes you, sure, but don’t drop cash on legal structure until you have actual cash coming in the door. I didn’t register my LLC until I had 11 recurring clients and $7,200 in my business bank account three months in. Anyone who tells you otherwise is either selling you registered agent services or has never had to choose between buying business cards and paying their electric bill.
I passed out those flyers for three straight nights after my bar shift, taping them to community bulletin boards at grocery stores, sliding them under the doormats of houses with overgrown lawns and piles of junk on their porches, leaving a stack at the local senior center. I got my first call 41 hours after I posted the Craigslist ad: a retired teacher 12 minutes from my apartment who needed a old couch, three broken bookshelves, and 17 boxes of 1990s National Geographics hauled to the dump. She paid me $280 cash. That first job covered my entire initial startup cost, plus left me $93 to fill up my gas tank and buy a $12 pizza on the way home.
Don’t fall for the “build an audience first” garbage, either. I see 22-year-olds on TikTok spending six months making Reels about their upcoming candle business, dropping $800 on wax and wicks and custom labels, before they’ve ever asked a single stranger if they’d pay $18 for a candle that smells like pine and regret. You don’t need an audience. You need one person who will pay you actual money for the thing you can do or make. If you can’t find one person to pay you $50 for your offering before you drop $1,000 on inventory, your offering sucks, or you’re too scared to ask people for money. Both are fixable, but neither gets fixed by posting aesthetic grid photos of your home office setup.
I turned down three “growth opportunities” that first month, too. A guy offered to build me a $1,200 website in exchange for a 10% cut of all jobs for a year. I said no. A local moving company wanted to white-label my services for 40% less than I was charging clients directly. I said no. A friend who’d “run three startups” offered to invest $5,000 for 30% equity. I said no. When you’re broke, every offer that looks like free cash or a shortcut feels like a lifeline, but most of them are just anchors. That $5k would have felt like a win until I realized I was giving up nearly a third of every dollar I made for the rest of the life of the business, just because I didn’t want to pass out flyers for a few more nights.
By the end of that first month, I’d made $2,140 cash. No ad spend beyond that initial $25 Craigslist post. No business cards. I still didn’t have a website. I’d bartered hauling services for a better set of tie-down straps from a guy who ran a landscaping company, traded a junk haul for a free oil change from the mechanic down the street, and got three referrals from that first retired teacher client, including her son who ran a small property management company that gave me 4-6 jobs a month for the next two years.
People love to talk about “hustle culture” like it’s a dirty word, like working 12 days straight when you’re launching is some kind of moral failure. Let me tell you what’s actually a moral failure: lying awake at night stressed about rent because you spent three years “validating” your business idea instead of just selling something to the first person who’ll buy it. You don’t need perfect. You don’t need funded. You don’t need a brand guide. You need to stop overcomplicating it, count the cash you actually have in your pocket right now, and figure out what you can sell for more than it costs you to deliver it, today.

Here’s the exact breakdown of that $187, because vague “spend less” advice is useless: $42 for 500 full-color flyers from the local print shop (the guy behind the counter gave me 100 extra when I said I was broke and would bring him donuts if it worked—I did, two weeks later), $25 for a 30-day Craigslist posting in the labor and hauling section, $97 for a used hand truck off Facebook Marketplace (the seller threw in work gloves for free when I showed up 20 minutes early in the rain), and $23 for contractor bags and duct tape from the dollar store. That’s it. No website. No LLC. No branded t-shirts. No Canva logo that looks like every other cheap service business cluttering Instagram feeds.
Wait, people lose their minds when I say skip the LLC first. Let’s be blunt: if you’re making less than $10k gross in your first 90 days, dropping $300 to register an LLC is a waste of money that could buy gas, supplies, or a week of groceries so you don’t tap out before your first client. File a $25 DBA if your state forces you to, sure, but don’t waste cash on legal structure until you have actual cash coming in the door. I didn’t register my LLC until I had 11 recurring clients and $7,200 in the bank three months in. Anyone who tells you otherwise is either selling registered agent services or has never had to choose between buying business cards and paying their electric bill.
I passed out flyers for three straight nights after my bar shift, taping them to grocery store bulletin boards, sliding them under doormats of houses with overgrown lawns and junk stacked on porches, leaving a stack at the local senior center. I got my first call 41 hours after the Craigslist ad went up: a retired teacher 12 minutes from my apartment who needed an old couch, three broken bookshelves, and 17 boxes of 1990s National Geographics hauled to the dump. She paid me $280 cash. That first job covered my entire startup cost, left me $93 for gas and a $12 pepperoni pizza on the way home.

I watch 22-year-olds on TikTok spend six months making Reels about their upcoming candle business, drop $800 on wax and custom labels, before they’ve ever asked a single stranger if they’d pay $18 for a candle that smells like pine and regret. You don’t need an audience. You need one person who will pay you actual money for the thing you can do or make. No. When you’re broke, every offer that looks like free cash or a shortcut feels like a lifeline, but most are just anchors tied to your ankle. title: negotiation book|finding out what the other side really wants
text:
Chapter 3: Uncover the Hidden Prize – What They *Really* Want
The rain hammered the windshield as I idled outside my daughter Lila’s middle school, mentally replaying the standoff from that morning. For three days, the 12-year-old had refused to sign up for the regional youth soccer league—the league I’d coached in for 8 years, the league all her friends were joining, the league she’d begged to play in six months prior. My initial negotiation playbook was straight out of the “win-lose” handbook I’d spent my early career relying on: I’d listed the pro-level coaching, the college recruitment exposure, the chance to win a championship alongside her best friend Mia. I’d even offered a new pair of the premium cleats she’d been eyeing for months. Every point landed like a rock in mud. “I don’t care,” she’d mumbled, slamming her bedroom door.

I almost defaulted to authority: *You’re signing up, end of discussion*. But 15 years of negotiating commercial real estate deals had taught me one hard-won lesson: the demand someone says out loud is almost never the thing they actually want. When Lila climbed into the car, I bit back the lecture. “I get it if you don’t want to play,” I said, pulling away from the curb. “I don’t want to force you. But will you tell me what’s actually bugging you? No arguments, no fixing it right now. I just want to listen.”

For two minutes she stared out the window, picking at a loose thread on her backpack. Then it came out, quiet: “Mia and I got placed on different teams. The draft was last week. Her coach is the dad who yells at kids for tripping, and mine is Mr. Henderson, who makes everyone run extra laps if they miss a pass. I don’t want to play against her. It’ll ruin our friendship.”

I’d spent 72 hours negotiating against a problem that didn’t exist. I thought the core conflict was *Lila vs. playing soccer*. It was actually *Lila vs. losing her closest friend*. The cleats, the trophies, the “exposure” I’d been selling were all irrelevant to her hidden priority. That’s the trap most negotiators fall into: we walk into conversations assuming we know what the other side values, because it’s what *we* would value in their shoes.

A week later, I watched the exact same dynamic derail a client deal I was mediating. The seller, a third-generation bakery owner named Rosa, had spent 3 weeks turning down offers that met her full asking price. The buyer, a regional café group, kept upping their bid, confused and frustrated: “What more does she want? We’re giving her every dollar she asked for.” What they didn’t know—what Rosa had never said out loud—was that she didn’t care about an extra $10,000. She cared that the new owners keep her 82-year-old master baker, Marco, on payroll for two more years until he qualified for full retirement benefits. The price tag was her stated ask. Protecting the man who’d helped her build the business was her hidden prize.

 Three Steps to Pull Back the Curtain
Most people won’t volunteer their real priorities on the first ask. Use these three tactics to draw them out:
1. Ask open “what” and “how” questions, not “yes/no” traps. Stop saying “Are you unhappy with the salary?” Start with “What would make this role feel worth taking for you?” or “How would this decision impact your team six months from now?” These questions invite explanation instead of defensiveness, and surface constraints you’d never guess on your own.
2. Test your assumptions out loud, and invite correction.
