When Lila first refused soccer, I could have said, “I’m guessing you’re worried about the time commitment with your advanced math class—did I get that right?” Naming a wrong guess gives the other side permission to correct you, which feels far less confrontational than a direct demand for answers. In Rosa’s case, the buyers wasted weeks until they said, “We assume the money is the biggest factor here, but tell us if we’re missing something that matters more.”
3. Map the difference between their stated position and their underlying interests. A position is what they say they want: “I won’t sign up for soccer,” “I’m rejecting your offer.” An interest is the why behind it: fear of losing a friend, loyalty to a long-time employee. Positions are almost always negotiable. Interests are the non-negotiable core you have to work around.

By the end of that month, Lila and Mia worked out a carpool schedule to make pre-season practices together, and both agreed they’d get ice cream after every game their teams played against each other, no hard feelings. The café group added a two-year employment clause for Marco to their contract, and Rosa signed that week. Neither deal required more money or bigger concessions. They just required stopping the sales pitch long enough to find the prize the other side had been hiding all along. (Word count: 698)

title: negotiation book|finding out what the other side really wants
text:
Let’s get one thing straight before you walk into your next negotiation, whether that’s haggling with a contractor, asking for a raise, hashing out a custody schedule with your ex, or locking in a partnership deal for your small business: 90% of the time, the demand the other side leads with is not what they actually want. It’s a placeholder, a shield, a number they picked because they think it’s the starting point that keeps them from getting played, and if you spend all your time haggling over that surface demand, you’ll leave value on the table, burn the relationship, or walk away from a deal that could have worked for both of you for no good reason.
You’ve probably done this yourself, right? You walk into a salary negotiation and lead with “I need a 15% raise” because you don’t want to say the real thing: you’re embarrassed that your teammate who does the same work makes 10% more, you’re burnt out from covering three extra roles after layoffs, and you’d turn down a higher cash offer if it meant you could get two guaranteed remote days a week to care for your aging mom. You lead with the number because it feels safer, more measurable, less vulnerable than naming the messy, personal priorities that actually drive your choices. The person across the table is doing the exact same thing.
So how do you cut through that placeholder to find what they actually care about? First, stop planning your counteroffer while they talk. I’ve watched hundreds of negotiators sit across the table nodding blankly while the other person speaks, mentally running through their list of concessions, calculating how low they can push the price, waiting for their turn to talk. That’s the fastest way to miss every signal that matters. When they state their opening demand, don’t jump to push back. Pause, ask an open, unthreatening question, and shut up. If a supplier says they can’t go lower than $20 per unit, don’t snap back that your last supplier charged $15. Say, “Help me understand what goes into that number for you. What constraints are you working around right now?” Half the time, you’ll find out their price isn’t about greed—it’s that their raw material costs spiked 30% in the last quarter, they’re short two staff on the production line, and they’re terrified of taking on an order they can’t fulfill on time, which would tank their reputation with every other client they have.
Second, pay attention to what they get defensive about, and what they circle back to when the conversation drifts. If you’re negotiating a job offer and the hiring manager keeps brushing off your questions about flexible hours but lights up when they talk about their fast-track promotion path, that tells you something: they can’t budge on in-office requirements, but they have way more flexibility to throw in professional development stipends, a clear six-month review timeline, or a performance bonus than they’re leading with. If your teen says they “absolutely need” a $1,200 new phone and gets frustrated every time you mention a cheaper refurbished model, don’t write them off as entitled. Dig a little, and you might find out their current phone dies halfway through the school day, they can’t access the tutoring app they need for AP math, and they’re embarrassed to ask for a ride home from practice because they can’t text to coordinate when it ends. The $1,200 price tag is just the solution they landed on for a set of problems they didn’t want to explain out loud.
Third, test for unspoken priorities with low-stakes hypothetical trades, no strings attached. You don’t have to make an offer to ask, “If we were able to lock in a two-year contract instead of a one-year deal, would that change how you think about the per-unit price?” or “If we could guarantee you 48-hour turnaround on feedback for every project milestone, would that let you be more flexible on the deadline?” These questions don’t commit you to anything, but they reveal tradeoffs the other side might value far more than the surface demand they opened with.
Here’s the part most people miss: finding out what the other side really wants isn’t about manipulating them into giving you what you want. It’s the only way to stop fighting over imaginary positions and build a deal that actually sticks. I once saw a landlord and small café owner spend three weeks haggling over a $500 monthly rent increase, both ready to walk away, before the landlord admitted he didn’t need the extra cash—he needed someone to plow the parking lot and keep the sidewalk clear in winter, a service that cost the café owner $300 a month to cover for his own storefront anyway. They traded that service for a rent freeze, both walked away happier than if they’d split the difference on the rent, and they renewed that lease three more times over the next decade. You don’t get those wins by arguing over opening demands. You get them by leaning in, asking more than you talk, and remembering that every person across the table is carrying a set of worries, constraints, and unspoken goals they’re not leading with. Your job isn’t to “win” the haggle. It’s to uncover those things, so you don’t waste weeks fighting over something neither of you actually cares about.

title: Christian purpose-driven living book|serving others as the path to a meaningful life
text:
I used to believe the “abundant life” Jesus promised in John 10:10 looked like an upgraded version of me: calmer mornings, clearer skin, a better budget, and maybe a kitchen where every mug had its own little hook.

I’m only half joking.

For years, I chased meaning the way I chase the ice-cream truck: urgently, loudly, and usually too late. I wanted purpose to feel like a mountaintop moment, cinematic music and all. Instead, God kept placing me next to ordinary people with ordinary needs—the kind that don’t look impressive on social media.

Like the Tuesday I brought soup to my neighbor Karen and accidentally spent two hours listening to her explain her cat’s digestive issues. I went in feeling like a ministry superhero. By minute twenty, I was mentally rearranging my pantry. But somewhere between “wet food only” and “the vet says it’s stress,” Karen said, “You’re the first person who’s sat at my table since my husband died.”

Oof.

Right there, God did that thing He does where He gently points out that I’m not the main character. I had come to serve, sure, but I also wanted to feel meaningful. Meanwhile, He was more interested in making me present.

That’s the strange, beautiful secret of the purpose-driven life: significance usually arrives wearing sneakers, holding a casserole, and asking, “How can I help?”

Jesus didn’t say, “Whoever finds the most impressive mission statement wins.” He said whoever wants to be great must be a servant (Mark 10:43). In God’s kingdom, the path up is the path down. The way to find your life is to lose it in love (Matthew 16:25). And yes, sometimes that means listening to cat stories.

If that feels intimidating, let me reassure you: serving others is not about being holy enough, talented enough, or having enough homemade soup. I have served while tired, irritable, late, and wearing socks with holes. God does not need our perfection. He asks for our availability—and maybe a sense of humor, because people are messy, and so are we.

Here are a few things I’ve learned while tripping along the servant path:

1. Start with the person in front of you.
You don’t need a burning bush or a five-year plan. Ask God to open your eyes. The lonely church member, the exhausted parent, the coworker nobody invites to lunch—your mission field may be closer than your mailbox.

2. Serve small, then keep serving small.
Meaning rarely comes from one dramatic sacrifice. It comes from faithful little yeses: a text, a meal, a ride, a genuine “I’m praying for you,” followed by actually praying.

3. Don’t wait until you feel qualified.
If Moses had updated his résumé before the burning bush, it would have said, “Shepherd, former fugitive, public speaking not my thing.” God loves using unlikely people because it makes it obvious whose power is at work.

4. Serve without keeping score.
Sometimes people won’t say thank you. Sometimes they’ll criticize the potatoes. Sometimes you’ll bless someone and never see the fruit. That’s okay. Your reward is not trending; it’s stored in heaven (Matthew 6:4).

I remember volunteering at a food pantry and feeling completely unspiritual. We sorted canned corn, laughed with the regulars, and dropped a bag of rice in the parking lot. A woman named Rita picked up her groceries and said, “I used to be ashamed to come here. Now this feels like family.”

Suddenly the corn felt holy.

Because that’s how the kingdom works. When we kneel beside someone else’s burden, we meet God there. Serving isn’t merely a duty; it’s a doorway. We enter the needs of others and discover we were designed for something bigger than comfort, control, and curating a cute life.

Purpose isn’t a treasure map locked in a drawer. It’s a towel wrapped around your waist (John 13:4–5), a basin of water, and the courage to wash feet that may be dusty, awkward, or attached to someone who votes differently, talks too much, or never returns your mixing bowls.

Jesus washed Judas’s feet, by the way. Let that wreck your expectations.

A meaningful life isn’t built by being served, admired, or comfortable. It’s built by love poured out. And the best part? When we give our lives away, we don’t lose them. We finally find them—bruised, laughing, rice on our shoes, and more alive than we’ve ever been.

title: self-improvement book|dealing with procrastination and perfectionism
text:
Let me tell you about the Tuesday I stared at a half-written book proposal for three full hours, not typing a single word. I’d already rearranged my desk twice, refilled my coffee four times, and spent 20 minutes deep in a YouTube rabbit hole of golden retriever puppy rescue videos—all because the opening line I’d drafted the night before felt “not quite right.” If that sounds familiar, you’re not lazy, and you’re not bad at time management. You’re caught in the toxic tango of procrastination and perfectionism, two sides of the same fear-coated coin that’s been robbing you of small wins for way too long.
I used to think perfectionism was a flex, you know? I’d brag to friends that I “didn’t submit half-assed work,” that I waited until the idea felt flawless before I put it out into the world. What I didn’t say was that I waited so long to turn in a college magazine feature my junior year that my editor ran a backup story instead, that I sat on my first book idea for two years because I was convinced no one would want to read “messy, unpolished” thoughts from a 20-something who still burned toast half the time. Procrastination wasn’t me being lazy—it was my brain’s weird, misfiring protection mechanism: if I never turned in the less-than-perfect work, no one could judge me for it, right? If I never started, I never had to face the gap between the perfect version of the thing I imagined in my head, and the clunky, real version I could actually make that day.
Here’s the trick that pulled me out of that cycle, the one I still use every single time I feel that familiar pull to scroll instead of starting: I give myself permission to make the worst possible first version of the thing. When I was stuck on that book proposal that Tuesday, I set a timer for 10 minutes, and typed at the top of the page: THIS IS GARBAGE, NO ONE WILL EVER READ THIS. Then I wrote the cheesiest, most clunky opening line I could think of, rambled through three paragraphs of half-baked ideas, misspelled half the words, and didn’t fix a single typo. When the timer went off, I didn’t have a perfect proposal—but I had something on the page. And here’s the wild part: editing that messy draft took 40 minutes total, less time than I’d spent scrolling puppy videos that morning. That proposal sold to a publisher six weeks later, by the way. The opening line they kept? The “garbage” one I banged out in those first 10 minutes, no tweaks needed.
Stop waiting for the perfect mood, the perfect outline, the perfect moment when you don’t feel scared to start. That moment never comes. The next time you catch yourself putting a task off because it doesn’t feel “good enough” yet, ask yourself: what’s the smallest, most unimpressive version of this I can do right now? If you’re avoiding writing a work email, write the dumbest, most casual draft first, no formal greetings, no polished phrasing. If you’re putting off a workout, put on your gym shoes and walk around the block, no pressure to lift weights or run three miles. Perfectionism tells you the first version has to be the final version, but that’s a lie. Every great thing you’ve ever loved started as a messy, unpolished first try. You don’t have to get it right first. You just have to get it going. (Word count: 598)

title: habit-building book|starting with habits so small you can't fail
text:
Chapter 2: The Push-Up That Changed Everything
The gym membership card burned a hole in my wallet for three months. Every morning, I’d stare at it while making coffee, promising myself that *today* was the day I’d go. I’d imagined myself walking through those doors, crushing an hour-long workout, and emerging as someone who “had their life together.” Instead, I’d end the day on the couch, scrolling through fitness videos, feeling like a failure before I even laced up shoes.

That all changed on a rainy Tuesday in October. I was burnt out from work, my back ached from hunching over my laptop, and the guilt of that unused membership was heavier than any dumbbell I could have lifted. Instead of making another grand promise, I told myself: *Just do one push-up.* Not ten. Not a full workout. One single push-up, right there on my living room carpet.

I got down, did one wobbly push-up, and stood back up. That was it. Thirty seconds, max. But something shifted. I hadn’t failed. I’d actually done the thing I said I would. The next day, I did one push-up again. The day after that, I did two. Within a week, I was doing ten without thinking about it. A month later, I was driving to the gym three times a week—not because I forced myself, but because the tiny habit had already rewired how I saw myself. I was no longer someone who *planned* to work out. I was someone who *worked out*.

This is the magic of starting so small you can’t fail: you strip away the pressure, the perfectionism, and the all-or-nothing thinking that kills most new habits before they start.

 Why Tiny Habits Win the Long Game
When we decide to build a new habit, our first instinct is to go big. We vow to meditate for 30 minutes a day, cut out all sugar cold turkey, or write 1,000 words every morning after a decade of not writing. These goals sound impressive, but they’re fragile. One busy day, one bad night of sleep, one unexpected errand, and the whole thing falls apart. Then we call ourselves lazy and quit entirely.

A “minimum viable habit” is different. It’s a behavior so easy, so low-stakes, that you have no reasonable excuse to skip it—even on your worst day. It’s not about the push-up itself, or one page of reading, or flossing one tooth (a classic example from habit researcher BJ Fogg). It’s about showing up for the identity you want to build. Every time you complete that tiny action, you cast a vote for the person you want to become. You don’t need 100 votes at once. One a day is enough to start.

 How to Design Your "Can’t Fail" Habit
First, shrink your desired habit until it feels almost silly. If your goal is to read more, don’t start with 20 pages a night. Start with opening the book and reading one sentence. If you want to build a meditation practice, don’t aim for 10 minutes of calm. Start with taking three deep breaths after you turn off your alarm. If you want to eat healthier, start with putting one piece of fruit on your plate at lunch. The action should take less than two minutes. If it takes longer, shrink it more.

Second, anchor it to a routine you already do without fail. Habits don’t live in isolation—they attach to existing cues in your day. My push-up habit anchored to the moment I closed my work laptop each evening. Your anchor might be “after I pour my morning coffee,” “after I brush my teeth at night,” or “when I sit down on the couch after dinner.” Use the formula: *After [existing routine], I will [tiny new habit].* This removes the need to remember or motivate yourself; the existing behavior acts as a trigger.

Third, celebrate immediately—even if it feels stupid. Our brains repeat behaviors that feel good. Right after you finish that one push-up, that one sentence, that three deep breaths, give yourself a tiny, genuine win: a fist pump, a quiet “yes,” a sip of your favorite drink. I’d grin at myself in the mirror after my daily push-up, corny as it sounds. That split second of pride wires the habit into your brain far faster than willpower ever could.

You don’t need to be impressive on day one. You just need to be present. The big results aren’t in the one heroic workout or the perfect two-hour writing session. They’re in the tiny, unremarkable choice you make even when you’re tired, busy, and convinced it doesn’t matter. One push-up doesn’t make you fit. But showing up for that one push-up, every single day, is the exact thing that will.

Tomorrow morning, don’t ask yourself to become a whole new person. Ask for one push-up. That’s all you need to start.

title: customer-service business book|building a company culture around delivering happiness
text:
Let’s get one truth out first: you cannot script your team into delivering happiness to customers. You can write 17 pages of call scripts, hand out branded smile pins, and mandate a “warm tone” in every email, and none of it will stick if your internal company culture doesn’t prioritize happiness as a core operating rule, not a marketing buzzword. I’ve sat in on leadership retreats where CEOs wrote “deliver happiness” on a whiteboard, then went back to their offices and approved a policy that docked frontline support reps 10% of their bonus for spending more than three minutes on a single customer call. That disconnect is why so many “customer-centric” initiatives feel hollow to both employees and the people buying from you.
Start by building a culture that delivers happiness to your team first, because every employee will treat a customer exactly as well as they feel treated by the company. If you force your support team to beg a manager for approval to issue a $10 refund to a frustrated customer who got a broken item, or write them up for taking two extra minutes to listen to a regular caller who just lost a spouse and wanted to chat about the product they used to buy with their partner, you are not building a happiness-focused culture—you are building a compliance machine, and compliance never sparks joy. Give your lowest-paid frontline team member the same authority you would give a senior manager to fix a customer problem on the spot, no hoops to jump through, no follow-up forms required unless it helps them learn for next time. I know a small online pet supply retailer that lets every support rep send up to $50 in free treats, toys, or handwritten condolence notes to customers who reach out upset about a sick pet, no approval needed. Their customer retention is 42% higher than the industry average, and their team turnover is less than a quarter of the sector standard, because people don’t leave jobs where they feel trusted to do the kind, human thing.
Next, stop measuring success only by average handle time, resolution rate, or net promoter score. Those metrics matter, but they don’t capture the small, unscripted moments that build real loyalty. Set aside 15 minutes in every weekly team huddle for people to share the small, happy moments they created for customers that week—not the big, viral-worthy stories, the quiet ones: the rep who stayed on the line for 10 minutes to walk an elderly customer through resetting their account password even though the issue wasn’t technically part of their job, the warehouse team who slipped a free extra pack of a customer’s favorite snack into their order because they saw the customer note mentioning it was for their kid’s birthday, the social media manager who replied to a random customer’s joke about loving your product with a silly meme instead of a generic corporate response. Celebrate those moments publicly, not with big cash bonuses, but with genuine recognition, because those are the choices that define your culture far more than any policy document.
Finally, don’t treat happiness as a destination you hit once you hit a certain revenue target or customer count. It’s a daily choice you model as a leader. If you walk past a support rep dealing with a furious customer and don’t stop to ask if they need backup, if you dismiss team feedback that a certain policy is making customers unhappy because “it’s better for the bottom line,” if you never take a customer support shift yourself to remember what it feels like to talk to the people who pay every employee’s salary, your team will notice, and they will stop prioritizing happiness too. Delivering happiness isn’t about being perfect. It’s about building a space where people feel safe to be human, first with each other, then with every customer who walks through the door, calls your line, or sends you an email. That’s the culture that doesn’t just make customers happy—it makes them stay, and tell everyone they know about you, too.

title: productivity book|single-tasking in a world built for distraction
text:
Here’s the dirty little secret nobody tells you about “productivity”: most of the advice is just distraction in a nicer outfit.

I learned this the hard way. There I was, laptop open, phone propped up like a tiny needy coworker, earbuds in, browser tabs cascading across the screen like a digital waterfall. I was answering an email while editing a paragraph while nodding along to a meeting I definitely wasn’t listening to. I felt like a genius. I looked like a hedgehog trying to pay taxes.

Then came the moment that broke my brain. I wrote the sentence, “Let’s circle back and circle back.” Two circle backs. In one sentence. My computer didn’t even flag it. Even autocorrect had given up on me.

That’s when I started paying attention to single-tasking.

Single-tasking sounds embarrassingly simple. Do one thing. Finish it, or at least work on it intentionally. Then do the next thing. But in a world built to interrupt you, doing one thing is a rebellious act. Your watch wants attention. Your fridge can send notifications now. I once got a marketing email while standing inside the store that sent it. They had hunted me down geographically to offer me 15 percent off candles.

We treat attention like an unlimited resource, but it’s more like a houseguest: easily startled and impossible to get back once it leaves.

Here’s what changed for me. I started writing with my phone in another room. At first, this felt like leaving a baby at home alone, except the baby was a rectangle that only showed me arguments and videos of raccoons. I lasted about eleven minutes. Then I walked to the phone, checked it, saw nothing important, and felt the exact emotional texture of eating a single stale Cheeto out of the carpet.

But something strange happened over the next week. The work got easier. Not because I became brilliant or stopped wanting snacks, but because my brain finally got room to think. Deep work isn’t dramatic. It’s usually just you, a document, and the horrifying realization that you don’t know what you think until you sit there long enough to find out.

If you want to try this, don’t overhaul your entire life before breakfast. That’s blogger nonsense, and I should know. Start small.

1. Pick one twenty-minute block and do only one work task in it. Close email. Silence everything. If you remember you need to buy toothpaste, write “toothpaste” on a piece of paper and return to work. This is not procrastination; it’s a hostage negotiation with your brain.

2. Keep a distraction list. When the urge to switch tasks appears, don’t obey it and don’t shame yourself. Just log it. You’ll quickly see that your brain offers the same three ideas: check phone, open fridge, dramatically reconsider career.

3. Put your body where the task is. If you’re writing, open the document. If you’re reading, hold the book. If you’re “doing admin,” don’t mysteriously end up shopping for lamps. Admin does not require lamps.

4. End tasks on purpose. Close the tab. Put the notebook away. Say, in your head or out loud, “I’m done with this.” Yes, it sounds like casting a small spell. That’s fine. Your brain enjoys closure almost as much as it enjoys notifications.

The myth of multitasking is that it makes you powerful. Usually it just makes you vaguely present everywhere and genuinely effective nowhere. You can answer quickly and think shallowly, or you can protect enough attention to make something better.

I still love my phone, obviously. I’m not a monk. I’m a person who has watched multiple videos about organizing containers while standing in a messy kitchen. But now I try to choose distraction deliberately instead of volunteering for it every six minutes.

Single-tasking won’t make you a machine. It will make you more human. You’ll remember what you were about to say. You’ll finish books. You might even feel calmer.

And if all else fails, hide your phone in a drawer. The raccoons will understand.

title: personal finance book for young adults|automating your savings so you never have to think about it
text:
Let me tell you about the laziest, most effective money move I ever made—one that turned me from a broke 22-year-old who once overdrafted my account buying a $7 burrito into someone who had a fully funded emergency fund and retirement account before I turned 27, without ever feeling like I was “sacrificing” fun. It’s not a fancy investment hack or a side hustle that requires working 20 hours a week. It’s automating your savings so completely that you never even see the money leave your checking account in the first place.
Back when I got my first real job out of college, I made $38,000 a year at a small marketing firm, and my approach to saving was… let’s call it chaotic. I’d tell myself “I’ll save whatever’s left at the end of the month,” which of course was always $0. Some months it was negative $120, because I’d splurge on concert tickets or takeout with friends and forget to check my balance first. I thought being “good with money” meant having to white-knuckle every purchase, track every coffee, say no to every weekend trip, and I hated that idea so much I just didn’t do it at all. Then my older roommate, a middle school teacher who somehow managed to travel to Portugal every summer on her $45,000 salary, sat me down at our kitchen table one Tuesday night and showed me her bank app.
She had four automatic transfers set up, all scheduled for the day after her paycheck hit: $150 went straight to her high-yield savings account labeled “Portugal 2019,” $200 went to her Roth IRA, $75 went to a separate “oops fund” for car repairs and broken phone screens, and the rest sat in checking for rent, groceries, and whatever random fun she wanted that month. “I don’t even think about it,” she said, biting into a slice of the frozen pizza we’d split for dinner. “If the money’s in my checking, I can spend it. If it’s gone before I open the app, I don’t miss it.”
I copied her the next day, but I started tiny, because I was terrified I’d overdraft again. I set up a $25 automatic transfer to a high-yield savings account I’d opened the week before, scheduled for the first Friday of every pay period—literally 12 hours after my direct deposit landed. I didn’t touch the retirement stuff yet, didn’t mess with big numbers, just $25 every two weeks. The first two months, I barely noticed. I still got my usual iced lattes, still went out for tacos with my coworkers, still bought that dumb cute sweater I saw at Target. After three months, I looked at that savings account and there was $150 in it, plus a couple bucks in interest. I upped it to $50. Then, when I got a $2 an hour raise six months later, I bumped the transfer up another $75 before I even got used to the extra money hitting my checking.
Here’s the trick no one tells you when you’re in your early 20s: human brains are terrible at delayed gratification, but they’re amazing at adapting to whatever amount of money is available to spend. If you make $3,000 a month after taxes and you automatically move $300 to savings before you ever log into your bank, you’ll adjust your spending to fit the $2,700 that’s left without even trying. You don’t have to make a budget with 17 categories, you don’t have to feel guilty for grabbing drinks, you don’t have to remember to transfer money at the end of the month when you’re tired and all you want to do is order sushi.
I’ve kept that system going for eight years now. Today, 15% of every paycheck goes straight to my retirement account before I even see it, 5% goes to my emergency fund, another 5% goes to a travel fund, and the money that lands in checking is mine to spend however I want, no questions asked, no guilt attached. Last year I took a two-week trip to Japan, paid cash, and didn’t once stress about derailing my bills or my long-term goals. The $25 transfer I started with? It’s the reason I never had to put a new set of tires on a credit card, the reason I didn’t panic when I got laid off for three months during the pandemic, the reason I don’t lie awake at night worrying about money anymore. You don’t need to be a financial genius to win at this. You just need to set it up once, then go live your life. The system does the hard part for you.
(Word count: 618)

title: minimalism and focus book|clearing your desk, your inbox and your calendar
text:
The Surface, the Feed, and the Grid

Let’s start with the desk. Not someday. Not when you buy the perfect organizer. Today.

A cluttered desk isn’t a personality. It’s a pile of postponed decisions. The coffee-stained invoice is a decision. The charger from 2019 is a decision. The book you’ll never read is a decision wearing a costume called “potential.”

Here’s the reset. Take everything off. Every drawer? No. Just the surface first. Monitor, lamp, laptop, keyboard, phone—move it all. Wipe the desk down. This sounds stupid until you do it. Then it feels like you fired yourself and hired a calmer person.

Now put back only what you use at least three times a week. Not what you want to use. What you actually use. The fancy pen can live in a drawer. The twelve notebooks can fight to the death; one survives. If an object doesn’t earn its real estate, it goes.

Use four zones. One zone for active work: the current project only. One zone for tools: pen, charger, whatever. One zone for waiting items: papers that need action within forty-eight hours. One zone for nothing. Empty space is not wasted space. Empty space is where thinking happens.

Paper gets three exits: trash, file, or calendar. If it requires action, put the action on your calendar or task list, then recycle it. If it’s reference material, scan it or file it. But be honest—most reference material is nostalgia in a cardigan. You are not going to build a comprehensive archive. You’re running an archive-themed landfill.

Keep your desk under ten visible items. That’s the number. Ten. Cables included. If you’re furious right now, good. Furious means the clutter has a bodyguard.

Now the inbox.

Your inbox is not a job. It’s a lobby. Too many people live there all day, greeting every stranger who walks through the door.

First, declare email bankruptcy without asking permission. Select all, archive. I said what I said. If something’s truly urgent, someone will resend it or call. The world will not end because you archived a coupon for mulch.

Then turn off every notification except humans. No badges. No sounds. No pop-ups. If your phone dings for a newsletter, your phone works for the newsletter.

Check email three times a day. Maybe 9:00, 12:30, and 4:30. Pick real times and defend them. Outside those windows, close the tab. The tab is a crack in the wall, and chaos has very thin fingers.

When you process, use four moves:

Reply in under two minutes? Do it now.
Need action? Put it on the task list or calendar, then archive.
Delegatable? Forward it with a clear request and deadline.
No value? Archive or unsubscribe.

Unsubscribe aggressively. If you haven’t opened five emails from a sender in a row, cut the cord. Shopping brands are not family. You don’t need a “last chance” every Tuesday for the rest of your life.

Inbox zero doesn’t mean no work exists. It means nothing is pretending to be work by sitting unread. Aim for zero. Miss sometimes. Fine. But stop treating 4,872 unread messages like a harmless quirk. That’s a haunted apartment.

Now the calendar.

Most calendars aren’t schedules. They’re crime scenes. Recurring meetings bleed into lunch. Focus work gets whatever corpse of an hour remains. No wonder you feel busy and useless at the same time.

Print the next two weeks or view them on one screen. Mark every meeting that has a purpose, an agenda, and an output. If it lacks one of those, cancel it, decline it, or ask the brutal question: “What decision are we making?”

Silence is not a meeting. Updates are not meetings. Thinking out loud together is not a meeting unless someone is responsible for a result.

Block deep work before anything else. Ninety minutes, at least four mornings a week. Treat that block like a flight. You don’t interrupt a flight because someone wants an opinion on a slide. During that block, no email, no chat, no phone. One task, one document, one problem.

Cap meetings at six a day. Six sounds generous, because it is. Seven or more means you’re collecting attendees, not doing work. Default meetings to twenty-five or fifty minutes. The missing five or ten minutes is how humans use the bathroom, breathe, and walk between rooms.

Also, put recovery on the calendar. A thirty-minute buffer after long calls. One lunch break that cannot be booked. A weekly admin block. If it isn’t scheduled, the meeting machine will eat it.

Finally, delete or decline anything that survives only because saying no feels rude. You can be kind and still say, “I can’t make that work.” You don’t owe discomfort to every person who discovered your calendar link.

Clutter gives you the illusion of importance. The crowded desk says, “Look how much I handle.” The exploding inbox says, “People need me.” The suffocating calendar says, “I’m in demand.”

Maybe they do need you. But the best version of you isn’t buried under a desk, a feed, and a grid. The best version of you has room to choose.

Start with one drawer. One archive button. One recurring meeting.

Not because small actions are cute. Because momentum respects motion.

title: leadership book for new managers|giving honest feedback without crushing morale
text:
Let’s get one thing straight first: your first few months as a manager, you will probably mess up feedback. You’ll either sugarcoat so hard the actual point gets lost, leaving your team member confused about why they’re passed over for a promotion three months later, or you’ll blurt out unvarnished frustration after a missed deadline and watch a usually high-performing person shut down for a week. That’s normal. What separates good managers from the ones who erode trust long-term is learning to deliver honest feedback without making people feel like their worth is on the chopping block.
Start by ditching the myth that “honest” means “unfiltered.” Raw, off-the-cuff criticism delivered when you’re annoyed isn’t brave—it’s lazy. Before you sit down for any feedback conversation, ask yourself one question: what is the specific, actionable change you want this person to walk away with, and how does that change tie to their goals, not just your to-do list? If you can’t answer that, you’re not ready to give feedback. You’re ready to vent, and that’s a conversation to have with your peer mentor, not your direct report.
When you do sit down, lead with context that proves you see them as a whole person, not a task-completing machine. Don’t open with the tired old “feedback sandwich” where a generic compliment sits on either side of a criticism—people see that trick coming from a mile away, and it makes every future compliment feel like a lead-up to a letdown. Instead, anchor the conversation to their strengths first, specifically. For example, if you’re talking to a junior designer whose last three client drafts missed the mark on brand voice, don’t start with “Your work has been off lately.” Start with “I’ve been so impressed with how you show up to brainstorming sessions—your idea to streamline the client intake form last month cut our back-and-forth by 20 percent, and that’s the exact kind of problem-solving I want to help you lean into. That’s why I want to talk through what’s getting in the way of your drafts landing right now, because I know you’re capable of work that blows these clients away.” That opening doesn’t soften the blow—it eliminates the blow entirely, because the person across from you doesn’t leave the first 30 seconds wondering if you think they’re bad at their job. They know you’re invested in their win, not just calling out a loss.
As you talk about the gap between their current work and the expected standard, stick strictly to observable facts, not judgments. Say “In last week’s client presentation, you walked through the data slides before confirming the client understood their core campaign goal, and three of their follow-up questions were about basics we covered in the kickoff” instead of “You rush through presentations and don’t pay attention to what the client needs.” The first statement is something they can fix. The second is a character judgment that makes people defensive, because it attacks who they are instead of what they did.
Most importantly, leave space for them to talk. Half the time, the person already knows they messed up, and they’re carrying stress or context you don’t have—maybe they were covering for a sick teammate, maybe they misunderstood a priority because a last-minute email got lost in their inbox. You don’t have to excuse the misstep to acknowledge that context. End the conversation with clear, small next steps, not a vague “do better.” If they struggled with client presentations, agree to do a 10-minute dry run with them before the next one, and set a check-in for two weeks out to talk through what’s working.
Honest feedback doesn’t crush morale when people know it’s not a verdict on their worth. It crushes morale when feedback feels random, personal, or disconnected from any investment in their growth. Your job isn’t to be the nice boss or the tough boss. It’s to be the boss who helps people get better, because they know you’re on their side even when you’re pointing out where they’re falling short. That’s the kind of manager people stay to work for, and the kind of leader whose team actually outperforms expectations long-term.

title: minimalism and focus book|clearing your desk, your inbox and your calendar
text:
The day I decided to get serious about focus, I couldn’t find my keyboard.

Not in the dramatic “someone stole it” way. In the sad modern way: under a layer of receipts, lip balm, three charging cables, a cookbook I’d never cooked from, and a tiny wooden duck my sister gave me because it “looked judgmental.”

She was right. The duck looked disgusted.

I was the kind of person who called mess “creative energy.” My desk had piles that had developed local government. My inbox had unread emails from 2019, which in internet years is the Cretaceous period. My calendar looked like a losing game of Tetris, except every block was a meeting and somehow none of them were useful.

Then I tried a little experiment. Over one weekend, I cleared three surfaces: my desk, my inbox, and my calendar. Not perfectly. Not in some monk-on-a-mountain way. I just removed the stuff that wasn’t actively helping me live or work.

The result was ridiculous.

Monday morning, I sat down and immediately knew what to do. There was no archaeological dig required. No emotional negotiation with a stack of paper. I opened my laptop, saw the one important task I’d left myself, and did it before I had time to become inspired by something stupid online.

That’s the secret nobody mentions: clarity isn’t magical because it makes you brilliant. It’s magical because it removes the delay between deciding and doing.

Start with the desk. I know, obvious. But your desk is a physical argument for what kind of person you believe you are. Mine was arguing that I was a hardware store having a nervous breakdown.

1. Take everything off the desk. Everything. Put it in a box if you have to.
2. Return only what you use daily. For me: laptop, notebook, pen, water glass, lamp, and the duck. The duck earned its place through accountability.
3. Relocate the “maybe later” stuff. If you haven’t touched it in two weeks, it doesn’t live on your launchpad.
4. Wipe the surface. This sounds dumb until you do it. A clean desk smells like a fresh alibi.

A minimal desk isn’t about being boring. It’s about giving your next action a stage with no hecklers.

Next came the inbox. I used to treat email like a slot machine: refresh, refresh, refresh, lose, lose, lose. I had 4,817 unread messages, which meant my brain was carrying around a small administrative village.

I did not “process” them properly. Let’s be honest. I searched for invoices, travel confirmations, and anything containing the words urgent, attached, or mom. Then I archived the rest. All of it. I felt powerful and slightly criminal, like someone who fakes their own death using spreadsheets.

The trick is maintaining it.

1. Check email at set times, not whenever your anxiety gets bored.
2. Use folders or labels for actions under two minutes, waiting on someone, and archive.
3. Unsubscribe aggressively. If a newsletter hasn’t improved your life in three issues, it’s just spam wearing a blazer.
4. End each day with the inbox empty enough that you can breathe. Perfect zero is less important than mental zero.

People fear missing something. I’m here to tell you that if it’s truly important, the message will return, possibly accompanied by a phone call, a calendar invite, and someone standing outside your house holding a sign.

The calendar was the hardest. I liked being busy. Busy felt like proof. Look at all these rectangles! I must be valuable! But most meetings were just adult show-and-tell with worse snacks.

I printed my week, circled everything that moved an actual project forward, and stared at the rest. Lots of coffee chats. Lots of “alignment.” Lots of recurring calls that had outlived entire empires.

I canceled, declined, or shortened what I could. I grouped similar tasks into blocks. I left empty space on purpose, which felt irresponsible until I realized empty space is where thinking happens. A calendar with no gaps is like a sentence with no spaces: technically full, completely unreadable.

1. Delete recurring meetings without a clear purpose.
2. Shorten defaults from sixty minutes to twenty-five or fifty.
3. Protect one or two focus blocks each week like they contain gold, because they do.
4. Leave blank time. That’s not wasted. That’s recovery, decisions, serendipity, and lunch.

Minimalism isn’t about owning nothing and living in a white room with one attractive chair. It’s about removing the noise so the signal has somewhere to land.

Your desk tells you where to start. Your inbox tells you what demands attention. Your calendar tells you what you actually believe matters.

Clean them enough, and you’ll notice something funny: the work gets simpler. Not easy, never easy. But simpler.

Even the duck seemed impressed.

title: small-business marketing guide|getting your first hundred customers through word of mouth
text:
Let me cut straight to the part no fancy marketing textbook will tell you: your first hundred customers don’t care about your polished brand kit, your algorithm-optimized social reels, or that 20% off launch discount you spent three nights designing. I learned this the hard way back in 2018, when I quit my corporate marketing job to sell small-batch, cold-brew coffee concentrate out of the back of my beat-up 2004 Honda Civic in Portland. I printed 500 glossy flyers, paid $150 for a local Instagram shoutout, and set up at a weekend farmers market ready to blow up. By the end of the first Saturday, I’d made four sales. Two were to my mom, who drove 45 minutes to be nice, and two were to a guy who thought my concentrate was iced tea.
I was ready to pack it up when my next-door neighbor Mabel, who ran a 12-seat plant shop three blocks from my apartment, leaned over her fence that night and said, “Quit yelling at strangers. Go talk to the people who already like you.” That’s the core of word of mouth for your first hundred customers: it never starts with random reach. It starts with the tiny, already loyal circle you didn’t even realize you had.
Here’s what I did next, and what I’ve watched 47 small business owners replicate to hit that 100-customer mark in 30 to 45 days, zero ad spend. First, I made a list of every single person I’d had a real, non-transactional conversation with in the last two years: my regular dog park crew, the librarians who saw me every Tuesday, the guys at the bike shop who fixed my flat tires three times a month, my old college roommates, even the barista who remembered my order at the café I used to work at. I didn’t send a mass text. I knocked on Mabel’s plant shop door first with a free cold brew bottle, and said, “I’m testing this recipe, no pressure, but if you like it, would you tell a couple regulars who complain about bad office coffee?” I did the same for the bike shop guys, left a six-pack of samples at the dog park bulletin board with a handwritten note asking for honest feedback, and dropped a bottle off for that library front desk crew.
By the end of the week, Mabel had texted me to say 11 of her regulars had asked where to buy my brew. The bike shop guys were handing out my phone number to customers who stopped by on morning commutes. One of the librarians brought a bottle to her book club, and eight people from that club placed orders that weekend. I didn’t offer referral bonuses, I didn’t beg for shares. I just gave them something worth talking about, and made it ridiculously easy to talk about: I printed cheap little business cards with my cell number on them, left stacks at Mabel’s shop and the bike store, and told every person who bought a bottle, “If you love this, just tell one person who complains about being tired at work. That’s all the marketing I need.”
Let me be clear: word of mouth is not “hope people talk about you.” It’s giving your earliest fans a specific, low-lift story to tell. My friend Lila, who launched a homemade dog treat business out of her kitchen in Minneapolis last year, didn’t ask people to “spread the word.” She told every person who got a free sample bag at her local dog park, “If your pup goes crazy for these, tell the person you always chat with while waiting for your dog to finish fetching. I’ll bring a free extra bag for you and their pup if they mention your name.” She hit 102 customers in 28 days.
The biggest mistake new founders make is chasing viral attention before they’ve earned the right to be talked about by the people right in front of them. Your first hundred customers aren’t metrics. They’re people who will bring your product to family dinners, rave about you to their coworkers, defend you when a big chain copies your idea, because they knew you before you had a fancy website or a sales team. Stop chasing strangers. Go say hi to the people who already want to see you win. That’s the marketing no ad budget can buy. (Word count: 598)

title: relationships advice book|staying faithful and keeping a long marriage alive
text:
Chapter 7: The Boring Truth Nobody Buys This Book For

Here's where I lose half the readers.

Staying faithful isn't sexy. It's not some grand romantic gesture. It's a thousand tiny, unremarkable choices you make when you're tired, or annoyed, or bored out of your mind. I've been married to Denise for thirty-one years. I've been tempted exactly four times. Three of those times nobody but me ever knew about it. The fourth time I told her, and she didn't speak to me for two days. That silence was worse than any fight we've ever had, and we've had some screamers.

Let me be blunt about something. If you think you're too smart, too committed, too in love to cheat, you're the person most likely to do something stupid. Arrogance is what gets people caught. Humility is what keeps them honest.

The first temptation happened in year six. Her name was Marcy, she worked in accounting, and she laughed at everything I said. Not the polite laugh Denise gives when I repeat the same joke for the third time. Real laughter. I felt clever again. I felt *seen*. And here's the ugly part—I wanted more of that feeling. Not sex, not exactly. Just the version of myself I got to be around someone new.

I didn't sleep with her. I didn't even have lunch alone with her. But I looked forward to Mondays in a way that made me ashamed on Sundays. That's the edge. Most people don't recognize the edge until they've already stepped off it.

Here's my rule, and it's not negotiable. You don't put yourself in a position where temptation has room to grow. No closed-door meetings with someone you find interesting in that particular way. No texting after nine. No drinks one-on-one, not even "just as friends," not when the friendship is starting to hum at a frequency your spouse can't hear. I don't care how modern and secure you think you are. I've counseled enough couples—fourteen years, over nine hundred of them—to know the architecture of these things. It's always the same blueprint.

Nobody wakes up on a Tuesday and decides to ruin their marriage. They drift. One small compromise, then another. A confidence shared. A problem brought to the wrong person. Suddenly you're hiding your phone, and you tell yourself it's because you value privacy, but really it's because there's something on it you wouldn't want read aloud at your kitchen table.

Now, the marriage itself. Keeping it alive. Thirty-one years, and I'll tell you the secret nobody puts on a greeting card: it's mostly maintenance. Like a house. You don't wait for the roof to cave in before you fix anything.

Denise and I have a standing date every Thursday. Has to be Thursday. We tried Fridays once and both of us were too drained. We don't do anything elaborate. Half the time it's takeout Thai at the same place on Ninth, the one with the sticky table by the window. But it's protected. You don't cancel on Thursday for anything less than a fever or a death in the family. Work doesn't get to eat it. The kids don't get to eat it. In thirty-one years I can count the Thursdays we've missed on one hand. Six, to be exact. Two funerals, one stomach bug, and three times I was an idiot and let work win. I still owe her for those.

Physical intimacy changes. Let's not pretend otherwise. In year two we couldn't keep our hands off each other. In year twelve, after the twins, there were months. Actual months. I kept score and that was its own kind of poison. Here's what I learned: resentment is the most effective contraceptive ever invented. You cannot spend all day treating your partner like a roommate and a logistics coordinator and then expect them to turn into someone eager at eleven o'clock. It doesn't work that way.

The small physical stuff matters more than the big stuff. A hand on the back of her neck while she's washing dishes. A real kiss, not the peck-on-the-way-out-the-door. Six seconds. That's what the researchers say a proper kiss takes, and I used to think that was nonsense until I tried it. Six seconds of actually being there, lips together, not already thinking about your email. It changes something. Not dramatically. Quietly.

And for God's sake, fight fair. We had a rule after year three, the year we nearly didn't make it. No divorce threats. Not once, not even as a punchline. The moment you introduce the possibility of leaving as a weapon, you've told your partner something underneath the argument that you can't take back. We've broken that rule twice. Both times cost us weeks.

Marriage isn't finding the right person. It's being the right person, repeatedly, on the days you least feel like it. That's not a sentence I'd put on a mug. It's just true.

title: entrepreneurship book|launching a small business with almost no money
text:
Chapter 2: The $17 Jam Jar That Launched My First Business
When I lost my barista job in March 2020, my bank account held $129.42, my rent was $850 due in 12 days, and the only “assets” I could scrounge up were a half-empty bag of foraged blackberries from the overgrown greenbelt behind my apartment, a stack of unused canning jars my grandma had left me, and a crumpled $17 bill tucked in the back of my junk drawer. I’d spent three days scrolling “zero-cost startup ideas” online, every tip boiling down to either “build a social media following first” (which takes months) or “invest in a cheap website” (which I couldn’t afford). That’s when I stopped looking for hacks and started looking at what was already within arm’s reach.
I’d spent my senior year of high school canning jam with Grandma, and I knew that blackberry vanilla jam cost roughly $1.20 per jar to make if I already had the jars. The $17? It bought a pound of sugar, a single vanilla bean from the bulk bin at the corner grocery, and a pack of 20 blank paper tags. That night, I simmered 19 jars of jam (one jar broke when I dropped it, a reminder that even zero-capital plans have waste), scrawled “Mia’s Backyard Blackberry Jam – $7 each, cash or Venmo” on the tags, and tied them on with twine I pulled from an old moving box.
Here’s the part no “zero-cost startup” guide tells you: You don’t need a brand, a website, or even a business license for your first 10 sales. You need to show up where people already are, with something they already want, without spending money to get there. The next morning, I loaded the jam into a reusable tote and walked three blocks to the weekly farmers’ market – but I didn’t pay the $60 booth fee. Instead, I set up on the public sidewalk right outside the entrance, where dog walkers and market shoppers filtered past, and held up one jar. I didn’t have a sign, a sales pitch, or a card. When people asked what I was selling, I told them the truth: I’d lost my job, foraged the berries down the street, and made jam to cover my rent.
I sold out in 47 minutes.
The practical rule I learned that day, and have applied to every no-money launch I’ve coached since, is what I call the Arm’s Length Test: Before you spend a single dollar (or fill out a single LLC form), list every resource you can access without paying: skills you already have, stuff sitting in your closet, people you already know, public spaces you can stand in for free. Most aspiring founders skip this step, because they’re chasing the “shiny” startup playbook: logo, website, ad spend, all before they’ve made a single dollar. When I sold that first batch of jam, I didn’t have a business name registered. I didn’t have a cottage food license (I applied for the $35 home food permit two weeks later, with money from jam sales). I didn’t even have a separate Venmo for the business – I just used my personal account.
After I sold those 19 jars, 11 customers asked if I had more, and three asked if I made other flavors. That’s when I did my second zero-cost trick: pre-sales. I texted every person who’d given me their number, told them I’d make a batch of peach jam the next week if they pre-paid via Venmo, and used that pre-order cash to buy peaches from the farmers who’d just unsold their last crates at the market (they sold them to me for 70% off, rather than hauling them back to the orchard). Within two months, I was selling 120 jars a week, had a $12/month Square account paid for by sales, and never once dipped into my personal bank account to fund the business.
A year later, I sold that jam business to a local bakery for $14,000 – enough to cover six months of living costs while I launched my small-business coaching practice, which I also started for less than $50. The $17 I spent on that first batch? It wasn’t an “investment” in a brand. It was a bet that I didn’t need to wait for perfect funding, a perfect plan, or a perfect product to start. The only thing you need to launch, when you have almost no money, is to stop looking for what you don’t have, and start using what’s already in arm’s reach. (Word count: 712)

title: habit-building book|starting with habits so small you can't fail
text:
My friend Sara once asked me what I thought the most dangerous phrase in personal growth was. I thought about it for maybe three full seconds and said, “Motivation.”

She said no. She said the most dangerous phrase was, “I’ll start tomorrow.”

Because tomorrow has this magical quality. Tomorrow you’re a different person. Tomorrow you wake up at 5 a.m., meditate for an hour, drink green juice without making a face, and maybe briefly levitate. Tomorrow-you is incredibly impressive.

Today-you, meanwhile, is on the couch wondering if a cracker counts as dinner.

I used to design habits for tomorrow-me like I was hiring someone much better than myself. “She’s going to run three miles,” I’d say proudly. “She’s going to journal, read, and learn Spanish. She probably loves broccoli.”

Then tomorrow arrived, and that woman refused to show up. Rude.

So I learned a weird little trick from the best possible teacher: desperation. I stopped trying to become impressive and started trying to become repeatable.

Here’s the idea: begin with a habit so small you can’t reasonably fail.

Not “work out for an hour.” Put on workout clothes. Not “write a book.” Open a blank document and type one sentence. Not “meditate for 20 minutes.” Sit down, close your eyes, and take three breaths.

This sounds annoyingly tiny. That’s the point. Your ego hates it, which is usually a sign it’s useful.

A few years ago, I wanted to start flossing. Normal adult goal, except I apparently had the dental discipline of a raccoon. I kept buying fancy floss, then ignoring it like an enemy on my bathroom counter.

So I made the rule: floss one tooth.

One. Just one.

If you’re a dentist reading this, please sit down. I know. It’s medically adorable.

But here’s what happened. Some nights I’d think, “This is stupid, I’m already flossing one tooth, I might as well do a few more.” Other nights I literally did one and went to bed feeling like a winner. And winners, it turns out, floss more often than losers who declare themselves gross failures and eat chips in shame.

After a couple of months, I was flossing regularly. Not because I developed massive willpower. Because I lowered the bar until I could step over it.

1. Start with a “two-minute-ish” version.

The actual action should take less than two minutes. “Read 25 pages” is a project. “Read one page” is a habit. “Go to the gym for 45 minutes” is an expedition. “Drive to the gym and walk inside” is still scary, but that’s why you can shrink it further: put on shoes, walk outside, stand on the porch like someone in a self-help folk tale.

2. Make the fail state almost embarrassing.

You want the minimum version to be so easy that refusing it feels dramatic. Can’t do 10 push-ups? Do one. Can’t do one? Kneel on the floor in push-up position. Congratulations, you trained. The goal is identity evidence: you’re collecting proof that you’re the kind of person who shows up.

3. Never negotiate after dinner.

Decision time is where habits go to die. Choose the minimum in advance. If your habit is “write one sentence,” then when the scheduled time comes, there’s no debate about whether you’re inspired. You’re not producing a masterpiece; you’re fulfilling a tiny contract with yourself.

4. Celebrate like a sociopath.

After one push-up, say, “Nailed it.” After one breath, give yourself an internal high-five. This feels fake at first because adults are deeply suspicious of easy wins. But habits attach to pleasure and recognition, not to grumpy obligation.

One guy emailed me saying he started exercising by putting on his shoes, walking to the end of his driveway, and coming back inside. His neighbor eventually waved. He said it felt humiliating. Then it became a joke. Then, after two weeks, he walked around the block. A year later he ran a 5K. The race didn’t begin on race day. It began at the end of his driveway.

Small habits get made fun of because they don’t look like transformation. Transformation rarely does at first. It looks like one tooth, one page, one breath, one shoe tied with suspicious maturity.

Don’t worry that the tiny version isn’t enough. Worry that the giant version never happens.

You don’t need a grand new life by Friday. You need one stupidly doable action today. Then another one tomorrow. Tomorrow-you can handle the grandeur. Today-you just needs to begin.

title: career advice book|quitting a stable job to do work you care about
text:
Let me tell you about the Tuesday I almost threw up in my corporate office parking lot. It was 2017, I was three years into a six-figure HR operations job at a Fortune 200 healthcare company, I had a 401(k) match that made my dad brag to his golf buddies, and a standing 10am meeting invite titled “Q3 Synergy Alignment” that I’d stared at for 12 straight weeks without being able to tell you a single actual outcome we’d ever delivered. That Tuesday, I’d stayed till 9pm the night before adjusting font sizes on a 47-slide deck no one was going to read, and as I sat in my Honda Civic watching a group of interns shuffle in with their branded lanyards, I realized I couldn’t remember the last time I’d woken up excited to go to work. What I did remember? Spent every weekend that year building free career workshops for first-gen college kids at the rec center down the street, coming home with glitter on my jeans and a voice hoarse from laughing, staying up till 1am drafting resume templates because I cared more about those 20 kids than I’d cared about any project in my corporate role in three years.
I know what you’re already thinking, because I heard it from every single person in my life when I said I was going to quit: “Stable jobs don’t grow on trees, you’re throwing away security.” Let’s get one thing straight first: I did not walk in and quit that day. I’m not here to sell you the viral TikTok lie that you should storm out of your office tomorrow with a middle finger to your boss and a dream. That’s not brave, that’s reckless, and it’s the reason so many people end up back in a soul-sucking job six months later, more bitter than when they left. I spent 10 months building my safety net before I turned in my notice: I stashed away 12 months of essential expenses, not “concert tickets and fancy coffee” expenses, so I knew I wouldn’t be panicking about rent if workshop sign-ups were slow the first quarter. I tested my side gig on nights and weekends till I had three consistent monthly clients paying me enough to cover 70% of my corporate take-home pay. I even practiced my resignation speech in the shower for two weeks so I wouldn’t accidentally cry or over-explain myself when I sat down with my manager.
And no, it wasn’t all Instagram-perfect coffee shop workdays and windfall profits. My first six months self-employed, I forgot to pay my quarterly taxes and had to dip into my emergency fund to cover the bill. I cried in a Panera Bread parking lot after a client ghosted me halfway through a contract. I had a three-week stretch where I ate nothing but frozen bean and cheese burritos because I messed up my cash flow projection. But here’s the difference between those hard days and the hard days at my corporate job: when I was pulling all-nighters to build a new scholarship program for the first-gen kids I worked with, I didn’t feel drained. I felt tired, sure, but I didn’t feel that hollow, dead-inside exhaustion I used to get after a full day of status updates that went nowhere.
I get DMs every week from people telling me they’re scared to take that leap, scared they’ll regret leaving the safety of a known paycheck. Let me leave you with this: I talked to a retired auto worker at my hometown diner last year, who spent 42 years on the assembly line to put his kids through college, and he told me the only regret he had in his whole career was turning down a chance to open a small bait and tackle shop with his best friend when he was 28, because he was scared to give up the union benefits. “The stable check paid the bills,” he said, stirring his coffee, “but I spent 40 years thinking about those fishing lures I never got to sell.” Stability is lovely if it’s funding a life you actually want to live. But if that “stable” job is making you drag your feet every Monday, if you’re spending all your free time daydreaming about the work you actually care about? You don’t have to burn it all down tomorrow. But you can start building the bridge today. (Word count: 598)

title: startup memoir|the early days of a search-engine company and its odd culture
text:
We thought we were revolutionizing information retrieval. What we were actually doing was sharing a refrigerator with eleven men who believed lunchmeat qualified as cuisine.

The office was 2,400 square feet above a dim sum place on Sanchez Street. Rent: $6,800 a month, which Sanjeev paid with a check that bounced the first time because nobody had remembered to invoice our one actual customer. There were twelve of us then, if you counted Anya's dog Bismuth, and most days I did because Bismuth attended more standups than our VP of Sales.

The product was a search engine. Not the cuddly kind that wants to know your hobbies. Ours crawled, indexed, and returned results in under 900 milliseconds, which in 2001 felt like witchcraft. We had 4.3 million documents indexed and were absurdly proud of this. Sanjeev kept the number on a whiteboard in the kitchen and updated it each morning with the reverence of a man carving scripture. Nobody had the heart to point out that our biggest competitor had indexed roughly the entire internet.

The culture, if you want to call it that, had organized itself around strange principles.

First: the desk. Nobody kept the same desk for more than six weeks. This was called "hoteling," and it was presented as a way to break down silos. In practice it meant you lost your chargers constantly and formed grudges against people based entirely on chair ergonomics. I once spent three days sitting on a stability ball because Derek from infrastructure had taken my Aeron, and I refuse to apologize for the things I said about his mother.

Second: the deploy. We shipped code every Tuesday at 4:47 p.m. Exactly 4:47. Not 4:45, not 4:50. This was because our first successful deployment had happened at 4:47, and Curtis, our lead engineer, had decided the time was lucky. Curtis was otherwise a rational person, a man who could explain distributed hashing at a chalkboard for ninety minutes without notes, but he would physically block the server closet if your pull request merged at 4:48.

Third: feedback. We did something called "radical candor," which mostly meant people told you rude things and then called the rudeness a gift. A man named Lars told me my presentation "lacked a thesis, structurally." This was true. It did not feel like a gift. It felt like Lars was a 26-year-old with a ponytail and a vocabulary borrowed from a business book he'd read in the bath.

We worked absurd hours, but not the heroic kind you see in films. There was no dramatic score. There was just lukewarm takeout and the hum of forty-one servers we'd bolted into a closet that absolutely had not been designed for them. The temperature in that room hit 104 degrees in August. We called it the sauna, which is what people in denial call a fire hazard. Twice the fire department came. Twice we charmed them into leaving with free schwag, which in 2001 still worked, because firemen apparently love novelty t-shirts.

Our traffic numbers were small enough that I knew individual users. There was a man in Ottawa who searched for vintage tractor parts every night at 11:12. There was a woman in Bristol who used us to look up medical symptoms, and I worried about her constantly, though I never knew her name. We had 19,000 queries on a good day. Google was doing that every couple of minutes, but when I watched our logs spike after some blog linked us, I felt the way a farmer must feel after rain. Stupidly, sincerely grateful.

The money situation was a horror movie with a slow soundtrack. We had $318,000 in the bank and a burn rate of $147,000 a month, which gave us roughly 2.1 months to live depending on who did the math. Sanjeev presented this to the company as "a tight runway with focused optionality." I did the arithmetic on a napkin and wrote TWO MONTHS, DUMMIES on it and taped it beside his monitor. He laughed. He also started sleeping at the office two nights later, so I don't think he thought it was that funny.

The strangest thing, though, was how happy people were. Not content. Happy in the specific, feral way that only happens when everyone has agreed to pretend the stakes are small while knowing perfectly well they're enormous. We played roller hockey in the parking garage on Fridays. We had a kegerator that poured a beer brewed by Curtis's roommate, which tasted like wet bread and had an ABV of either 5% or 11% depending on the batch. Engineers argued for hours about stemming algorithms and then went together to buy burritos. Nobody had a title. Everybody had an opinion.

Bismuth slept under the index-build desk and growled whenever the sales guy from downstairs came near. She was, in retrospect, the best manager we had.

The night we crossed ten million documents, nobody went home. Sanjeev opened a bottle of something cheap and sparkling that had been sitting under his desk since launch. We drank it out of mismatched mugs because the office didn't own a single champagne flute, which was correct. A flute would have been a lie. The crawl finished at 1:52 a.m. Curtis wrote 10,000,000 on the whiteboard, then stood there with the marker in his hand like he didn't know what came next.

None of us did. That was the job.

title: leadership book for new managers|giving honest feedback without crushing morale
text:
Section 2.3: The Sticky Note That Changed How I Give Feedback
I was 26, six months into my first management role leading a small content team at a scrappy edtech startup, and I was convinced I was a feedback rockstar. I’d read the management blogs: no feedback sandwiches, be direct, call out gaps immediately. So when my newest hire, Lila—an eager 22-year-old fresh out of journalism school, who’d brought homemade matcha cookies to her onboarding and stayed late three nights in a row to fix a broken quiz tool—turned in a first draft of a high school study guide riddled with factual errors, awkward tone, and misaligned curriculum standards, I pounced.
I pulled her into the glass-walled conference room 10 minutes after reading the draft, slid the marked-up document across the table, and said, “This isn’t where it needs to be. The facts are wrong, the voice feels like it’s talking down to teens, and you missed three core state standard requirements. Let’s get this revised by EOD Friday.” I leaned back, proud of my clear, no-nonsense delivery. No sugarcoating, no beating around the bush—exactly what the books told me to do.
Lila nodded, mumbled “Got it,” and walked out. She didn’t ask a single question. For the next three days, she barely spoke in team meetings, skipped our usual casual check-ins by the coffee pot, and turned in the revised draft without a note. It was technically perfect, but it was flat—no spark of the snappy, teen-centric voice that had made me hire her in the first place. I’d gotten compliance, but I’d crushed the curiosity and enthusiasm that made her a great hire. That night, I found a crumpled sticky note in the conference room trash, written in her loopy handwriting: I’m bad at this. Should I quit?
That note hung on my home office desk for the next seven years, because it taught me the lie at the heart of so much bad feedback advice: radical candor doesn’t require you to lead with the flaw, and honesty doesn’t have to land like a punch to the chest. Over the years, I refined a framework I call the 3:1 Context Pivot, built explicitly for new managers who fear they have to choose between being liked and being honest.
First, anchor the conversation in specific, observed appreciation before you name the gap—not generic praise like “great work,” but tangible proof you see their effort, so they don’t walk into the conversation braced for rejection. With Lila, I should have opened with, “I noticed you stayed late three nights last week troubleshooting the quiz tool when the engineering team was swamped, and that line you wrote about cell division feeling like a messy group project made me snort-laugh at my desk—you have a real gift for making hard stuff feel approachable.” That’s not fluff: it’s proof you’re paying attention to them as a whole person, not just a list of mistakes.
Second, frame the gap as a shared problem to solve, not a personal failure. Instead of “This isn’t where it needs to be,” try, “I noticed the study guide is missing a few of the state standard requirements, and a couple of the biology facts are off—let’s walk through where those gaps are, because I didn’t loop you in on the updated curriculum doc last week, and that’s on me.” When you take shared ownership of the misstep, you eliminate the shame that makes people shut down instead of leaning in.
Third, end with a clear, specific invitation to grow, not a vague demand to “do better.” For Lila, that would have been, “I want you to lead the next two study guides, because your voice is exactly what our students need—let’s block 30 minutes tomorrow to walk through the standard checklist together so you have all the context I failed to give you this time.”
I went back to Lila a week later, apologized for my harsh delivery, and used that framework to reset the conversation. She stayed on the team for three years, eventually leading our entire high school content line, and later told me that conversation was the moment she stopped feeling like she was one mistake away from being fired. Honest feedback doesn’t have to hurt to work. It just has to start with seeing the person in front of you, before you see the mistake. (Word count: 698)

title: productivity book|single-tasking in a world built for distraction
text:
You sit down to work with one honest intention: finish the report. Within ninety seconds, a notification blinks, a message pings, and your phone lights up with a headline you did not ask for. You tell yourself you are just checking quickly. Ten minutes later, you are scrolling, answering, opening tabs, and mentally rearranging the day. The report remains open, but your attention is elsewhere.

This is not a failure of character. It is the natural result of living and working inside environments designed to interrupt you. Apps, devices, open offices, chat platforms, and endless inboxes compete for moments of your awareness. Many reward speed, reactivity, and visible busyness. Few reward the sustained concentration that meaningful work requires.

Single-tasking is the practice of giving one thing your full attention for a chosen period. It sounds simple, but it can feel unnatural at first because your mind has been trained to expect novelty. Every time you switch from writing to email, from listening to browsing, or from planning to checking messages, you pay a hidden cost. You lose the thread of your thought, spend time re-entering the task, and make mistakes you later have to repair. Multitasking often feels productive because it creates motion. In reality, it fragments focus and drains energy.

The first step is not to demand perfect concentration for an entire day. That is too much, and the world will not cooperate. Instead, choose one meaningful task and protect a short block of time. Twenty minutes is enough to begin. Close the tabs unrelated to the task. Put your phone out of reach, not merely face down. Silence notifications or leave the device in another room. If you work on a computer, use only the document or application needed for that task. These are not magical acts. They are boundary-setting acts.

Write down in advance what you intend to accomplish in the block. “Do email” is too broad. “Draft the opening section” is clear. “Work on the presentation” invites wandering. “Create three slides with main points and data sources” gives your mind a target. When attention has a specific destination, it is less likely to drift toward the nearest interruption.

Distractions will still appear. Some arrive from outside: a colleague messages, a child calls, a meeting reminder appears. Others arrive from inside: boredom, worry, hunger, restlessness, or the sudden urgent need to look up something trivial. Single-tasking does not mean never having distracting thoughts. It means noticing the urge without obeying it immediately. Keep a blank page beside you and jot down the thought. “Call dentist.” “Check statistic.” “Ask Sam about budget.” Then return to the task. The page becomes a holding area, so the thought does not have to hijack your attention to be remembered.

You also need to manage expectations. If people are accustomed to instant replies, your silence may feel strange. Establish communication rhythms rather than remaining permanently available.
